Fie said: Madam Speaker, this bill was before this Flouse on two occasions in the last session. The bill attempts to change the Criminal Records Act so that when persons have an absolute discharge or a conditional discharge and conditions have been satisfied they do not carry a criminal record.
It was the original intention of the criminal records provisions in the Criminal Code that criminal records not be attached to people given an absolute discharge or conditional discharge by the court. Nonetheless, the system operates in such a way that even a member of this House convicted some short while ago of a very minor offence and given an absolute discharge bears a criminal record and will for the rest of his life unless he makes a formal application to have that record dismissed.
An absolute ridiculous situation exists and ought to be corrected. I am surprised the government has not already introduced legislation to do so. In the absence of the government acting sensibly, I introduce this bill again.

He said: Madam Speaker, I am pleased at this time to present to the House for first reading an act to amend the Canada Labour Code relating to unjust dismissal.
The bill would provide that no employer may suspend, discharge or impose any financial or other penalty on a person employed by him or take any other disciplinary action by reason of that person having refused to perform an act that he has reasonable cause to believe is prohibited by law.
This would form an essential component of any whistle-blowing legislation. It is not really directly related to the matter of health and safety but rather to those areas where no current protection exists, such as employee assistance in the enforcement of environmental protection laws, public safety in the shipping and storage of hazardous materials and transport of goods across international borders.
It would assist employees and supervisors alike to help ensure the law of the land is indeed upheld.

Motion agreed to, bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.

speechtext:
That a Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons be appointed to inquire into and make recommendations to Parliament on the Government of Canada's proposals for a renewed Canada contained in the documents to be referred to it by the Government;
That fifteen Members of the House of Commons and ten Members of the Senate be the Members of the Special Joint Committee; such Members on the part of the House of Commons to be designated upon the report of the Standing Committee on House Management, which report shall be deemed concurred in upon presentation or; if the House is not sitting at the time of such Standing Committee on House Management Report such report shall be deemed concurred in upon its being filed with the Clerk of the House of Commons.
June 18, 1991

That the Committee have the power to appoint from among its Members such sub-committees as may be deemed advisable, and to delegate to such sub-committees all or any of its powers except the power to report directly to the House;
That the Committee have the power to sit during sittings and adjournments of the House of Commons;
That the committee or sub-committees have the power to travel and to hold public hearings within Canada;
That the Committee provide Canadians with an opportunity to participate fully in the development of the government of Canada's plan for a renewed Canada;
That the Committee have 1he power to hold joint sittings with the committees of legislatures or individual members of provincial and territorial legislatures;
That the Committee develop procedures to ensure aboriginal peoples participate fully in the development of the Government of Canada's plan for a renewed Canada and, in particular, on issues of special interest to them;
That the Committee have the power to send for persons, papers and records, and to examine witnesses and to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be ordered by the Committee;
That the Committee be authorized to put in place mechanisms designed to encourage and facilitate the participation of individuals and groups of Canadians;
That the Committee be empowered to authorize television and radio broadcasting, as it deems appropriate, of any or all of its proceedings or of proceedings of its sub-committees, pursuant to the principles and practices governing the broadcasting of the proceedings of the House of Commons;
That the Committee be granted allocations for expert assistance;
That the Committee be empowered to retain the service of professional, clerical and stenographic staff as deemed advisable by the Joint Chairs;
That the Committee submit its report not later than February 28, 1992, provided that if the House of Commons is not sitting, the report will be deemed submitted on the day such report is deposited with the Clerk of the House of Commons and with the Clerk of the Senate;
That changes in membership of the Committee be effective immediately after a notification, signed by the Member acting as Chief Whip of any recognized party, has been filed with the Clerk of the Committee;
That the quorum of the Committee be thirteen Members whenever a vote, resolution or other decision is taken, so long as both Houses are represented, and the Joint Chairs are authorized to hold meetings, to receive evidence and to authorize the printing thereof, when nine Members are present so long as both Houses are represented; and
That a Message be sent to the Senate requesting that House to unite with this House for the above purpose, and to select, if the Senate deems it advisable, ten Senators to act on the proposed Special Joint Committee,
Government Orders
He said: Madam Speaker, for some time, almost a year ago this week, this House and this country have been dealing with the consequences of the failure a year ago to achieve agreement on the Meech Lake Accord. We have all known that there are very profound constitutional questions that have been raised. We know that this time it will be more difficult to deal with those issues than it would have been had we succeeded a year ago. We are not here to lament the past. We are here to try to construct a strong future together.
It is important, I think, that we understand some of the particular challenges that face us now. With the Meech Lake approach, it was possible to take issues one by one in the method that had been set out by the premiers of Canada when they met in Edmonton to agree on the approach that was later involved in that accord. That is now behind us. We no longer have the luxury as a country or as a Parliament of dealing with those issues one by one. What we have to do, and it is far more complex, is find ways in which we can deal with several difficult issues together.
A way of expressing this is to say that this is the Canada round of negotiations. That is meant to make it very clear that the concerns of aboriginal people will be prominent in these issues, that the concerns of institutional reform will be prominent in this process, that other issues which are of particular interest to groups in the country or regions of the country will be prominent in this process.
I think all of us in this House understand that while the other issues are of course of very real importance, a central issue that must be resolved here is the means by which this country, which was founded more than a century ago as an extraordinary partnership between two peoples who then went out to draw others in, can maintain the essence of that partnership so that Canadians whose first language is French and Canadians whose first language is English will choose to live together as partners in this common country.
What this particular motion is about is the terms of reference for a committee. There have been some discussions among parties, and I have been privileged to be a part of some of those discussions myself. There are some disagreements as to needs. I believe there are no disagreements as to the purposes or the ends that we are seeking to achieve here. We are looking for a way in which the Parliament of Canada can carry out its functions to create a climate and consider a series of recommendations that will allow the nation to make substantial progress to achieve profound changes in our constitutional arrangements.

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
Everyone knows that this country is at a crossroads. There are two paths before us. One is the path of partition. The other is the path of renewal. In the months ahead Canadians will decide which path they want to follow. The choice is straightforward. It is the choice of agreeing to live together or deciding to live apart.

It is a choice that Canadians will make themselves. This dusty document that we call a constitution will never be enough to keep us united. Our country, Canada, will remain united only through the will of its population and the strenght of a consensus. If this will and this consensus do not exist anymore, no constitution will have any significance, not simply because we will not be able to reach an agreement, but because a country is more than a mere legal document. Countries do not survive because they have their names on geographical maps. They survive because they have a place in the soul and the heart of their population.
That reality will never change. But there is another reality which also defines the task before us: It is the fact that, everywhere in the country, Canadians want to be directly invloved in the discussions that will determine our collective future. Canadians want to have a chance to express themselves.
They want to participate in the process which will determine whether Canada will continue to exist or not. That is a legitimate request, and we have the obligation to grant them this right.
We members of Parliament, also have another obligation: We must make of this assembly-of representatives elected by the Canadians-a part of the solution that we are seeking together. We are far from being perfect, as individuals as well as an institution. However, this assembly represents the whole country, and it is the only institution to do so. If someone can claim to speak on behalf of Canadians, it is us, the Parliamentarians. The time has come to speak for Canada and to decide together how to bring about the profound changes that our nation requires.
This is, Madam Speaker, the object of the motion before the House. It is aimed at bringing closer the parliamentarians of the people, and at bringing closer together the parliamentarians from Ottawa and those from the provinces and the territories. This motion is also aimed at enabling Canadians to discuss, to change and to develop together specific proposals for a renewed Canada.
In its Speech from the Throne, the government presented the outline of a four stage process for the renewal of the Canadian pact. It is, in my opinion, the most opened process ever devised to enable Canadians to decide the future of their country.
The first phase of this process is almost over. In the next few days, the Citizens' Forum on Canada's Future and the Special Joint Committee on the Process for Amending the Constitution will table their reports. These committees have done an excellent job.
The two reports will help the government develop a series of proposals for a renewed Canada. These proposals will be presented this fall. They will be specific in nature and they will also be made public. They will provide for changes in the division of powers, in our national institutions and in our way of dealing with native Canadians, among other things. The Canadians will be invited to review these measures and improve on them.
The mandate of the Special Joint Committee will be to move us from general ideas to specifics, from assertions to solutions, out of the past and on the way to a promising future.
Before setting up this committee, we consulted with the official opposition and the New Democratic Party. As we debate this motion, I want to put on record that this government will consider carefully any serious amendment to the comittee's mandate that could help Parliament carry out its duty.
I would like to outline the primary criteria which governed the establishment of this committee.
First, it must be a committee of parliamentarians, by this I mean a committee made up of people whose present duty is to help Canadians ultimately find a way to stay together.
It must also be, and this is the second criterion, a committee of the people. It will not be the kind of committee that will sit only in Ottawa listening just to the views of its own members or of lawyers and bureaucrats. This committee will travel to Canadian communi-
June 18, 1991

ties to meet the people and ask them to share their views and tell them what they think of our proposals.
Third, this committee will reflect, through its approach, the co-operative nature of the federation it will help renew. For the first time in the history of this country, a committee will the allowed to consult with other committees or groups of legislators in each province and territory.

These parliamentarians will not meet across the table. They will meet around the table, and they will not simply meet each other. They will be empowered to hold hearings together, joint hearings, in a process designed to make our federalism an instrument of co-operation among Canadians, not division. That unique dialogue can become both a means and an example of the consensus we seek.
I am writing today to the premiers and territorial leaders of Canada to ask for their support. Decisions about their legislatures are for them and for their colleagues to make. However I hope that all provinces and territories will find a way to work with this unique committee of Parliament.
Fourth, the committee will develop special procedures to ensure that the aboriginal peoples of Canada participate fully in the development of Canada's renewal, both respecting general questions which interest them as Canadians and particularly where there is a distinct aboriginal interest.
I have met with leaders of the four national aboriginal associations in Canada to ask their help in designing an agreed mechanism. Most recently I spoke by telephone with Mr. Ovide Mercredi, the new national chief. The language in the terms of reference provides maximum flexibility to create a system which respects the power of Parliament to decide yet recognizes that aboriginal Canadians have interests and have a unique perspective that cannot be met in a normal committee context.
An alternative proposal was to designate certain aboriginal leaders as ex officio members of the parliamentary committee. I considered that carefully. It could create a demand for other ex officio representatives which would have the effect of diluting the position of both the
Government Orders
committee and the aboriginal peoples. The model that we are examining gives aboriginals a wide opportunity to influence decisions that ex officio status would not.
I make the point clearly so that there is no doubt. What we are proposing is a system that would not change in the least the capacity of national aboriginal organizations to come as witnesses, but in addition to that right which is open to them and to other Canadians, there would be a particular capacity to have the perspectives of aboriginal Canadians considered regularly and in depth by the committee that must make recommendations regarding the future of our country.
Finally, this parliamentary committee will be given all the flexibility and all the resources it needs to be open, to be inclusive, to be innovative. The committee can create as many subcommittees as it wishes. If it chooses, some of those subcommittees can take on the character of a constituent assembly on particular issues, always reporting back to the joint committee of Parliament.
The committee will be able to authorize whatever radio and television broadcasts it deems desirable. The committee will be able to create new mechanisms, whether they are round table discussions, specific issue panels or innovative communications channels, to make the discussion and the debate as deep, as democratic and as productive as possible.
I believe that this process and this committee form our best opportunity to bring this country together. The committee is both parliamentary and participatory. The committee will meet with its counterparts across the country, a federal-provincial-territorial experiment, which I believe can help renew federalism itself.
The committee will meet in public. The committee will reach out to Canadians from sea to sea to sea. It will be flexible, not rigid. It will be open, not closed. It will be inclusive, not exclusive, and its work will matter. It will be on the basis of the substance and the success of this committee that Canadians will then decide how we give effect to change that can renew our federation.
This committee has the potential and it has the mandate to change the tone and the content of constitu-

If it meets that potential, it can express a consensus on what changes should be introduced by the Canadian government, on what changes should be introduced by provincial and territorial governments, and on what changes should be approached by all of us working together.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. member who was elected as a federalist and now flies other colours says: "Not all" of us. He will have the opportunity to participate as a member of Parliament-his party does not have the status of a party in the House-in these discussions. We hope that he will take an open-minded approach to these discussions. There are people here who would be interested in his point of view. There are people across the country who would be. We hope profoundly that he will be open-minded enough about the country which has given him so much that he will be prepared to consider the perspective and the point of view of others.
I do not believe it an exaggeration to state that never before in the history of this country has a committee had such a responsibility placed upon it. If this committee succeeds, it can be a central instrument of the renewal and the reform of this country.
Some would propose a different mechanism to bring this country together. A popular and prominent alternative is the constituent assembly. I do not dismiss that proposal, nor do I question-the sincerity of those who prefer that option. However, after serious discussion and deliberation, it is our view that that would not be the best choice now. I do not rule it out for the future. Our judgment on those and other options will be influenced both by the recommendations of the joint committee looking at the amending formula for the Constitution as it will be by the success of the committee, the formation of which we are discussing here today.
However, I would like to make some observations concerning the concept of a constituent assembly. First, there is no consensus in the country on how such an assembly would be constituted and how it would work. Even such a prominent proponent of this option as the premier of Ontario recently acknowledged this reality. The breadth and depth of substantive differences in this
country are already such, I would have thought, that we should think twice before adding a new difference on a new process which has never been tried.
How long would it take before agreement could be reached on the forum and the operation of a constituent assembly? What new tensions and emotions might that process evoke? Once the forum was agreed, if it was ever agreed, how long would the process take?
Second, it would be less than sensible, it seems to me, to embrace a process which has been rejected by the province whose participation we require to make our Constitution whole. What purpose would it serve? What message would it send if we adopt the very process to achieve that goal which the province of Quebec has ruled out? It defies logic, it defies common sense to attempt to arrive at consensus on the Constitution through a mechanism which from the beginning would leave out those whom we wish to bring in.
The interests of this country are best served by improving this institution of Parliament, not by replacing it. Premier Ghiz said recently: "We have existing traditions and I don't think we should abandon them". Premier Bourassa echoed those views when he said: "Moi, je fais confiance a la democratic parlementaire".
Finally, as I have argued today, I do not believe the choice of a parliamentary committee implies rejection of the best features of a constituent assembly. Indeed that is what we are trying to do here. We are trying to select the best of both options by adopting special measures to ensure the full and meaningful involvement of aboriginal peoples by putting in place means to encourage joint meetings with committees of provincial legislatures and by mandating this committee to identify and implement innovative ways by which individual Canadians and groups can participate in the work of the committee by these and other means. I believe we have identified and acted upon the best of the parliamentary tradition and the best of the concept of a constituent assembly.
When I look at all the other proposals for a constituent assembly, I overcome my modesty enough to suggest that what I have designed is the most workable proposal that has come forward from any other quarter, although I am naturally prepared to hear other suggestions that
June 18. 1991

Government Orders
will serve all of the interests that we seek, including the capacity for the participation of Quebec.
This committee will require energy, imagination, and the help of Providence as it embarks on its historic task. The tempers of a year ago have subsided but they can Hare again. The wounds which many suffered are beginning to heal, but the healing is by no means over. The sense of exclusion, misunderstanding and mistrust which has permeated this country remains, and it must be addressed.
In the eight weeks I have been in this job, I have listened to Canadians from coast to coast to coast. I have gone deliberately to those who have felt left out or mistreated. I have travelled to the north, to the west, to the Atlantic provinces. I have talked to aboriginal Canadians and several of their leaders. I have visited Ontario and Quebec, met with representatives of women's organizations, of the ethnocultural community and others. While Canadians are still angry at how things have gone wrong in our country, they are now looking for ways to help set things right.
I believe the committee mentioned in the motion before the House today can be one of those ways. It will seek the response of Canadians on specific proposals. It will help Canadians get to know each other, to understand, accept and I hope even treasure the diversity which blesses this country, the diversity which has built Canada and made it the tolerant, understanding and free country that it is.
In the months ahead Canadians must reflect on this country', on what it has accomplished, on the peaceable kingdom it has become, and on the bright future it can hold if we hold together. The Canadian achievement is unlike any other, a country that cares and dares, a country where rich provinces help poorer ones, where health care is a right and not a privilege, where the proud boast of our Armed Forces is that we are the best peacekeepers in the world.
We sometimes forget or deny just how special we are. We forget that this country secured its freedom without bloody revolution. We forget that we have maintained our unity without civil war. We forget that while so many others have chosen conquest and empire, Canadians have pioneered the pursuit of co-operation and of comity.
I want to quote Joseph Howe, Nova Scotia's great statesman, but before doing that I want to say that I note, as you undoubtedly will, that he spoke in a different age with a little less sensitivity to gender equality. But what Joe Howe said more than a century ago was: "Brag about your country, boys". Well, Canadians don't brag much, but there are others in this world who know what we should brag about.
When the Japanese want to learn about peacekeeping, they come to Canada to see how we do it. When anyone in the world interested in how people live together in human communities wants to see cities that work, they come to Canada to see how we do it. When Argentina's Mothers of the Disappeared wanted to learn about putting in place an institution to guarantee human rights and how they could secure those human rights, they came to Canada to learn from our achievement. When the brave democrats of the new eastern Europe want to find out about democracy or want to find out about municipal government, or want to find out about how they can build a social safety net, they come to Canada. When Americans want to figure out how to put together a better health care system, they come to Canada. When South Africans, black and white, want to learn about elections that are fair, legal systems that are just, and human rights that are universal, they come to Canada.
As we enter into this phase of this debate we have to ask ourselves: Is everyone else wrong about this country? Is Canada as ordinary and as common and as disposable as some would have us believe? Have we not built something here which is special and which deserves to be sustained?
Canadians need to ask those questions and we need to answer those questions. Canadians need to get to know each other; not to convince each other that their views are right but to come to accept and to celebrate the diversity that has blessed this extraordinary country. We can only build consensus around Canada if Canadians everywhere come to understand why others have priorities which are different from our own.
I remember several weeks ago coming out of a meeting in the West Block on Parliament Hill. I had just been meeting with members of the Alberta caucus of my party

and then with members of the Quebec caucus of my party. That is quite a bit for one night.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In my case it is both caucuses and in the case of the hon. member I suppose it is both members.
However, I came out of the West Block and there was a bus full of students. They were shouting at me. That is not as unusual as I would like people to believe, that people shout at me, except that these w'ere friendly shouts. I went aboard the bus and I talked to the students w'ho were there. They were here as part of the Forum for Young Canadians. One young Montrealer said to me: "Mr. Clark, last week I was a separatist, but that was because I had never met anyone from the rest of Canada, and I am not a separatist now".
Too many Canadians have not met people from the rest of Canada. We see each other through filters, which are often false. We keep our distance. We keep our counsel. We should not do that.
The committee this House is considering today will help Canadians reach out to each other and to us, who they have elected, to build upon what is best about this country. Next year Canada will be 125 years old and next year can either be a requiem or a celebration of this country. That choice is one that Canadians will make. Our obligation today is to give them the opportunity to make that choice intelligently, to make it directly, to make it well, and to make it wisely.
It is in that spirit and for that reason that the government has proposed the establishment of this committee which will be the instrument which can carry the discussions, which can have the effect of leading Canadians into a renewed united future.

Madam Speaker, I am glad to participate in this debate today and my first words will be along the line of the minister's conclusions.
It is quite clear that many Canadians do not realize what is happening in this country. Some would like to break it, while so many around the world would like to come here. That people in this country would no longer believe in its fundamental values and would seek to
break it is a source of great puzzlement around the world.
I would like to say, right from the start, that the Official Opposition in this House shares the views expressed by the minister, on behalf of the government, that an objective and just solution to this constitutional impasse must be found quickly. This is why, on behalf of the Official Opposition, I am happy to tell the minister that we are willing to go along with the approach suggested by the government.
On April 21st of this year, our leader outlined the main thrust of an approach aimed at solving Canada's constitutional problems. "It's time for a new Canada Round of negotiations" he said. "We must have a constitutional process and framework, based on principles which will allow for a quick solution to the current impasse, a solution which is faire to Quebec and to the whole of Canada."
The Leader of the Opposition reminded that it was up to the present government, the Conservative government, to make public rapidly its proposal for constitutional reform, so that hon. members of this House and Canadians in particular, could respond to the initiatives put forward by the government.
The Leader of the Opposition promised at the time- and I renew that promise today-that the Liberal Party would work constructively with the other parties in the House to help solve the national unity issue. The Leader of the Opposition, on our behalf, suggested that the government hold a national referendum to give legitimacy to its constitutional reform project. By trying for a large consensus in a referendum, we might help the acceptance of constitutional resolutions by the Parliament of Canada and all ten provincial legislatures.
Clearly, the Leader of the Opposition mentioned the need to act quickly. Why did he propose a fast process? This is because, in our Party, we recognize the deadlines set by Quebecers.
There was, in Quebec, the creation of an extended parliamentary commission, the Belanger-Campeau Commission, which recommended to the Quebec National Assembly the establishment of two parliamentary committees, one to study the consequences of Quebec's separation or sovereignty, and the other to receive
June 18. 1991

proposals for in-depth constitutional changes from the Canadian government and other provincial legislatures.
The Bclangcr-Campeau Commission recommended that, after completion of those studies by the two parliamentary committees, a referendum be held in Quebec either on those constitutional offers from the other Canadian provinces and the Canadian government, or just simply on Quebec's sovereignty.
We, in the Liberal Party of Canada, believe that those deadlines are true, are very clear and we want to abide by them, as expressed by distinguished Quebecers who sat on that extended parliamentary commission. It seems very important to us that this constitutional review process be very expeditious.
Of course, we would have preferred that the government of Canada react faster to what was going on and is still going on in Quebec. It is why we looked with some skepticism, some curiosity and even some amazement at the creation of the Spicer Commission, a sort of collective inhibition relief commission which, no doubt, played some role in getting the views, the suggestions, the comments, and particularly, the frustrations of many Canadians. But we were fully aware that that commission did not have the mandate to change the Constitution of this country and to solve the constitutional impasse.
So, several months later, we are also looking forward to sec the recommendations, the findings of that commission and we hope that all of these millions of dollars will not have been spent needlessly.
Moreover, we agreed with the establishment of the Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons, commonly called the Beaudoin-Edwards Committee, whose mandate was to study the constitution amending formula, and to achieve better public involvement in the process. But, right from the beginning, speaking for the Official Opposition, we introduced an amendment which would have broadened the mandate of the Committee, because we felt that limiting the study to the amending formula was obviously not the key to the present constitutional frustration or deadlock.
The creation of this new Committee, with its mandate from the government, is really at the heart of the constitutional debate. For that reason, we welcome the
Government Orders
government initiative and agree with the appointment of this Parliamentary Committee, because we think it is receiving the mandate that should have been given to the Beaudoin-Edwards Committee in the first place.
Thus, the government somewhat is belatedly assuming its responsibilities. But we are very happy to learn that it finally does, and that it intends to table a concrete constitutional amendment proposal, as the Leader of the Opposition suggested.
We are all the more happy because the minister told us that it will not be a take-it-or-leave-it proposal, but one which could be improved and amended not only by those who will sit on the Committee, but mostly by those who will appear, who will express their views before the Parliamentary Committee. That is precisely what the Leader of the Opposition had requested. Why are we experiencing this constitutional deadlock? Must I recall that unfortunately the last initiative taken by the Tory government was introduced on a take-it-or-leave-it basis? The famous Meech Lake Accord could not tolerate an improvement. And unfortunately, when a parliamentary committee studied the Meech Lake Accord, many representatives of the natives, of the French minorities outside Quebec, of women's movements told us that they could not accept this Accord for because they had their own reasons, that their objection had nothing to do with an opposition to Quebec legitimate requests.
Many of those people who appeared before this committee created to study the Meech Lake Accord and the companion resolution, the famous Charest committee, told us many times that they accepted the five requests of Quebec, but that the Accord included items that were absolutely unacceptable to them and that they felt rejected, cast aside and left out of. this constitutional reform exercice. I have in mind in particular several witnesses representing the various ethnic groups who now make up the Canadian mosaic which is very different from what it was at the beginning of the century, when the Constitution was written.
Now, all these people told us: We have nothing against Quebec, but this Meech Lake Accord includes elements that we cannot accept because we feel rejected and the Accord will make the Constitution virtually impossible to amend in the future. That is why we cannot accept it.

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
Now, the reason I say this, Madam Speaker, is to remind members in what context we are living today. That is why it is very important for the constitutional process of the government to be an all-Canadian process this time, and not a Quebece process or one which favours some groups at the expense of others. The Canadian government's constitutional proposal must not only seem to be just and fair for all Canadians, including of course Quebecers, it must be so.
That is why the Leader of the Opposition insisted so much, in his remarks of April 21 last, that this coming round of negotiations be a Canada round. And I am very happy today to note that the minister has just told us that it was the government's intention to make a proposal which would answer both the legitimate aspirations of Quebecers and the long frustrated aspirations of the native peoples of Canada, who insist more and more on having their place in the sun, on being recognized as Natives of Canada and on being treated with justice and fairness as full-fledged citizens of this country.
The government's constitutional endeavour must take into account the legitimate aspirations of the regions of the country. Westerners have for a long time felt that they were incorrectly or inadequately represented at the federal level. So, how is it that today, so many western Canadians insist on Senate reform, on an elected Senate, a Senate better adapted to the needs and aspirations of the regions?
A review of Canadian governments shows that very often electoral forces were such that a Liberal government was represented mostly by members from the center of the country, that is Quebec and Ontario. So, very often, the most important portfolios or Departments were given to members from Quebec and Ontario, since they were few from the west.
Because of this situation, too often people from western Canada did not feel adequately represented by ministers and the Prime Minister. Then, the Conservative Party came into office and for the first time in a long while Westerners were represented by ministers from their own province, their own region, ministers who had important protfolios. These people thought they would be adequately represented at the federal level at last.
However, one of the first measures taken by the Conservative Government was to grant the CF-18 contract to a Montreal company though the lowest bidder was a Winnipeg concern. The western provinces were outraged by this decision and I would say it has marked the Conservative government's decline in the west. For the first time in a long while, they thought they would be equitably represented in the Parliament of Canada. They rejoiced because they were represented by Ministers at last. However, because of the Conservative government's decision the Westerners realized that as long as Ontario and Quebec members would be in force, they would never have an equal opportunity to have their fair share.
That is why Senate reform and a stronger, more numerical and more significant representation of western Canada-and that applies also to the Maritimes- have become so important in the constitutional amendment process that we will be asked to approve in the months to come.
Therefore, Madam Speaker, it is important that in its constitutional approach the governement say yes to the demands of Quebec while answering the aspirations of all the other Canadians who want a Constitution that fully satisfies them.
That is why the Leader of the Opposition proposed a constitutional reform plan in nine points. He first suggested a statement on the nature of Canada.
I listened a little earlier to the Leader of the Opposition's splendid description of our country. Now, his words could well be included in the Constitution to give a true description of what Canada actually is. When the Fathers of Confederation wrote the Constitution in 1867, Canada was not as it is today.
Now, it would be useful and important to have a statement on the character of Canada indicating the will of Canadians to cohabit in a federal State, describing clearly the fundamental principles of how such a State would operate and also listing the values we share as Canadians, our attachment to the two official languages that we consider to be absolutely essential, fundamental, the cornerstone of the Canadian State. We would also recognize this new reality, our reality of today, of a modern Canada in this ending 20th century with the diversity of our cultural heritage. We should also recognize clearly and specifically the place, the role and the
June 18, 1991

importance of the aboriginal peoples in the Canadian society.
We also think that Canada, in its constitutional reform, cannot go backwards. In 1981-82, Canadians gave themselves a Constitution, which finally sits at home, a Canadian Constitution, with a Canadian amendment formula, but also with a Charter of basic Rights and Freedoms which is enshrined into the Constitution and which is also another cornerstone of our Constitution.
Thus, it would be important to tell and reaffirm to all Canadians, because we have seen how strongly they want it, our commitment to the reinforcement and preservation of their rights and freedoms through the Charter. We believe it is essential that the constitutional changes suggested by any government, present and future, cannot and should not reduce the primacy of this Charter. I think that, in all those testimonies, people who came before various parliamentaiy committees have praised the merits of this Canadian Charter and stated clearly that they want the Charter to have primacy and remain the most important document for the protection and guarantee of rights, which we gave to Canadians ten years ago already.
We believe that, in light of the evolution of the world economy, the time has come to recognize that our federation has to give itself the required economic tools to better compete in the world market. At a time when we have just signed a free trade deal with the United States, at a time when we witness the explosion of borders in Europe and the creation of an economic common market on that continent, it seems essential to us that our Canadian Constitution guarantee the free movement of goods, services and people in all provinces of our country. How will we, Canadians, be able to compete with the great economic nations of the world if we do not have an economic market in our own country?
We think the time has come for us to reinforce the Canadian economic union through the free movement of persons, goods and capitals. We think the time has come for us to abolish all interprovincial trade barriers in Canada.
Of course, it is a decision that the government of Canada cannot make alone. Provinces have to recognize this new reality. We find it rather interesting that three
Government Orders
premiers from the Maritimes met recently to discuss this issue. The Belanger-Campeau Commission in Quebec made a similar recommendation. Moreover, my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, has also proposed a similar approach for the Prairie provinces.
Everywhere, this initiative gets a very favourable response. Now the government of Canada has to take this opportunity to be in the forefront of this change and include in the constitutional talks that are about to begin the means to reaffirm this Canadian economic union which is essential to our country's prosperity.
I am all the more convinced when I say that because I am under the impression that the government is about to make concessions to provinces in some areas. We, of the opposition party, will certainly be the first ones to hope for a better division of powers and to hope that provinces can have, in certain areas, responsibilities that should have been theirs in the first place. If a new sharing of jurisdictions between Ottawa and the provinces is to take place, Ottawa should not only transfer powers to the provinces in this constitutional reform, but also assert the necessity for the Government of Canada to retain jurisdiction in certain areas.
The Official Opposition cannot accept any excessive reduction in the importance, role and mandate of the central government. We are deeply convinced that what is at stake is the prosperity of all Canadians. A thriving Canadian economy depends on a Canadian government endowed with the means and responsibilities to play an economic role.
Of course, we feel that the time has come to rewrite certain aspects of our Constitution concerning the sharing of powers. In 1991, it is not possible to think of the Canadian Constitution the way it was done in 1867. A modernization of our Constitution is in order. Some powers that are now in Ottawa and some shared responsibilities should be reallocated in the best interests of Canadians.
The approach recommended by the Leader of the Opposition is a practical one. Speaking for the Liberal Party, he said that no power should be considered sacred. The Canadian Constitution can be completely revamped. However, that should not be done in order to give a little more or a little less to any level of government, but in

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
order to find the most practical, economic and useful approach for Canadians.
That should be our main goal in our constitutional reform. We should strive to find a sharing of jurisdictions between the Government of Canada and provincial governments that is for the well-being of Canadians. How can we best serve Canadian men and women? Which government is more apt to do the work as efficiently as possible. So, it is from this perspective that we are ready to receive and consider with an open mind all the suggestions that the government of Canada will make in this regard.
We also mentioned that it was essential to remember, during this constitutional reform process, a group of Canadians that we often neglected and that, unfortunately, we even treated unfairly occasionally. I am talking about the native people. We all remember what happened when the Meech negotiations were coming to an end; at that time, we felt very clearly that the Native leaders wanted to be part of any and all constitutional reform. I, for one, was a member of the parliamentary committee chaired by the hon. member for Sherbrooke, Mr. Charest. Time after time, all the witnesses told the committee that they had been forgotten in this round of constitutional negotiations, that they could not accept such a situation anymore and that they insisted on taking part, in the future, in any constitutional negotiations.
Now, the Opposition leader clearly said, on behalf of our party, that it was important that the government recognize, in its constitutional reform proposal, the right of Natives to self-government and that it was absolutely essential to examine the status, rights and claims of the Native people. We think that there is enough understanding and tolerance in this country so that we can establish a relationship on a new basis with the Native leaders; we also think that dialogue and cooperation must be part of the future Canada where we would like to live.
That is why there is a certain feeling of apprehension as we on this side of the House prepare for the proceedings of this parliamentary committee. We are very glad to see the government has agreed to make these hearings public, to have them televised, to have the committee travel across the country and try to meet as many people and as many groups as possible, and that the committee will be able, if possible to have joint
sittings with representatives of the various legislatures and territorial governments. We think it is the only sensible and practical solution, at this point.
As I said at the beginning of my speech, Madam Speaker, we are running out of time. We must act quickly. The country's elected representatives, the members of the House of Commons, can and must do a job they were elected to do. That is why we believe that in this particular context, setting up a constituent assembly, although it may look good on paper, is not particularly useful.
We have a constitutional deadlock, and there are deadlines we must meet. That is why although theoretically, we in the Liberal Party might favour setting up a constituent assembly, we feel we cannot afford to experiment with Canada's future. And above all, we cannot accept the proposal made by the New Democratic Party to create a constituent assembly consisting of 50 elected members of Parliament and 50 people chosen by parliamentarians. To have one hundred people travelling across the country and talking about the Constitution would be like a traveling road show and might compromise the constitutional future of our country.
Canada's road show!

We cannot afford the kind of experiment that might compromise the future of our country. Since we all know that the Government of Quebec has clearly and categorically rejected the concept of a constituent assembly and that it prefers to receive specific proposals from the government, we in the Official Opposition wonder why certain parliamentarians insist on promoting an option that has already been rejected by one of the major players in Confederation.
We feel it is useless to impose a procedure that is not acceptable to one of the major members of our Canadian entity. That is why we prefer the government's proposal, which allows for public involvement and participation through a number of subcommittees to be created by the parliamentary committee.
We also believe it is essential to send invitations to all Canadians who will want to appear before this committee. As we see it, there will be three ways of involving the public, which I think makes more sense that having a constituent assembly that would consist of a chosen few,
June 18, 1991

a restricted elite that would meet in a committee and, on its own, determine what our future Constitution will be.
We do not think that is the right answer. We prefer to involve the Canadian public in three ways. First of all, there would be subcommittees of the parliamentary committee proposed by the government, whose members would represent groups with an interest in constitutional amendments; second, public hearings where individuals and associations will be invited to testify and suggest amendments to the government's original proposal. We feel this approach is absolutely essential.
Finally, the really democratic way to involve Canadians would be to hold a referendum on the parliamentary committee's final proposal. The important thing is to avoid making the same mistake we made in the last phase of the Meech Lake Accord. The Canadian people must be involved in a positive way-from the very beginning, during the process and at the end of the process.
That is why the Leader of the Opposition suggested that the referendum be held after this parliamentary committee finishes its work and that the committee's proposal be submitted for approval to the Canadian people. We feel it is important that Canadians also be given a chance to get involved in the preparations for this new Constitution we want to give our country.
There is nothing as rewarding and patriotic as voting for one's Constitution. I think Canadians are ready and want to express their approval of the work that will be done by the government, in consultation with the provinces and with those who want to improve on the government's proposal.
We in the Liberal Party of Canada believe it is not up to a chosen few, an elite of 50, as suggested by the Democratic Party, to make decisions about our Constitution. It is up to the Canadian people who, in a referendum, will be able to express the views of the majority, across the country and in each of Canada's major regions, on constitutional reform.
These are the tools we have to help us make major strides towards resolving the present constitutional crisis. We think it is essential that, above and beyond political parties and partisanship, the men and women who sit in Parliament-in the House of Commons and
Government Orders
the Senate-were together to offer all Canadians a constitutional proposal that is fair and equitable to all Canadians, in Quebec and elsewhere. The needs and aspirations of every one of us must be reflected in this new constitutional proposal, and no one in this country should feel left out of the process. Above all, we must not give the impression we only want to deal with the problems of one particular group or province.
We must deal fairly and equitably-which is the Canadian way- with a constitutional problem that is a concern to us all, wherever we happen to live in this country.
Madam Speaker, in concluding, we may remind hon. members it is essential that the parliamentary committee be as representative as possible. The motion before the House proposes to appoint 15 members of the House of Commons. We think this is not sufficient to adequately reflect the Canadian mosaic.
In this Parliament, we have the good fortune to have members, both men and women, who are more than adequate to the last of representing the interests of those groups that make up our countiy.
We also have the good fortune to have members in this House who represent the many ethnic groups that came after the first settlers and who are now an integral and in fact a major part of Canada. We think that expanding the membership of this committee to a certain extent would be a way for the parties to reflect this new Canadian reality.
We also have the good fortune to have as members representatives of our native people, and we think that this time, in this constitutional round, those who sit in Parliament for our native people should be entitled to sit on this parliamentary committee.
That is why we suggest that the government increase the number of members to allow for more equitable representation. It is essential that members representing Canada's official language minorities also have a seat on the parliamentary committee. There are more Francophones outside Quebec in Canada today than there were at the beginning of Confederation. This French fact outside Quebec is very important, and I must say I regret that some Quebecers think the French language is the

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
exclusive purview of the Government of Quebec. The French fact goes well beyond Quebec's borders. The French fact in Canada is the best protection we could have against the influence of American culture. Frenchspeaking minorities in the other provinces around Quebec are living proof of the success and survival of the French fact in North America. We must never forget that.
There is another important minority whose existence we must not forget, and that is the English-speaking minority in the province of Quebec. Quebec has known periods of prosperity that were closely linked to its generous and equitable treatment of its English-speaking minority. I say without hesitation that quite often, Quebec's economic misadventures have been directly related to the existence of a separatist, sovereigntist movement in Quebec. When the sovereigntist movement gains strength in Quebec, the economy suffers. When the sovereigntist movement weakens, Quebec prospers. I would ask Quebecers to remember this: Quebec's survival and economic prosperity depend on the fair and equitable treatment of this English-speaking population in Quebec.
For all of these reasons, I wish to remind the government that it is important to treat opposition parties fairly. I assume the New Democratic Party will make its case to the government for improving this parliamentary committee. There are three comments I would like to make in the form of three small amendments which, we feel, are vital, considering the job to be done by this future parliamentary committee. We earnestly hope the committee will be appointed and will be able to report as soon as possible because, as I said earlier, this is a very urgent matter, and we are running out of time.
Madam Speaker, needless to say, the uncertainty created by this constitutional crisis is having a negative impact on our economy. Flow many investors have changed their minds because of the following consideration: Will Quebec which represents a quarter of Canada's population still be in Canada in two or three years? How much investment is not taking place in Quebec and other parts of Canada because of this constitutional uncertainty? We have no figures, but the impact is there. It exists because of this uncertainty which we must clear up as soon as possible.
That is why we suggest that the government table its proposal and that the parliamentary committee submit its conclusions as soon as possible, and above all, that Canadians be asked to vote on this new Canadian Constitution that will satisfy Quebecers and correspond to the aspirations of other Canadians.
In concluding, I move:

That the motion be amended by deleting the word "fifteen" in paragraph 2 thereof and by substituting therefor the word "twenty" and by deleting paragraph 12 thereof and by substituting therefor the following: "That the parties represented on the Committee be granted allocations for expert assistance with the Committee work in proportion to the representation of the said parties in the House of Commons;" and by deleting the words "February 28, 1992" in paragraph 14 thereof and by substituting therefor the words "December 31, 1991".

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Chair will take this under consideration for a few moments. I will come back and put it to the House a little later.

Madam Speaker, I have listened attentively to the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs and to the Official Opposition, and I certainly welcome this opportunity to participate in this important debate. It is a debate that really establishes the foundation for how we are going to build our constitutional future. Therefore it is an essential debate, it seems to me, for the future of our country.
What we are talking about today is simply trying to find the best way to ensure the future of our nation, finding that road that will enable us to be a stronger nation, to have a renewed federalism-not just for today-that will lead us into the 21st century.
My party and I start with the premise that we want to see a renewed Canada, a just Canada and a united Canada. However, in this party we believe that it will take more than a commitment to a constitution. It will also take a commitment to building a fair and prosperous economy, to having those kinds of national social and health programs that mean that each Canadian has equality of access to those programs and to restoring health to our shared natural environment.
Today we are debating the constitutional resolution and how we, as a Parliament, will respond to Canadians and how we, as a Parliament, will seek that consensus that will truly bring us to the 21st century.
June 18, 1991

I believe that we as parliamentarians share a commitment to the future of this nation, and we share as Canadians a commitment to our children's future. We want Canada and all that it represents to the world to succeed.
I believe and my party believes that the success of Canada is dependent upon the full participation of Canadians in the process of national renewal.
I regret to say that the motion put before us by the government does not allow for that full participation. Once again the government is proposing a parliamentary committee. I would like to propose an amendment to this particular motion of the government. The amendment 1 would propose is, of course, to fundamentally create a structure which would include all Canadians right at the outset, but I know that it will be ruled out of order. In the 20 minutes that I have, I do not want to take up time debating that, but rather to put forth the point of view that there is another way, there is a different way to do this, and there is a way that will lead to success.
Once again, the government is proposing a parliamentary committee in which-remember-the government has the majority control. The purpose of the committee is to discuss the government's proposal. Once again we have a committee made up of senators and members of Parliament in which Canadians are invited to visit, but a committee that belongs to politicians and politicians alone.
Once again, Canadians find themselves on the outside looking in.
My party cannot support the government's motion. We are saying it is time for a new way. It is time to bring Canadians fully into the process. This is an extraordinary time and it requires extraordinary measures. We have to meet the challenges facing our nation with innovation, imagination and openness. Canadians must be involved and must feel involved in this process.
While both the government and the Liberal Party are supporting the joint parliamentary committee, my party has proposed, both in the House and elsewhere, that we should be seeking to establish instead a constituent assembly. We arc proposing this form of assembly because a nation can onlv create a Constitution through
Government Orders
creating a social consensus. We believe that the best way to do that is through the kind of assembly we are proposing, an assembly which would represent a broad cross-section of Canadians in the most promising way to reach that consensus.
There is no perfect way. We are not pretending to suggest that we have the perfect way to do it, but we feel profoundly that we must look at new ways and we must take the time to do that.
The member for Papineau, speaking on behalf of the Liberal Parly, says that those new ways would be playing around with the future of Canada. I reject that. What we want to see is the future of Canada with Canadians involved in defining that future and speaking for Canada.
The member from Papineau, speaking on behalf of the Liberal Party, says that a constituent assembly that would respond and listen to the voices of Canada is a flight of fancy. It seems to me that it is time to really listen to Canadians because if the attitude of parliamentarians in this House is that the voices of Canadians are simply stating a flight of fancy, where can we go to find the consensus we must reach in order to save this country?
I want to contrast some of the differences that I see between a joint parliamentary committee and a constituent assembly. In doing so, I think this House will find some of those arguments extremely compelling in favour of a constituent assembly.
The government argues that the public will have a role in the parliamentary committee. The committee will travel so that Canadians will have the opportunity to appear before it, and in that way Canadians will be able to have their views heard.
In the government's opinion this is a full public role, but surely there is a difference between being a witness at a committee and being a member of a committee. A witness may have his or her opinion ignored or lost in the further discussion when a consensus is negotiated, but a committee member's view cannot be ignored. A committee member can ensure that his or her view is truly heard.

That is why, Madam Speaker, we must set up an entity such as a constituent assembly, made up of Canadian men and women from various groups and communities which are somewhat left out of the electoral process and under representend in it. I am referring to women,

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
native peoples, ethnocultural groups and Canadians from all walks of life.
This way, we will make sure that the views of every Canadian are reflected in the final product of a genuine consultation process.
I spoke with the leaders of a number of organizations representing millions of Canadian men and women. They told me that they have had it with preparing briefs to submit to various committees only to realize that their views and opinions are always ignored.
Just yesterday, I met with members of the National Action Committee on the Status of Women who told me in no uncertain terms that they will no longer take part in this obsolescent consultation process. Why should they. Madam Speaker? Why would the thousands of Canadian men and women who testified before the Beaudoin-Edwards Committee want to come before this committe? Why would they indeed when they see the government go ahead with its plans, pursuing its own agenda, and this even before these committees table their reports and conclusions?
It is an insult to the intelligence of the Canadian people who have submitted well-thought-out and constructive briefs to the Spicer Commission and the Beaudoin-Edwards Committee, Madam Speaker! This government did not even have the decency to wait for the commission and the committee to table their reports and listen to what they had to propose.
This is not consultation, Madam Speaker. It is a waste of time, effort and energy for Canadian men and women.

Madam Speaker, one cannot also avoid, when discussing the proposed committee, the fact that its membership is government dominated and the content of its discussions will be documents referred to it by the government. In other words, the government will have control over the committee, over the scope of the debate, over the writing of the final report. When the governing political party has such control, I find it difficult to attach credibility to the government's frequent proclamations committing itself to non-partisanship because to my party, the Constitution of Canada does not belong to the Conservative government, it belongs to the people of Canada.
Hear, hear.

This House and Canadians have had experience with such government controlled committees before. There were committees after all on the trade deal with the U.S. There were committees on the GST. They all had public hearings and we know what Canadians thought about that.
To the surprise of no one, those committees supported the government. The government went ahead with its policies and ignored the views of Canadians. That must not be allowed to happen on this fundamental issue.
We cannot leave a committee on the future of Canada open to such dictates. It must not serve the interests and agenda of one political party. It must serve the interests and the agenda of the Canadian people.
Hear, hear.

Madam Speaker, one final word on the composition of this proposed committee.
The Liberal Party has proposed that we have more members on the committee, but I have to confess that I cannot believe that when Canadians are calling for a larger role in this debate, the government's response is to appoint 10 unelected, non-representative senators to the committee.
Why have they been given such a major role on the committee and why have the views of those Canadians who are not represented in this House not accorded any voice? This is the question that Canadians will be asking of this government. This is the question that this government must answer.
I suspect that the government has decided to strike a joint parliamentary committee and the Liberal party has agreed with that because that is what they have always done. There have always been joint parliamentary committees, but this is the 1990s and this is an extraordinary situation.
We are not opposed to committees, of course We are not opposed to even joint parliamentary committees, but we are saying that in this extraordinary situation it is time to find new solutions and new ways. It is time to be creative and stop turning to the old ways.
June 18, 1991

Government Orders
My party and I believe that a body like a constituent assembly could be that new way that Canadians are looking for. It would bring Canadians into the process of Canadian renewal and it would ensure that their participation is meaningful, that their voices are heard, and that their views count.
The majority of Canadians, I might add, agree with my party on the issue of having a body such as a constituent assembly which would listen to Canadians. I am told that in the Edwards-Beaudoin committee 158 groups supported the principle of a constituent assembly, which only 23 groups opposed.

Both this government and the Liberal Party are against the principle of the constituent assembly. The government gave two reasons to explain its position. It claims that Quebec would be excluded from the process and that the assembly would by-pass elected representatives.
I would like to rebut these two arguments. First, I would like to ask the government who will represent Quebec on this committee. Members of Parliament or non-elected senators?
A constituent assembly would also include Quebec members of Parliament, Madam Speaker. It could also include representatives from the labour movement, women organizations and other Quebec society groups.
In short, a constituent assembly would allow for a greater participation of the Quebec men and women and a more detailed expression of their aspirations.
I would like to remind this House that the people of Quebec are not against the idea of a constituent assembly. The Quebec government simply said that it would not take part in it. It does not object to the creation of that kind of a forum.
In fact, sooner or later, there will be a constitutional proposal. The question is how will we come up with one? Will it be formulated by a governmental committee or by the people? I think that the people of Quebec, like other Canadians, would rather like it to be representative of the largest possible section of the population.

The Conservative government and the Liberals also argue that a constituent assembly would mean that we were in some way not respecting parliamentary tradition and the parliamentary process. This simply is not the case. A constituent assembly would include elected officials and it would report back to Parliament.
I reject the argument that the parliamentary system would be by-passed because in fact under our current Constitution it is the Parliament which must make the final decision along with the provinces. I reject that argument. We know that the buck stops here. We know that parliamentarians will have the decision on the proposals. The question is how do we reach a consensus so that together in this House we can work toward the kind of future for our nation that we all so badly want to see.
The other parties in this House argue that it is up to elected politicians alone to come up with the answers. As much as I agree that an elected politician has an important role to play, a principal role to play, I must say that we as elected politicians certainly do not have a monopoly on creativity, intelligence or concern for the fate of our nation.
To suggest that we are the only proper representatives of the people's will is not only inaccurate in latter 20th century democracies, but also arrogant.
Hear, hear.

The reality is that we have been told by the government that this House represents a form of constituent assembly. It is true that we have all been elected to represent the citizens of our particular riding. The majority of people in this House do that well, but there are other eyes and other voices that are not as well represented in this House. The House fails to accurately reflect the Canadian population. When you look around the House of Commons, you do not necessarily see a microcosm of Canada. You do not necessarily see the reflection of the face of Canada in 1991.
For example, women who make up over 50 per cent of the population make up only 14 per cent of the House of Commons. Visible minorities and other ethnocultural communities are seriously under-represented. Aboriginal people are seriously under-represented. Disabled people are under-represented. Labour is under-repres-

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
ented. Middle income Canadians and working families are under-represented in this House.
These people have ideas to bring to the debate on the future of our nation. They have something to say. We must create a forum where they can be heard, and will be listened to. We must create a forum that will ensure that this constitutional round is a constitutional round for all Canadians.
Hear, hear.

Madam Speaker, as we undertake this task- and a very serious one it is-we are really talking about painting a grand new canvas, a portrait of our nation as we want it to be. We cannot leave the painting of the portrait to a small group of artists who interpret Canada from one perspective. There must be a great gathering of painters and artists, a diverse group, each offering something unique and all joining together to achieve a shared vision, a common landscape, a portrait in which all Canadians see themselves.
We can create a new, a more prosperous, more generous and more understanding Canada if we bring Canadians into this task. A constituent assembly is the way to do that, and it is a far better way than that proposed by the government.
I want to close simply by saying that I take no pleasure in standing here in this House to say that the New Democratic Party cannot support a government initiative on the Constitution. I say with honesty that I would like to agree with the government on this. I would like to agree with the Liberal Party, but I do not agree and it is the responsibility of my party, a responsibility which we proudly assume, to provide a voice for those Canadians who seek a new way to build our nation.
I will persist in opposing the repetition of constitutional processes that have so clearly failed in the past. I will persist in repeating my party's message that the process must be open to all Canadians. I have no certainty that there is only one right way, but I do know that millions of Canadians believe that it is time to have the voices of Canadians throughout this country from different origins and different walks of life as an essential part of the process with a voice and a vote.
To us, an open participatory process shows the greatest promise for national renewal. It provides the greatest
hope for a Canada that is more just, more caring and more united. I assure you, Madam Speaker, that I will not let go of that vision. I will continue to speak out my party will continue to speak out until that Canada becomes a reality.
Hear, hear.
