speechtext:
Madam Speaker, after having been so eloquently interrupted, allow me to talk about this new parliamentary joint committee that was just proposed this morning. The appointment of this committee is timely, considering there is, as we say, some bickering going on.
Madam Speaker, over the years this instability has brought on a certain cooling off in the federal-provincial relations, as well as real disillusion within the population. In short, the constitutional fabric does not seem to be thick enough anymore to keep the country warm. The data provided confirm those fears. Our future is certainly in jeopardy when 70 per cent of Quebecers expect to leave the rest of the country; when 61 per cent of Western Canadians say: "If they want to leave, let them leave!" We need much more than wishful thinking to settle the conflicts between the different regions of the country. However, we are not yet at the stage where we have to rely on miracles. Let's just say that the time has come for some acts of faith and confidence.
Yet, there is something new. For the first time in our history, a government is committing itself to appointing a committee which, thanks to a new and more aggressive approach, will enlist the participation of all of the provinces and territories into a new highly democratic adventure.
More concretely, the committee will have the power to hold joint sittings with the committees of legislature or individual members of provincial and territorial legislatures. It will also have the power to appoint sub-committees from among its members and to delegate numerous powers to those.
At a time where partnership is what it's all about, the Government of Canada is getting into high gear. It advocates a versatile approach and a philosophy based on widespread consultation, which will enable every group in the country to become equal partners and to choose together their common future.
Madam Speaker, this committee will also give a chance to Canadians to participate fully in the development of an action plan for the renewal of the country. However, the constitutional structure will only hold if there is a solid base and if we use the most adequate techniques.
The parliamentary joint committee on unity is a democratic model comprising two parts: first, a committee made up of federal parliamentarians representing all Canadians; secondly, elected provincial and territorial representatives who, by dealing with their federal counterparts on the same level, will express the needs and expectations of very distinct regions.
Madam Speaker, I purposely use the expression distinct regions. It is an expression that the Quebec nation, of which I am proud to be part of, has taught Canadians from coast to coast last year. However, the differences

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
must not make us forget our links and those links, must not, in turn, become chains.
I therefore invite very sincerely Quebec to fully participate, with the enthusiasm, the perseverance and the energy that it has displaid so often in the past, to the setting up of this new special joint committee on Canadian unity. I also urge all the other provinces and territories to do the same. I invite them to clearly express their own views, while recognizing, at the same time, that there are, within our borders, other visions, other distinctions that also deserve to be appreciated and preserved.
In that regard, Madam Speaker, I am very pleased that the committee will give particular attention to the presence and the participation of the First Nations. There presently exists some 604 aboriginal tribes in the country. This translates into as many lifestyles, perceptions and experiences that will contribute to the work of the committee. Those are legitimate concerns that the country as a whole will have to deal with.
At the table, the First Nations will sit in the front row next to the provinces and territories. At provincial meetings, parallel talks with native groups might even be considered. Because of all these initiatives proper attention will be paid to every view point and every need.
In spite of the problems tugging at the country right and left Canadian men and women are still quite fortunate-some may even call it a privilege-to be living on a free and prosperous land. We have acess to the best medical care possible, our children receive the finest education, our universities, industries and institutions train specialists whose knowledge and skills are prized world-wide.
The new joint committee on national unity intends to make good use of this unique natural resource. It will give top billing to scientists, thinkers, entrepreneurs, academics and other Canadian experts.
It will give them a unique opportunity to put their knowledge and ideas to the service of the entire nation, to help the people achieve a consensus. To this end, various activities are contemplated, such as round tables or even conferences to find, through the exchange of ideas, answers to sensitive or complex questions.
Madam Speaker, the measure I am outlining to you today is not meant to heal Canada's constitutional wounds. It should not be seen as a trade-off to make people forget about past failures. Lessons from the past have to be learned for the future.
We learned a great deal from the disappointments of the past decade. They revealed that Canada is not a homogeneous entity, but a nation made up of a number of small regional nationalisms just waiting to bloom under a flexible central government that would respect their rights.
They made us take a good hard look at our multifaceted national identity. They made us aware that, in Canada, a Canadian is a Canadian, whether his or her ancestors settled the virgin land of Abitibi, slaved away in the rice fields of Asia or survived in the desert.
That being said, we must not let ourselves get discouraged by the challenge in our search for national identity. If Canadian men and women are more divided than ever on this issue, is it not ground enough to make this difference our rallying cry?
The joint committee on unity will echo this cry. Following in the footsteps of the Spicer Commission, the public opinion will never have been so sought after and prized, whether through open lines or other means aimed at providing every opportunity for an exchange of ideas and meetings.
Travel broadens the mind, as we say. In the months to come, they will also shape this nation. The committee and its various sub-committees will travel across this country.
Not only will they meet their provincial and territorial counterparts on several occasions, but they will also hold public hearings and listen to the views and suggestions of all the groups and individuals concerned.
All of my colleagues in this House and myself must not take a back seat in this process. In your ridings, in your regions, it will be up to you to encourage your fellow citizens to get involved. You should start an informal dialogue with members of communities that you represent and that have put their confidence in you. They should be able to take every opportunity to stand for the future of this country.
June 18, 1991

In the months ahead, Canadians will not only be called to play a role in the constitutional renewal, they will also be kept informed of the latest progress on this essential matter, since the government will issue a number of information documents written in a clear and precise language. But it will do much more.
The television coverage of the committee proceedings will allow the public to follow on a regular basis the progress made, either on cable or community television that will show highlights of the most recent hearings of the committee, or by way of short factual reports on the most recent provincial meetings. One thing is sure, the Government of Canada will take the necessary steps to convey efficiently his message of unity.
Madam Speaker, I know that we have had a difficult period. As a Canadian, I was able to note the increasing weaknesses of the present constitutional system. As a member from Quebec I have heard all kinds of comments.
Our childhood was carved in the immensity of the land. The vastness of our land has always fascinated newcomers. Isn't it time to draw some kind of inspiration from our vast and generous country? One thing is sure, we will not build our future by setting up one committee after another. We have to show goodwill.
Yet, because we need the tools to bring about changes, because we need processes, structures, committees, let's get to work, each on our side. Let's talk about it. Let's watch each other acting. Let's work together for a better future.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask two questions to my hon. colleague. First, I don't know if he had the time to read our amendment, but its purpose is really to enlarge, if you want, the membership in order to make sure that there is as many members as possible representing the different "Canadian realities", the essence of Canada. My second question relates to certain comments that were made by the New Democratic Party: do you believe that the proposition made by the government this morning may nevertheless involve in a very important way a number of groups and, I would hope even those groups mentioned by that party?
Government Orders

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, I am familiar with the proposals and amendments put forward by the Liberal Party, and in many regards they are interesting. I think that the government-and I am not speaking on its behalf since I am not a member of the executive committee or the Cabinet-has nothing to gain from arguing about the number of members. I am drawing a parallel with his second question on the constituent assembly. As long as- Yes, we might not want to argue about numbers, but there is a limit. When I look at the proposal from the New Democratic Party, where it is assumed that a single constituent assembly might reflect the future of Canadians, I think there is a limit. The New Democratic Party did not give any clear indication as to the making of this assembly. Also, with such an assembly, you know where you start, but not where you stop. Their problem is that they travelled across the country, listening to just about everybody who had anything to say, because they told them that they should be heard. If you say to everybody "you should be heard, you should have a seat in a constituent assembly" you are making empty promises. So who would be there? I would like- However they did not submit any list of people who should be on such a constituent assembly lest they forget someone. There is also the fear of continuous amendments, because with a constituent assembly nobody knows when to stop.

Madam Speaker, I listened to the hon. member explain why he was against the concept of a constituent assembly. I am not sure I understand, because in Quebec, we had our own constituent assembly. We had our constituent committee. It was called Belanger-Campeau. And when I hear the Liberals and the Tories say that they agree on something, I must say I have my doubts. There is something conspiratorial about this, because they both use the same arguments. Well, I want to deal with these arguments once and for all. How can you represent everyone in a constituent assembly? You can't. You can't represent everyone.
The Leader of the NDP said no system is perfect. We do not expect perfection, otherwise most of us wouldn't be here. But we are looking for democracy. We want non-political people to be involved as well, and not as participants on the panel, as suggested by the government and apparently endorsed by the Liberals, a panel on which people would be consulted.

June 18, 1991

In concluding, Madam Speaker, I have often been consulted as a consumer advocate, and I think consultation doesn't mean a thing if you don't have the right to vote and the right to act on a committee like Belanger-Campeau.

speechtext:
There is something contradictory in what he just said, Madam Speaker. Does that mean members of a constituent assembly will have the right to vote? I don't think I ever heard that mentioned.
What I would like to say is that the members of Belanger-Campeau are mostly members of the Legislature. This was not a constituent assembly, it was a committee formed by the Legislative Assembly, consisting mostly of members of that Assembly.
Furthermore, as a member from Quebec, you know perfectly well that you can ask your leader to table proposals. You know perfectly well-and you in the NDP have abandoned Quebec -you know perfectly well that Quebec has rejected the concept of a constituent assembly. This is another example of the NDP's totally ignoring 20 to 25 per cent of the Canadian population, in a process that should include as many people as possible.

Madam Speaker, the hon. member-and I listened carefully-referred to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Papineau-Saint-Michel, and more specifically to the first part that requests an increase in the number of members. I think his response was that the government was flexible, and I assume this was a positive response on behalf of the government. In other words, the proposal was received with interest.
The second part of the amendment asks that funds be made available to the other parties in this House, in proportion to the number of members on the committee.
I think this was done with other committees in the past, and I think it is a worthwhile proposal. Perhaps the hon. member would care to comment.
Third, the change in date. It has always been our position that Canada urgently needed to resolve this issue, and we suggest changing the date on the motion from February 28 to December 31, 1991, in other words,
we are moving the date up. We want to compress the committee's proceedings and cut about two months off the time. Could the hon. member discuss his position on the amendment in question, with respect to funding and the time factor?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am glad the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier made it clear that the amendment was favourably received by me. It is not up to me to decide, but I think the three proposals are quite interesting.
First of all, regarding the number of members, I think we should be generous with our resources. Of course, cabinet will have to consider the matter and report back to the House tomorrow. The matter of funding is very important. I think that the matter of funds that could be made available to the committee for research services is in fact even more important than the other element of the Liberal proposal.
Although, having December as a starting date may- The study may take a little more time. There is certainly room for using the talents of Canadians as a resource for the people who will be on this committee.
As for the date, I agree the matter is urgent. This committee's work should have already begun. I call people and I ask them, since they have a lot more experience than I do in this area, to be realistic about dates. If you honestly think we can get something done by December-in fact with what we found out through the Spicer Commission and Beaudoin-Edwards on the amending formula, a lot of preparatory work has already been done. We have to collate all this. So I think it is a possibility.

Madam Speaker, I would like to make a very short preamble.

In the spirit of co-operation it has already been indicated that my party wants to participate. It wants to contribute to the building of a new Canada, a stronger Constitution for all Canadians.
I would hope that in the same spirit the government will consider our amendments, the three points that have just been made, that is the possible enlargement of the committee, more members to ensure greater representation, the funding question, as well as the date that has been proposed for completion of the report.
June 18, 1991

I would like the New Democratic Party to make some constructive criticisms as well. The leader has said that there are no perfect solutions, no perfect approaches. I would hope that she would in fact admit that this one proposed by the government is neither more perfect nor less perfect necessarily than her own.
Hopefully, for the sake of Canada and all Canadians, there will be some constructive points made so that we can get on with the job. Canada and Canadians need us now. They need us to come to grips with this problem, so let us not cop out when there is a tough job to do. Let us not give it to others.
Canadians are calling upon us as parliamentarians, so let us get on with the job. Let us not give it to others when we think there might be significant heat in the kitchen and when we know it is not going to be an easy mandate. At the same time, let us not exclude others who want to be heard and who need to be heard.
I want to address four points.

First, the objective, that is the intentions or the raison d'etre of the committee. Secondly, I will talk about its make-up, thirdly, the process and, finally, the fourth major aspect, namely the substance or the content of what will be proposed.

Let us remember as we undertake this monumental, historical task that the Constitution belongs to all Canadians: to you, to me, to all of us. We must keep that as a prime objective. Let us remember as well that we are now trying to correct what is not working and to respond to our many current problems. Let us remember that we want to make lasting changes to create a Canada that is united, with greater economic, social and political stability.
Let us remember that we should address what Canada is all about. What is this great country all about? How will it work? We must indeed have increased fairness, a more just society, and a more competitive society in the true spirit of the time so that wc can in fact be much more sensitive to the needs of all Canadians. Let us make sure in the final analysis that we have a better Constitution for all regions, all provinces and, indeed, all Canadians wherever they happen to come from.
Government Orders
Those are the purposes that I see at the present time. Let us remember that as we undertake the composition of this committee we need to be sensitive to provinces, to the various regions of Canada, and I would include most definitely the territories. We need to be sensitive to the peoples of Canada: aboriginal Canadians, those of French origin, those who are of English speaking origin and those of origins other than aboriginal, French or English.
Let us remember as well as we make up the composition that we need to have gender parity. We need to represent men and women as equally as possible.
Let us remember as well-this is a fundamental point-that we are attempting to correct, to change and to build a Constitution for Canadians and for those who were here before us. We must reflect upon the past but at the same time, we must not forget that we are creating a Constitution and a country for the youth of our nation.
We often forget the youth of the nation when we undertake projects such as this one.

Madam Speaker, let us not forget our vision of Canada in terms of social, cultural, economic, and other policies. The prejudices that I have and the ones that those who were here before me are not the same as those of today's youth.
Canada is not the same today as it was before. It must compete at the international level and when we deal with this fundamental issue, we have to make sure that we take into account our youth, those young men and women, your children, my children, your grandchildren. We want to build a country that will fulfill their needs, that will make their lives better and that will bring greater justice at every level.

When we attempt to rebuild a country, let us not forget that it is for all Canadians, but especially let us not forget that it is for the young people. It is so easy to build something for yourself and forget the others.
I want to speak briefly about the process. We have already said that this must be a round for all Canadians. We want to make sure that we can reach out to each and every Canadian who has something to say about the Constitution, the fundamental law of the land. Let us

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
ensure that it is an open process, that there are no hidden agendas, that there are no seamless webs. Let us ensure that we listen intently, sincerely and profoundly to what Canadians have to say. Let us make a commitment today to involve all Canadians who want to speak about the fundamental law of our land.
I have spoken about our aboriginal peoples. I have spoken about Canadians from French, English and other origins. Let us not forget the poor. They do not always have the voice that they need. Let us not forget our Canadians with disabilities who cannot always speak as loudly, as often and as forcefully as they would like. Let us not forget organized, non-organized labour and business people.
Canadians, generally, must be given the opportunity to be heard and we must make a commitment to listen to them no matter what region of this country or province they come from and no matter what their background happens to be.
Let us respond as well, once we have listened and listened carefully to all Canadians, in an open kind of way. Let us really attempt to hear and to bring forth solutions that will in fact correct and solve a lot of those problems.
I was a member of the Beaudoin-Edwards constitutional committee whose report should be coming soon. As I travelled across Canada and talked to my constituents, they told me that they want a solution to the constitutional crisis and they want it now. They want national unity because they believe that national unity brings economic stability. It will bring social progress and political stability as well. They arc tired of this continual haranguing about where we are going, who is in, who is out and under what circumstances.
Let us come to grips with it, perhaps not for all times but for a significant period of time.
I want to address the question of substance. There is a number of principles that I think we must abide by and I shall share a few that my party has developed. In fact they come from a statement of the leader of the party.

There they are. I believe that we really need a statement on the nature of Canada and I would like this statement to include a number of issues that I have alluded to, namely that we recognize the regions, the provinces, and the people of different origins. I would also like us to show a profound attachment to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. If we want to be a first class country, it is fundamental to attach the greatest importance to this Charter.
I would also like to see a strengthening of the Canadian economic union. I find it hard to understand why we talk about free trade with other countries when there are still, in our own country, all kinds of barriers that keep us from working together in a much easier and simpler way.
I would like to see, like everybody else I believe, an institutional reform, so that our great institutions, whether it is the Supreme Court, the Senate, the House of Commons and many other ones, meet the needs of Canadians. The distribution of powers is also another issue that must be dealt with. I tried to bring this issue up when I was sitting on the Beaudoin-Edwards Commission. We discussed it a bit, but it was not an integral part of our mandate. It was thus put aside, and I think it is unfortunate. However, this time, we cannot put it aside.
Spending power is a matter of the great importance, not only to Quebec but to any province or region in Canada. It is a matter this committe will have to settle.
The immigration issue is a very sensitive one. Certain agreements were signed that Canadians are not quite familiar with. Moreover, I am not convinced, and this is not meant as a nasty remark, that we know just where we are going on this issue of immigration. Nevertheless, we must tackle it and try and find a solution. The Supreme Court of Canada is most important. Are changes needed here? The native peoples were also mentioned over and over, and I am so proud that we, as parliamentarians, as well as the Canadian people have given further recognition to the importance of and the key role played by natives, the native peoples of Canada.
Finally, it seems likely that we will be able to meet in a very concrete and significant way to their needs, or so I hope. In my view, the amending formula should be flexible, responsible and responsive to the needs of a
June 18, 1991

modern nation, a nation changing very rapidly to compete with the rest of the world.
If need be, there should be a national referendum to settle this business, maybe not once and for all, but for a long time I hope.
{English]
At the end of this process I think that Canadians need to be able to say something like the following: Canadians need to say at the end of the process of this new commission that it was indeed a Canada Round, that we were concerned about Quebec, the north, the Atlantic provinces, the western provinces, and of course Ontario as well. It must be a Canada Round, and at the end of the process people must say: "Yes, it was indeed a Canada Round". Canadians must be able to say that parliamentarians reached out to Canadians, that they really went out of their way to find them, to listen to them and to respond to them.
Canadians have to be able to say as well at the end of this whole exercise that the process was indeed open, that partisanship virtually did not exist, that the most important goal was Canada and the future of Canadians, and that that is reflected in all the travels, the debates and the discussions.
They must be able to say that parliamentarians listened with open minds. They must be able to say that they as Canadians have had fair representation, that our aboriginal peoples were represented, that there were representatives from the French language communities, from the English language communities and from the ethnocultural and multicultural communities as well. They must be able to say that there was a good balance of gender, and that wc were sensitive to the whole question of youth, the poor, the handicapped and other Canadians who feel that they must be heard, that they must be reflected in this fundamental law of the land.
Canadians at the end of the process must be able to say that there was a significant, substantive, sensible, sensitive response to that which was communicated and shared with the members of the committee. They must be able to say: "We do have a good solution; no solution is perfect, but this is a good solution".
I think that Canadians need to be able to say at the end of the process that the important nations of the world which are watching us today and will continue to do so
with respect to our constitutional and other crises will acknowledge our success, that they will say: "We now see a Canada that is stronger, that is more united, that has a better sense of direction, not only on constitutional matters, but on other matters as well". If we are able to do that, I am certain that we will have a better country.
With respect to the amendments I just want to say a few words. I mentioned them briefly at the beginning.

I pointed out that we got involved in this as a party in a spirit of co-operation. I hope that the government will consider the amendments we proposed with the same open-mindedness to see if there would not be a way to accomodate what we proposed. We believe, as I said earlier, that this would help us, as parliamentarians, to meet the needs of the Canadian people regarding their Constitution.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member will have a couple of minutes to conclude his comments when we resume debate on this motion.
For the time being, as it is one o'clock p.m., I will now leave the chair until two o'clock p.m.
The House took recess at 1 p.m.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, several times during the past month, a number of my constituents suggested that all taxpayers should be treated the same by governments, whether they are married, single or living common law, and whether a family's income is earned by one or several people, all other things being equal.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the exceptional work being done by the Conservative member for Calgary North, A1 Johnson, who with the Conservative committee on family tax measures is trying to find solutions to these problems.

June 18, 1991

Mr. Speaker, this week is Occupational Health and Safety Week in Canada, a time when we should express our gratitude to those thousands of working Canadians, both volunteer and full-time who work hard every day to make Canada's work places safe and healthy.
We must also, as parliamentarians, rededicate ourselves to ending the all too familiar litany of death, injury and industrial disease which continues to victimize Canadian workers and their families at the alarming rate of one death in every three working hours.
I am sure we are all sincere in our expressed aims, but two questions come to mind. First, why did both the Ministry of Labour and the Liberal Party fail to respond to an invitation from the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety to join deliberations in Sudbury last week to rescue the financial viability and independence of the centre?
Second, why has the government still not proclaimed the health and safely parts of the Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act passed five years ago, which would accord Parliament Hill workers the same health and safety protection as other Canadians?
Let us put our actions and dollars where our mouths are.

Mr. Speaker, I was glad to hear that the Minister of National Health and Welfare tabled the government's response today to the campaign against tax rates launched by tobacco companies. Although taxes are never popular, I know Canadians agree we should use all reasonable means to discourage our young people from smoking, a habit that often becomes addictive. In response to the efforts of tobacco companies that focus on taxes, while the real problem is public health, our government has used taxes as part of its national strategy for reducing the use of tobacco. Canada ranks first in the world on cutting the smoking habit, and the minister made it clear that despite the
objections of tobacco companies, he intends to maintain the government's current policy. The minister also stressed the need to promote the government's program, to make Canadians aware of the dangers of smoking.

Mr. Speaker, due to this government's policies, small businesses are failing in record numbers. The recession which this government's policies helped induce has placed many small businesses in a very tenuous position.
The GST which came into effect last January has had a significant negative impact on small businesses across the country.
On July 1, this government's payroll tax increase of 24 per cent in unemployment insurance payments will come into effect.
Last week the proposed bankruptcy legislation was introduced and small business persons across this country were shocked to find out that this government will be hitting them again with another payroll tax to finance a wage insurance fund. This will mean added costs and more paper work for the already over-burdened small business sector.
At a time when jobs and economic growth are badly needed, this government seems determined to implement policies which will discourage small business from hiring more employees, discourage small businesses from expanding and propel many small businesses right out of business altogether.

Mr. Speaker, after centuries of disrespect the common pig is now gaining new stature. Even as I speak, futuristic pigs are producing human haemoglobin in their blood.
In the best studied pig at the New Jersey Research Station, 10 to 20 per cent of haemoglobin is human. The amazing pig will soon be saving human lives. These unselfish animals are potentially virus free blood donors
June 18, 1991

and after receiving their 100th donation certificate, they can still wind up on your barbecue.
The next time you pass a pig or a pig farmer on your way to work, do not look at them with disdain. Take them to the football game or buy them a beer.
The pig now commands a new respect. The life he saves could be your own.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday, June 14, two fishermen in my riding came close to losing their lives due to a serious silting problem at the mouth of Dingwall Harbour. The cost of this dredging has been estimated at $350,000 and although this is not a long-term solution, this government has not seen its way clear to providing even this amount of money.
Silting is a major problem in the harbours in my constituency. Bay St. Lawrence, Sugar Loaf and Ingon-ish are other places where silting has caused difficulties for individuals employed in the fishing industry.
Except for the fact that these two fishermen had a very powerful engine in their boat, they could easily have capsized and drowned.
A request for funding is now sitting in the Minister of Fisheries' office and I hope the minister will examine this request and approve it immediately. He comes from an area where fishing is the mainstay of small communities and must realize the daily dangers that fishermen face.
What is more important to this government, the lives of fishermen or $350,000? I urge the minister to act immediately on this very important matter.

Mr. Speaker, we note with regret that Senator Stan Waters is suffering from fatigue. According to his own admission, his fatigue is a result of his trying to promote the Reform Parly, no doubt an exhausting undertaking.
He is also reported as saying that this task requires about 80 per cent of his time with only 20 per cent left over for senatorial duties.
The question Canadians are asking is will Preston Manning's conscience require Senator Waters to return 80 per cent of his wages to the federal bank account, or does the leader of the Reform Party condone the spending of public funds to support his populist movement?

Mr. Speaker, Canada Post announced that it will be closing the post office in Brandon, Manitoba next month. This post office services over 38,000 people. The decision sent a clear warning to all Canadians. No post office is safe.
I and thousands of Canadians are angry that Canada Post took this step and in doing so, gave the residents of Brandon only six weeks notice before this arbitrary decision would become fact. Many other communities, including Guelph and Charlottetown, are receiving drastically reduced postal services at the post office. Many rural communities are losing all postal outlets.
Canadians deserve first class postal service. Instead they are forced to find insurance outlets or pharmacies which are often not equipped to provide efficient and secure services.
Canada Post spent nearly $200,000 on a luxury box at SkyDome to entertain its corporate friends. This kind of expense is obscene when average Canadians are being denied basic services.

Mr. Speaker, the government has admitted that it has collected a windfall in profits from the Goods and Services Tax, a windfall collected at the expense of co-operatives across Canada.
The GST applies to share capital investments made to a co-operative.
Their competitor food companies do not pay GST on any risk capital invested in their companies.

June 18, 1991
5. o 31
For example, this unequal application of GST costs a retail co-op in Moncton approximately $20,000 a year.
The GST is also applied to the co-operative weekly fees. The co-ops have broken down their sales and determined that 40 per cent are GST taxable and 60 per cent are zero-rated. This unfair GST tax on food costs the same retail co-operative about $40,000 per year. This creates an unlevel playing field for co-operatives.
Months ago co-operative representatives suggested amendments to the legislation similar to that for credit unions. They are still waiting to hear back. These amendments would appear to be easy to accommodate and would help to correct some of the inequities of the GST as it applies to co-operatives.

Mr. Speaker, if there is a way of measuring a community's compassion, it is perhaps through gauging the way it cares for its sick and elderly. By that standard the community of Georgetown, Ontario, in my riding is truly both compassionate and caring.
For the past 30 years local civic leaders and volunteers have been instrumental in seeing to it that the Georgetown Community Hospital protects and heals the citizens who have come to depend upon it.
I am proud to rise in my place in the House of Commons to both thank and praise these people.
In a few days the hospital will officially mark three decades of operation. During that time the facility has expanded and now includes an excellent centre for the care of the aged.
In Georgetown we arc proud of this achievement and while I know this House is often filled with rancour and complaint, I want to remind all members that our communities arc enriched by local institutions such as these to which we must all offer our deep thanks.

Mr. Speaker, Ontario is calling for a massive overhaul of the province's general welfare assistance system and the
Region of Peel is outraged. Why? With the changes, a self-declaration system is advocated.
People will be able to apply for welfare by mail. Home visits will be abolished unless requested, and the welfare system will be opened to 16 and 17 year olds.
Welfare will become a hand-out rather than a hand up. Costs will skyrocket.
The region cannot bear this extra burden, nor can we.
Our federal government contributes 50 per cent of the funding for this program and has a 50 per cent interest in the well-being of the people in the province of Ontario.
We should be outraged too.
We should have the right to call for negotiations between funding partners.
We should ensure that the welfare system does not break the back of an already strained region.
We should, but will we?

Mr. Speaker, I spoke at the environmental gathering which was organized by the Aboriginal Cultural Society in Winnipeg yesterday. This gathering was to enhance the solidarity among aboriginal peoples by examining environmental issues facing our planet and sharing traditional values about Mother Earth.
I commend the organizers and the participants of this important event. David Suzuki participated and, as members know, his ability to reconcile the interests of science with those of humanity has made him one of the most well known and perhaps greatest scientist of our time.
Jeannette Armstrong from the Penticton Reserve stated "the native people of this land developed a lifestyle through a unique world view, based on the health of the whole individual".
There were many people in attendance, including elders. It is our elders and people who still live on the land who reinforce my conviction that native people can protect the planet through a combination of traditional
June 18, 1991

and spiritual environmental values and new scientific knowledge.
I believe the environment is the foundation of our well-being. This is what the elders have taught us. This is what I call traditional knowledge. I believe that all Canadians want to protect the environment from destruction. In the end, this is the vision which will unite our country.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that the family unit is central to the quality of life in Canada.
It is the family unit where values are shaped, where faith is nurtured and strengthened and where tolerance, good will and generosity are developed.
Therefore, I become very upset when any government introduces any legislation that directly, or indirectly, erodes or discriminates against the family.
Our current tax system penalizes many married Canadians by charging them billions of dollars more than if they were unmarried, according to yesterday's report by Statistics Canada.
The report said that due to differing deductions and credits, 58 per cent of married-couple families had less disposable income under the tax and transfer payment system in 1989 than if they had formed a family but remained unmarried.
I want to congratulate the Conservative member of Parliament from Calgary North for his leadership in researching and investigating this issue over the last two years. Let us act quickly to correct these unfair tax measures.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George -Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ever since this government signed the softwood lumber tariff memorandum of understanding with the United States, thousands of jobs have been lost in the forest industry.
Canada's ability to manage our forests has been turned over to the Americans.
Grandfathered into the free trade deal, this tariff is another example of why this government's trade agenda is seriously flawed.
To date, the government has failed to get Canada out of the MOU.
The minister should tell American officials when he meets them later this month that we want this tariff scrapped. The government should act before more jobs are lost.
Since this government traded away our sovereignty, let us get it back.

Mr. Speaker, like the member for Regina-Wascana, I am very sorry that Senator Waters has had to spend time in the hospital because of fatigue.
I wish him a speedy and complete recovery.
What concerns me is the fact that Senator Waters attributes only 20 per cent of the problem to his senatorial duties, and the rest because he has been so busy working for his party.
For one who has made such a public issue of donating a small part of his salary to charity, perhaps he should show real charity and collect only the 20 per cent of his income that he says he is working for, and apply the balance to reducing the cost of government which he is so fond of criticizing.
It is a good time for the senator to put his rhetoric into action.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today in celebration of 100 years of Ukrainian immigration to Canada.
Drawn by the promise of a better future for themselves and their families, the first Ukrainian immigrants arrived in Montreal on September 7, 1891. They were followed by nearly 200,000 who were a founding people of Canada's west.

June 18, 1991
Oral Questions
Today, there are over 600,000 citizens of Ukrainian descent living in Canada. We share their deep love and loyalty to Canada and we respect their unique heritage and contribution to our country.
In the words of a former Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, Canadians of Ukrainian descent have added something of value, of strength and of colour to the Canadian character.
As this House will be in recess on the anniversary of this historic beginning, let us thank our Ukrainian neighbours today and together let us work toward many more years of the prosperity they helped to bring to our country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister.
Canada is again facing a major trade dispute: U.S. Customs is investigating Asian manufacturers who produce cars in Canada. We are told that the government intends to charge customs duty retroactively on cars manufactured here in Canada, because they say these cars do not meet the standards of the Auto Pact.
I therefore want to ask the government whether it is true that Asian manufacturers who produce cars in Ontario and Quebec, do not meet the standards of the Auto Pact.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I think the Leader of the Opposition is well aware, this is a report in the media. It is not a report based on something that we have received, nor has the company received it.
There is a leak here that we are not in a position to comment on. If it appears that there is something that does not meet the requirements of the free trade agreement, in the eyes of the Americans, then certainly that is something we will look into.
However, I should point out to my friend that we saw last week, with the very successful result of the pork countervail case, the result of the application of the extraordinary challenge, where Canada was successful in the position that it took; a three to nothing decision. I think that shows very clearly that the dispute settlement mechanism works.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, either these companies respect the auto pact content requirements or they do not. I am very surprised that the government does not know anything about it. It should monitor these things.
If the government does not know about it, why not? If it does know about it, what does it intend to do to ensure that the government trade action is not detrimental to Canadian workers?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is a very silly comment by the Leader of the Opposition.
At this point, the matter is the subject of a regular, normal and confidential audit by the United States authorities, comparable to audits that we do in Canada in respect of the rule of origin rules that are the subject of the free trade agreement.
For him to suggest that there is something wrong and that we do not know what is going on inside the Government of the United States is silly. When we find out what the results of this audit are, we will be able to take action if it is appropriate to take action.
I think the hon. member would be well advised to wait for the facts to come out before he starts making these allegations.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am terribly surprised that the minister does not know what is going on. He should know if these manufacturers meet or do not meet the requirements of the auto pact. It is his job, not my job.
Mr. Denis Desrosier, a very respected automobile analyst said: "With the trade negotiations with the Americans and Mexicans coming up, the potential exists to fundamentally blow the auto pact apart." Can the minister assure Canadians and this House that the auto pact is not on the table in the negotiations between Canada, the United States and Mexico?
June 18, 1991

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the answer is yes, I can assure the hon. member of that, but I also would like to advise him that between Canada and Mexico the largest single element of our trade is in automotive parts and assembled vehicles. There are some serious trade barriers that the Mexicans have that inhibit our trade, particularly trade in automobiles into Mexico, and I would expect that the Leader of the Opposition would be encouraging us to make part of these negotiations to help the export of our cars into the Mexican market.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister for International Trade. The United States trade representative has stated that the United States and Mexico are negotiating separate agreements on immigration, oil mineral rights, and on the environment without Canada's participation.
Did Canada choose to absent itself from those talks or was it excluded? Has Canada in fact secured full and equal participation in trilateral negotiations, or can Canada be excluded from some aspects of the talks if the United States and Mexico decide to do so?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we arc full and equal partners in the trade negotiations. There are some elements that are outside the trade negotiations that are a subject of discussions between the United States and Mexico, as there are between the United States and Canada. We have a bilateral arrangement with Mexico in matters of environment that the Prime Minister signed when he was in Mexico about a year or so ago.
Those discussions arc ongoing, but we agreed at our meeting last week that these bilateral discussions could turn into trilateral discussions. There will be full openness among all of us as to what is going on in these discussions, and if it appears appropriate to make certain bilateral discussions into trilateral discussions, that is something we can easily do.

Mr. Speaker, let me be a little more specific. The United States trade representative has announced that the United States has now agreed that ownership of all Mexican oil mineral
Oral Questions
rights is not on the table in the North American free trade negotiations.
Will the minister explain to the Canadian people why the ownership of all oil mineral rights is excluded in the case of Mexico, but not in the case of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sorry, I missed the last part of the question.

Mr. Speaker, I should be glad to repeat it. I wonder whether the minister would explain how it is that the ownership of all oil mineral rights is excluded in the case of Mexico, but included in the case of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the ownership of the mineral rights in Canada is a provincial matter. They are the governments responsible for the ownership. In fact they own the mineral rights themselves and it is up to them to decide how they should deal with them.
Our position in the free trade agreement with the United States was that we wanted to use the free trade agreement to ensure that we had access to the United States market to sell the products that come form those mineral rights, oil and natural gas in particular.
That was our choice. That was our decision as the government at that time and I believe it was the right one.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. Yesterday I asked the minister of health about the secretive, closed-door federal-provincial conference of ministers of health which will meet in Toronto on Wednesday. I now understand that this meeting has no agenda and will be restricted to ministers only. Clearly any minister can propose changes to our health care system such as provincial autonomy, disentanglement, user fees, or extra billing.
Can the Prime Minister tell this House if the proposals of his government that it will make at this meeting will include the federal government continuing to play a

June 18, 1991
Oral Questions
major role in medicare, including direct cash funding and the maintenance of national standards.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Minister of State (Youth) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect to the secretiveness of the meeting, it cannot be that secret if my hon. colleague knows all about it.
My colleague, the Minister of Health and National Welfare, will be there at the conference and I am sure he will be pleased to report back to the hon. member when he returns.
Canadians are clearly worried about their health care system and they certainly do not get assurance from the questions and answers we are receiving from the other side.
Oh, oh.

My supplementary is to the Prime Minister. yesterday, the minister of Health said the Canadian health system was admired as the best in the world. Can the Prime Minister tell this House how much longer the Canadian system will remain the best when its own government will cut S62.4 billion from medicare financing by the year 2000. What specific financial guarantees will he take to the provincial ministers of health tomorrow so that Canadians will continue to have the best medicare system?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Minister of State (Youth) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure Canadians would be much more reassured if we put the questions ourselves. But of course, that is the privilege of the hon. member of the opposition.
With respect to the conference, as I said, my colleague the minister of health is going to be there tomorrow, and I am sure after the conference he will be in a good position to indicate what transpired at that conference.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the minister responding for the minister of health. In a recent letter to the editor of Saturday Night the Deputy Minister of Health wrote that: "the government has developed an approach to regulation of prosthetic devices based on risk management, voluntary compliance and international co-operation."
There have been serious questions about the safety of the Meme breast implant. There are persistent rumours that the Meme will be back on the market by fall. Will the minister assure women that the Meme will not return to the market until it is proven safe.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Minister of State (Youth) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as hon. members know, many questions have been asked about that matter of the minister of health in the past. He has given indications of what measures National Health and Welfare have taken with respect to that particular matter, and I am sure the minister will continue to assure my hon. colleague that everything with respect to health and welfare and the protection of the user will be maintained.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister for International Trade. Last Friday, the US trade secretary said that her country and Mexico will negotiate, in the context of the free trade talks, a distinct environmental agreement, without Canada's participation. This formula was used in certain countries- there are a few, but I will not list them-hit by a revolution or a civil war, and it was to write a new Constitution.
But I want to ask him a very specific question. It is about the referendum, which can be very useful, but also very dangerous for some of us who are afraid. It is true that a referendum, if it is used to confirm a project of society, to confirm an agreement, that is fine. subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF A SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we must first agree that the wish expressed by the government to appoint a Special Committee of the House and the Senate to examine what is going on in this country and to see how the government and the institutions as a whole must deal with the situation, is a legitimate one.
As for myself, I can only support the wish of the central Parliament, of the federal Parliament, of the supreme institutions of Canada to deal with a crisis that is dividing the country and to try to see first the reality, and then what can be done about it.
In this sense, we must also commend all the parties in the House for seeking to rise above partisan lines, to form a sort of very large group, the largest possible, in order to look at the reality. Why do the parties have such an unusual instinct? We know well that parties generally fight at much lower levels and clash over the issues that divide them. Why, this time, do the parties feel the need to unite themselves in this endeavour? Why? Because

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
they know well that the crisis is such that we must include, all aspects of the problem. We cannot afford, in the face a such a situation, to be divided, to hide the reality. So, we want all the parties to be there, because all the parties, by their very existence, show that political reality takes various forms, that it is not monolithic, that there are several aspects and that we must represent them all, which is what the parties do through the election that brought them here in this House. However where the approach of the parties in this House is misleading, where it distorts reality, is that it fails to reflect, in the composition of the committee, one of the aspects of the political reality in this country, that is the move of Quebec towards sovereignty.
In other words, the kind of unanimity we see in this Chamber, this search for the truth, for honesty, does not go beyond these walls. There is some kind of framework which this Chamber does not want to get out of. We choose to ignore the most critical aspect of this crisis, the fact that it generated a sovereignty movement in Quebec, the fact that according to the latest polls 57 to 59 per cent of Quebecers want sovereignty.
I understand that it is a problem for a federal Parliament, for a country like Canada, an enormous problem for which a solution has to be found. If I were a federalist, I, too, would try to find a solution to such a problem. However the majority of the people in Quebec are moving toward sovereignty. Therefore, the normal reflex in this House is to create something which would be above the parties, in order to see what the reality is.
By doing that, Mr. Speaker, the government and the opposition parties are burying their heads in the sand while saying: "Yes, we are going to review all aspects of the problem, but not sovereignty." But the problem is sovereignty, and the committee is not going to look at it, is not going to look at the fundamental problems of Quebec.
The process being launched today is therefore heading for immediate failure. This attempt is doomed to failure. It is obvious that what you embark upon today, without us-not because you exclude us, as individuals, but because you exclude what we represent-is a process doomed to failure in the same way as the two previous
attempts. In other words, you will look at everything, except the problem.
Mr. Speaker, it is not only the attitude demonstrated by the the creation of the committee and the exclusion of the representatives of the Bloc quebecois that shows that we live in a surrealist world, there is in particular, the speech of the hon. member for Papineau-Saint-Michel, this morning, who, following the example of all those who speak here about the sovereignty of Quebec, condemned this movement. He tried, once again, to talk in a derogatory way, of something perfectly legitimate that reflects a deep reality, that is in keeping with an historic continuity of a people reaching towards the ultimate fulfilment.
When we talk about sovereignty the way we do, Mr. Speaker, we are once again burying our heads in the sand. When we are told that the fundamental values of the country are embodied only in federalism, we forget that the sovereignty of Quebec is as legitimate as that of Canada and that even Canada, in its present arrangement, does not reflect the values that it embodied in the beginning.
The Canadian dream, Mr. Speaker, does not work anymore, even with the values that were there originally. It is not Quebec's fault, Mr. Speaker, it is not the fault of sovereignty if, for the last twenty years, Canada has lost its place in the world, its competitiveness, its productivity and is not recognized anymore as a major international partner. It is not Quebec's fault, it is a crisis in self-confidence, Mr. Speaker. Moreover, Quebec cannot be blamed for that coup de force that was imposed on it in 1981-1982, as you well know.
Well, the House turns away from the facts and forgets what caused the situation we are now experiencing. But one must not forget, Mr. Speaker, because we, Quebecers, do remember! We are well aware that you also remember even if you do not talk about it, even if you ignore it when you take your decisions. Quebecers do remember that, in 1981-1982, nine provinces plus the federal government, with the support of the Parliament of Westminster and the Supreme Court, imposed on Quebec the shredding of the Confederation Pact. They acted to amend the constitution of a democratic country in order to reduce the powers of one of its two signing peoples, one of its two founding peoples, so that, in spite of its repudiation, in spite of its protestations, Quebec
June 18, 1991

Government Orders
had to accept a constitution which still governs it today, eight years later, even though it did not sign it.
This democratic Parliament-for it is substantially and essentially democratic, I do recognize that-this Parliament nevertheless voted for a constitution against the opposition of Quebec, despite a nearly unanimous vote in the Quebec legislature by more than just the Pequists and Separatists, as they are often called here. The Parliament in Quebec, the rightfully-elected Quebec institution, all that exists in Quebec, had to accept a Constitution from which we, Quebecers, are excluded, although it governs us legally, although it is not politically legitimate, because we all know that a constitution is more than a piece of paper, Mr. Speaker, it is more than a legislation. A constitution embodies the values that bind us together. You could give your life for it, if necessary, and defend it with your own blood. A constitution is the soul of a people, because we are one country. But, this constitution, Mr. Speaker, does not speak for us, it is not our soul. This constitution was, in a very unacceptable way, pushed down our throat.
Mr. Speaker, we did try for many years, in 1987, 1988, 1989 and 1990, to sign it. We, who come from the Province of Quebec, had decided to make one more show of confidence in Canada by signing the Constitution, even if it was a sign of disgrace for us. We were ready to accept the strict minimum, that is the recognition of Quebec as a distinct society. It did not even change anything concerning powers. Everyone knew that it would not alter the balance of power.
But, they said no to us. That means that not only did they push an injustice upon us, an unspeakable injustice, which will stay forever in the Canadian history, as long as they will not come back and admit it, which they do not want to do, even today, at the risk of losing Quebec. Furthermore, they even refuse to make amends for that injustice, Mr. Speaker.
So, no one can tell us that sovereignty is a negative move to destroy this beautiful country. This country is on a self-destruct course, Mr. Speaker, if it has not already destroyed itself through its intolerance, its refusal to accept reality. We have a political problem, Mr. Speaker. I do not think that the Meech refusal was inspired by malicious intent.

I do not believe Canadians were motivated by malevolence against Quebec when Meech was refused. I think English Canadians think they have a country, Canada. They love their country. It is the country of their heart and they have a right to behave like this. I understand them very well. Their sons, their fathers, their grandfathers shed blood for it and they stand ready to do it any time.
That is why when you ask them to change their country on something which is perceived as being substantial they will say no because this is their country. I do understand that.
But you must admit the reciprocal reality because Quebec is not recognized in this country. This is your country, the federal institutions, the whole way of governing the country. It might be legitimate for you but it is not for us. There are two visions of the country, two loyalties, as respectable in one case as in the other. It means we have to put forward a political solution.
There is a requirement for political maturity now and a need to admit that Quebec has a right to have its own country. English Canadians have a right to have their country, and we also have the same right.
Some things are really very mature but are difficult to do now because we must start from reality. But what are you doing now? You are attempting to ultimately solve the problem but like ostriches you refuse to see reality, which is the main aspect of the problem.
What I hear is the Canada round. This will be the Canada round. When was the last Quebec round? When was it? The last Quebec round was in 1867 when Macdonald and Cartier sat down and struck a compromise and decided to build a country. More than 100 years after that one of the parties tore up the pact.
I think that this is a failure. This committee will be a failure like the Spicer committee, like the Beaudoin-Ed-wards committee. Why? Because some people do not have the courage to admit the fact that we have to examine two realities. That is why I believe that some change should be made. I am making an honest proposal because we sovereignists know perfectly well that the decision will be made in Quebec next year. In the meantime if something rational, responsible and realistic is to be done here, it should be first to accept our

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
proposal to serve on the committee. We do not like to be on the committee. We are not here for that. It would be, as we stated in the letter, a way to allow English Canada to do more about the motivations of Quebec and to know what is going on in Quebec and why. So it would be a service to reality and to democracy.
Second, I really think it would be a question of responsibility and realism to look into what will happen when Quebec makes its decision. It would be wishful thinking to hope that Quebec will not make the decision.
Right now the National Assembly is debating a bill to oblige the government to set up a referendum on sovereignty by next October, 1992 at the latest. Then the government of Quebec will be obliged to put the question to Quebecers. We think their answer will be yes, we stand for sovereignty.
What happens to Canada if the answer is yes? It will not be a nice cosmetic report from a committee where sovereignty will have been hidden, taken away, that will make English Canada ready for this. English Canada must prepare itself for what will happen next year when Quebecers will take responsibility because they will have to take responsibility. That is why the second modification to the proposal should be to enlarge the mandate of the committee and allow the members of the committee to look into what should be the behaviour of Canada when Quebec becomes sovereign.
There will be huge decisions to make then. What kind of economic arrangements can be struck? What kinds of arrangements will have to be made relating to, for example, the monetary system, the debt, the partition of the assets, everything? Tliose are monumental questions to address. Even in Quebec we are doing that. Not only because we are trying to know what will happen when we become sovereign, but we have also set up a committee in the National Assembly to look into the next offers that will come from the federal government. Do not forget that those offers will not be studied by the committee if they do not immediately bind, as now, the federal government and the provinces.
Let us be frank, let us be courageous, let us be realistic. This country was not built on wishful thinking; it was built by people who looked at hard reality. We are
not doing that. We are hearing speeches from cosmetic orators, people who, like the minister, cannot even answer a question on the substance of the motion and on the heart of the crisis; people who stand up and only throw insults at us and play games. It is time for the truth and we are calling for the truth now.

Mr. Speaker, I note with much regret and sadness that we have brought this debate down to very low standards. Person-nally, I consider that debate to be an important debate since the future of my country is at stake. I, for one, do believe passionately that I can remain Marcel Prud'homme for ever within this country called Canada where I can evolve, breathe and be myself.
The only thing I would like to say to this House and in the presence of the responsibile minister, is that I regret that that member would not remain silent! The reason for that is quite simple because on some other occasions or during other debates, Heaven knows we can always indulge in that sort of exchange, but not when we are talking of the future or the possible desintegration of this country.
As I said, I am very concerned by the tone of this debate and I must say that the hon. member, who is a friend, did not help much to raise the level of the discussion. I listened carefully to the comments of the member of the new party-I do not mean the New Democratic Party because they just do not know where they are going-but the member from the Bloc Quebecois and he got me thinking. I would have hoped that we all had the decency to listen to what he had to say.
I was in agreement with him when he said that we must return to the spirit of the Cartier-Macdonald era.
