speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this very important debate to establish a special joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate to consult with Canadians and to develop proposals with respect to our Constitution, proposals which might be discussed with the provinces and, in particular, with the province of Quebec.
The question might be asked: why is this necessary and how did we get here? I will summarize very quickly. As many Canadians know, in 1981-82 we repatriated the Canadian Constitution with a new amending formula. Before that time, we did not have a proper amending formula in our Constitution. We also, in patriating the Constitution, established a Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and introduced other measures in our Constitution which were not there before, measures such as a recognition of aboriginal rights, an entrenchment of the right to equalization and so on.
At that time there was a Parti Quebecois government in power in Quebec. For one reason or another, and I guess in particular, because that government's option was not for Canada but rather for a separate, indepen-
When Mr. Bourassa came to power a few years later he made a five point proposal to the federal government and to other provinces as a basis for Quebec signing the Constitution of 1867 plus 1982, the composite Constitution as it developed, and those five points were put under discussion.
As a result of that discussion, the federal government with the provinces developed the Meech Lake Accord which was a series of amendments to the Constitution of Canada which would have addressed the concerns of Quebec and in particular the five point program put forward by Premier Bourassa. It also addressed some other matters that Mr. Bourassa had not raised at all, but which came out of the discussions with the other provinces.
We all know what happened. About a year ago the composite set of proposals to amend the Constitution known as the Meech Lake Accord did not get the necessary support. Parts of it required seven out of 10 provinces agreeing. There was easily that acceptance of it, but I think three major parts required the unanimous consent of all the provinces. It ended up that two provinces did not agree, and so the Meech Lake Accord failed.
In the aftermath of that failure there was a great reaction in Quebec. Many Quebecers, in part due to false information and in part due to a lot of demagoguery on the part of certain journalists, certain politicians and so on, felt rejected by the rest of Canada. This was a false situation because it was forgotten, and I think unfortunately forgotten, that eight provinces supported the Meech Lake Accord and the federal Parliament supported the Meech Lake Accord. The majority in all parties in this House supported the Meech Lake Accord and the Senate supported the Meech Lake Accord. I say that despite its flaws.
Our own party had, on two occasions, proposed nine amendments to the Meech Lake Accord, but the government, which I think was wrong in doing so, was totally inflexible. It did not accept any amendments. However, despite the fact that the Meech Lake Accord was flawed, on balance it was supported by this House, it was supported by the Senate and supported by eight prov-

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
inces of Canada. There was no rejection of Quebec by the other provinces, what is called in Quebec sometimes "English Canada". I refuse to accept that description of Canada outside of Quebec as English Canada because it is made up of many elements, including one million francophones but also people from all over the world including our aboriginal peoples.
The rest of Canada did not reject Quebec. That was the perception and there was a great reaction which led to the re-emergence or reinvigoration of the indepcndan-tiste movement, the separation movement, or the sovereignty movement-whatever you want to call it-in Quebec. As a result, the Government of Quebec under Premier Bourassa set up the Belanger-Campeau commission in conjunction with Mr. Parizeau, the leader of the Parti Quebecois. This commission carried on its work for the greater part of the last year. The Quebec Liberal Party, the provincial party, also conducted its own study with the Allaire commission. As well, the federal government set up the Keith Spicer commission and the Beaudoin-Edwards committee of this House and the Senate. All were dealing with different aspects of the Constitution and how we might resolve the constitutional crisis that arose from the failure of the Meech Lake Accord and, going back still further, the fact that Quebec had not signed the Constitution of 1982.
The government has put forward this motion to further the work at the federal level and has suggested this committee. Our party agrees to it. We have suggested some changes to the mechanics and the membership of the committee, but in principle we agree with what the government is trying to do, that is to develop in consultation with Canadians all over the country, openly and in depth, constitutional proposals that will be satisfactory not only to Quebec but to all Canadians.
I am an optimist. I was bom in Montreal. I have lived in Montreal for the greater part of my life. I have also lived in Ontario and New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, but I am a fifth generation Quebecer. I talk to my friends and acquaintances, the people I have worked with in law firms in Quebec-at one time I was the only anglophone in a law firm of 45 Montrealers. I have played hockey in Quebec on teams where the great majority were French Canadians, who were francophones. I still am in touch with these people. It is my deep-rooted feeling that we
in all parts of this country have much more in common than what divides us, much more in common.
We share great values together. We share the land. We share the beauty and resources of this country. Consequently, what we are searching for is a constitutional formula which will represent the commonality of views and values and so on.
I think it is possible. If there was great division among the individuals and peoples of this country that outweighed the things that we have in common then I would say it is a hopeless task. However, deep down I know that I as an anglophone Quebecer have much more in common with my francophone colleagues in Quebec than I have with any American, than I have with people even within this country, from British Columbia and from Alberta. If we cannot find a legal constitutional formula which will represent this commonality of views, the spirit that Canadians share together, then what hope is there for the world?
That is why statesmen around the world are speaking out in amazement that we would even think for a minute of splitting up this great and wonderful country. They see Yves Fortier at the United Nations. They see Claude Jodoin, one of the greatest labour leaders that this country has ever produced. We have had three prime ministers from Quebec, we have produced outstanding people at the national level.
I am not talking about at the Quebec level. Of course, at the Quebec level it is evident that francophone Quebecers would rise to the top. However at the national level francophones have risen to the top in all facets of life: in the theatre, in dance, in music, in politics, in labour, in the academic world and so on.
I am an optimist. There is much more in common between us than that which divides us. What we have to do and what we hope to do in this committee is determine how to translate the commonality of interest into a constitutional formula.
My interest in these matters goes back a long way. I was a member of the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons in 1970-71. That was the committee chaired by Senator Molgat and Mark Mac-Guigan of this House. By the way, that joint committee
June 18, 1991

sat for more than a year, and many of the recommendations in the report are still very worthwhile.
We travelled all over the country and heard people in much the same way as the government is recommending that this new committee do. Times were different then, but this was in the beginning years of the separatist movement in Quebec. There were other constitutional pressures from the west and the east at the time.
Again, I sat with the joint committee in 1980-81, the Joyal-Hayes committee, which studied the proposals to repatriate the Constitution and set up a charter of rights and freedoms.
I also had the good fortune to be a full member of the special committee on Indian self-government in 1981-82 which travelled this country for more than a year, meeting with aboriginal peoples. It finally recommended that we come out in favour of aboriginal self-government in this country.
The message that I want to give to the minister and to the members of the House of Commons is that in discussing these proposals, we cannot forget the minorities in this country. Some have said that this country is made up of minorities, that there really is not any majority.
That may be so. However, sometimes when the leaders of provinces get together, they represent the majority view of those provinces and too often have forgotten the minorities.
When I first came to this Parliament, we spoke of the two founding nations. At the time that might have made some sense. As we began to discuss these things with the Indian people in Canada, the Inuit and the Metis, we soon learned how ridiculous it was to consider the English and the French as the two founding nations when thousands of years before them were the first nations, the Assembly of First Nations as they call themselves now.
Government Orders
put pressure on others because they do not have the political structures to do so. Approximately 1 million aboriginal people are spread throughout this country.
We have to find a way. I was pleased that the minister and our leader are committed to finding a way of involving those people in the constitutional discussion. If we do not do that, we will never have a Constitution which will serve all Canadian people in a just and lasting way.
I can recall very well last summer when I was in Geneva for a disarmament conference at the time the Oka crisis broke out. Canada was on the front pages of the European newspapers, but not in a very positive way. The headlines said that Canada was oppressing its aboriginal peoples, its native people.
In too many cases the news was oversimplified. It did not totally explain the situation. However, the message, which deep down is correct, was that we have forgotten, we have ignored and we have not treated our aboriginal people properly. This is an opportunity to do that.
With respect to our two official languages, it is recognized that Canada is made up of many peoples. Our leader has proposed that in a new Constitution the preamble should recognize the peoples who have come together to build this country, including the English, the French and the aboriginal people-I am not listing them in any priority-and the millions of people who have come from all over the world and now make up more than one-third of our population. They have come from Europe, Asia, Latin America, Africa and form a great and positive force in this country. We have to recognize them all.
We have a policy of multiculturalism in this country so that we can take the best of all those cultures. We are not a melting pot. We do not want to forget the greatness that comes out of those nations when these people come to this country. We want to keep the best of their cultures and make it part of our own.
These people, the Cree, the Micmac, the Ojibway, the We have two official languages and I cannot under-Montagnais and so on were here for thousands of years, stand those people who try to diminish the use of the two They have been forgotten in the constitutional discus- official languages, who attack them, who look on them as sions. Of course, except for the Northwest Territories a burden. For me to have two official languages is an and to a certain extent in the Yukon, they do not form outstanding asset for a country and in particular to have the majority in any political unit in this country. Conse- as our two official languages English and French, which quently, they cannot bring their political views to light or are among the two greatest languages in the world.

June 18, 1991

Not only are they widespread throughout the world, but they have great literature and culture associated with them, great theatre, great writings, great philosophers, and great political theorists. To have these two great languages as our official languages should be an asset. Canada, different from many other countries, can do business in French and English. We can do diplomacy in French and English. We write books in French and English. We produce theatre and television in French and English. We have great universities in French and English. We have great libraries in French and English.
The United States, Great Britain, France, Germany, and Italy only have one language. They can only do all those things to which I referred in one language. We have this great asset and advantage of two official languages and we should make the most of it. We should use the fact that we have two official languages to attract tourists, business, international associations of the United Nations or whatever. I can recall right after the Second World War that ICAO and IATA were attracted to Montreal because Montreal was a city with two official languages and many other cultures such as Italians, Greeks and so on. That was an attraction for international organizations to move there. Great international conventions would come to Canada because we can work in two languages. We can make it an asset. We can look at something positive.
There have been rumours that in order to get a constitutional agreement there could be suggestions that we cut back on our commitment to linguistic duality or to the two official languages. By the way the policy of bilingualism is not and has never been that all Canadians must speak the two official languages. The policy is that the government must be able to serve Canadians in their language, either English or French, where they are in sufficient numbers and that makes good sense. That does not hurt anybody. There has been some talk that we should move to the Swiss model. In Switzerland, where I lived and worked for a while, there are 22 cantons, the great majority of which are either German, Italian, or French-speaking, but there are only two cantons that I know of with two languages.
In Canada there are one million francophone Canadians living outside Quebec. As was already stated in the debate today, those million francophones are greater than the entire number of francophones living in Quebec
at the time of Confederation in 1867. There are also- fewer today than there were a while ago, unfortunately- about 700,000 to 800,000 anglophones living in Quebec who have very deep roots in Quebec. They developed many parts of the Eastern Townships and, with the Inuit and the Indians, developed the north through the Eludson's Bay Company and the fur trade in the very far north of Quebec. They have very deep roots in Quebec.
To move to a situation where we would say that Quebec would be a French-speaking province-I will refine that in a minute-and all the other provinces would be English-speaking, I think is wrong. I have always recognized that the principal language of Quebec should be French and I have always recognized that Quebec should be a distinct society. It has been a distinct society since it was on this continent.
In the Constitution of 1867, Quebec was the only province that was to have civil law. All the others were to have common law. Quebec was the only province at that time that had the responsibility of two official languages under Article 133. Quebec was the only province with protected counties.
Since that time, other things have developed. Quebec has its own pension plan la Regie des rentes. The other provinces have the Canada Pension Plan. Quebec collects its own income taxes and the other provinces do not. Quebec and Ontario are the only two provinces that do not have the RCMP as their provincial police force.
My point is this: Quebec has had very distinct traits for over 100 years. We should recognize that and where it is essential, provide the powers that go with that distinctiveness. This does not mean that we would go as far as the Allaire commission report, but we could achieve a balance which would provide justice to Quebec and to the rest of Canada. That is what this committee strives to do.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF A SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to have this opportunity today to speak on this motion to appoint a special joint committee to inquire into constitutional proposals for a renewed Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the special joint committee being proposed combines the more attractive features of a constituent assembly, with the accountability of our parliamentary system. Ultimately the Parliament of Canada will set the direction for our country and mould its future. Parliament represents the highest authority, the level within our political system where issues and problems are transformed into ideas and solutions. It is therefore highly appropriate that a parliamentary committee should be given the responsibility of taking the government's proposals for a renewed Canada to the people, and then returning with those proposals, reshaped, altered, modified and augmented for eventual disposition by this House.
This Parliament, this House of Commons, is the ultimate constituent assembly of Canada.
The committee will have the good wishes of all members for success, and I am sure the support of all sides of the House.
The task before the committee is a daunting one, but the reward is nothing less than a reunited, recreated and rejuvenated nation.
Canadians are eager to participate in this process and this committee will provide the mechanisms through which the hopes and aspirations of the people of Canada can be transformed into legislative reality and into the building blocks of Canada's future.
I am sure that all of us in this House believe we are the most fortunate people on the face of the earth. None of us would choose to live elsewhere. Unlike the crises that have gripped most other countries of the world, the current national debate in Canada is not over economics, not over religion, not over basic human rights. Rather, it is a debate over whether or not we choose to continue to live together, whether we have the capacity and the will to better understand one another's needs and concerns, whether we have the strength as a society to embrace and welcome those cultural, linguistic and other features that make us different as individuals and groups and yet, collectively, make us a far stronger, richer and more mature society.
As we all know, our country, Canada, is today going through one of the most critical development periods in its history. We have a vision of a rich and generous nation, one of great material wealth but more important, a country of very high human values based on the diversity of two official languages and many cultural origins, not the least of which are the aboriginal peoples which originally inhabited this land. It is a vision unparalleled throughout today's world, both in the richness of its potential and in the complexity of its application.
Unfortunately, however, for reasons which are obscure to most of us who live here and really beyond comprehension to people in the rest of the world who look upon Canada virtually as the promised land, our rich vision is clouded by preoccupation with the problems of attaining that vision. We have experienced confrontations about language, aboriginal rights, bigotry and racism, regional alienation, financial stability and, political responsibility.
Almost as we speak, in these veiy days there are forces gaining momentum that seek to destroy the vision of Canada that most of us hold so dear. Those forces must be confronted and turned aside, not with violence or
June 18, 1991

hostility, but rather with knowledge, understanding, tolerance, the strength of reason and the will to see our vision survive.
Each one of us has the responsibility to think through our own vision of Canada and to help identify with the cause of the nation as a whole.
For me, one expression which I can leave with you to describe my feelings as a Canadian is the sense of real freedom which is to be found in this country: freedom to exist and live in a land so vast, with lots of room for everyone; freedom to grow and develop in a society that is open and generous and tolerant; freedom to participate in a democracy that is just and accessible; and freedom to dream in a potential which is overflowing with opportunity.
Those are the feelings I get when I think about the unique privilege of being a Canadian. They represent a state of mind not easily attainable in most other parts of the world today where landscapes are becoming more limited, population densities more burdensome, societies more volatile, democracy more fragile and dreams more distant.
It is critical in my view that in any vision of Canada we must always be mindful of that special reality of individual freedom which it offers for each one of us. That is a value above all others and should be the foundation for any vision of nationhood.
Economic arguments may be important, but they will not carry the day. Understanding, sensitivity and an abiding desire to build our nation together are the forces that will shape our future.
Perhaps first and foremost we have to learn to listen better. We want to encourage an outburst of public interest, even fervour. Canadians are not given to flag-waving and public displays of patriotism, unfortunately. But most of us feel a deep love and affection for our country.
This special parliamentary committee will provide the focus for these feelings. This parliamentary committee will talk about Canadian citizenship, and I would like to repeat some words I said to this House a few weeks ago. There are few words used throughout the world which convey the vision of freedom and democracy more clearly than these words, "Canadian citizenship". It is often said, for example, that a Canadian passport is the
Government Orders
most prized document in the international community. Yet among Canadians here at home there frequently seems an apathy about the values of our own citizenship, almost as though we have lost the meaning of our country, our sense of pride in it and our spirit of patriotism for it.
Surely this is a state of mind that we must revitalize for ourselves and for future generations of Canadians. Surely the common denominator of Canadian citizenship must be reinforced as the mantle under which the rich potential of our bilingual and multicultural heritage can be attained and fulfilled. That is a current challenge for each of us, more important now than ever before.
There will be no winners if we cannot resolve the serious differences that exist in Canada today. Our very independence would be placed in doubt and certainly, at best, our capacity for independent action would be greatly diminished. Nobody, except perhaps for a few impractical dreamers, wants a fractured Canada. But other nations have drifted in just that sort of a situation through indifference and lack of will to act courageously and intelligently when the time was right.
The situation is serious right now, but we have much in our favour. Most importantly, we are a civil people, used to coming to decisions after agonizing debate, soul searching, praying, cajoling and yes, even compromising. We have done this for nearly 125 years and I am convinced we have the capacity to do it, if necessary, for another 125 years. Our children and grandchildren have the right to expect us to make our very best effort, to put aside selfish, partisan interests and to work toward solutions that are acceptable to all parts of the country.
There will be only losers. All Canadians will be losers if we do not succeed in bringing forward a workable solution to the current impasse. We must redouble our efforts because our reputation as a stable and reliable nation is already suffering. This is costing all of us, every single one of us.
Some sincere, concerned Canadians have argued strongly for the convening of a constituent assembly. The government has not ruled out such a course, but adding another layer of legislative, consultative activity to our already complex system is hardly a sure cure for our ills. It would be no quick fix. Ultimately it will still be in Parliament where we will have to make the final decisions, no matter what course is chosen. We will achieve

June 18, 1991
Private Members' Business
nothing by abdicating our responsibilities to another body, especially when the groundwork has not been prepared. We would only delay the process, and this is a case where delay will not solve the problems. Delay will only make matters worse because those who would destroy our country are not marking time, they have momentum and their goals are to achieve separation before the rest of us can even catch up.
Whatever means are chosen to get us to our objective of a united, strong Canada, those means must have the full support and participation of all players. We do not go into a game like this with only part of a team; we must go in to win. I am convinced that this parliamentary committee that is proposed will have the resources, the substance and the power to bring about a consensus within Canada that will eventually lead to the unity of this country.
In the absence of time, I am going to cut my remarks short. I would like to propose a motion, seconded by the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry:
That the amendment of the member of Papineau - Saint-Michel be amended by deleting all of the words after the words "House of Commons".

speechtext:
that Bill C-201, an act respecting referendums and plebiscites in Canada on questions of public importance, be read the second time and referred to Legislative Committee G.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak about the Canada referendums and plebiscites bill by first saying a few words about its purpose. Second, I will make some comments about the sources of this bill and third, I will touch on the legislative process which lies ahead of us. I will conclude by making some general observations about the whole process of referendums and plebiscites in our country.
As to the purpose of Bill C-201, the Canada Referendums and Plebiscites Act, it is quite simply, to provide Canada, at our national level, with the enabling legislation under which direct voting could take place at such time as Parliament would see fit to submit questions to the people.
It is a fact that seven of our provinces have such enabling legislation on their books. In the case of Prince Edward Island, it is a very simple statute of five or six sections. In the case of Quebec, it is an extraordinarily comprehensive statute. It is time for us, in the national Parliament of our country, to likewise have available at such times as it may suit the nation's purposes and the wishes of the Parliament and the people of our country to have direct consultation on an issue and have the legislation in place for that.
There has been, of course, a lot of discussion in the country lately by many people as to whether we should have referendums or not. It goes back and forth. Sometimes it strikes me like the debate that might be going on among a number of teenagers about who should get a driver's licence. Nobody has ever checked to see if in fact there was a vehicle to take for a ride in the event that there was a licence to drive the car.
This legislation is the vehicle under which direct votes could take place and it would be a very fine thing for our country to have it ready and available when the need arises.
It is parallel to the situation with the Canada Elections Act which is the enabling legislation under which votes take place when there are elections to Parliament.
The purpose of this legislation is to set out all of the rules and procedures: who votes; how the voters' lists are prepared; how the questions are decided upon and the vote by both Houses of Parliament to approve them; the formation of two umbrella committees, one for the "yes" side and one for the "no" side; rules governing the raising and spending of money; rules dealing with broadcasting, advertising and campaigning. These are all of the procedures that, in the late 20th century, Canadians have
June 18. 1991

to come to expect in order to have fair and free electoral processes.
The bill is, as I say, comprehensive. It was first tabled back in July 1988 and I have resubmitted it on four occasions since. I wish to make some general observations about the role of referendums and plebiscites in our country. I think it is important briefly to do this so that this bill is seen in some context apart from the context I have just described as the need to have enabling legislation.
The first point I would very much like to stress is that no one should see a referendum or a plebiscite as something which is threatening to our parliamentary institutions or rivalling the role of elected representatives.
I am an elected representative. I certainly am not trying to under cut the role that we as elected representatives have in the process, but it can be and it has in our history already been a process, the direct voting, which is complementary to the role of Parliament. It is supplementary to the role of Parliament. Particularly in this bill there is provision for continual close involvement of the Parliament of Canada.
I think there is a necessary safeguard there regarding concerns which have been expressed by many members of Parliament and by the right hon. Minister responsible lor Constitutional Affairs enabling us to see, for example, the role of Parliament in voting to approve the wording of any question that would be submitted to the Canadian people, and also the role of parliamentarians setting up the oui committee, the "yes" committee and the "no" committee, the umbrella organizations.
This is not separate from Parliament. This is not antithetical to Parliament, but it is complementary and can be seen in a positive way, especially in light of our history with our two previous national plebiscites, over
60 plebiscites or referendums at the provincial level, and some several thousand plebiscites on municipal questions at the local ballot boxes which are certainly part of our democratic infrastructure in Canada. Some 94 or 96 separate statutes across our country at the provincial level accord the right to vote to citizens on specific questions.
The second point of a general nature regarding plebiscites has to do with their educational role. After the last election there was a lot of debate as to whether that election had been a plebiscite or a referendum on the free trade issue. In 1911 there was a lot of discussion as to whether that election had been a referendum on reciprocity with the United States, or in Quebec a referendum on the naval bill.
The fact is that when you are into a general election, a lot of issues are mixed together, as are the personalities of all the candidates and the party leaders. It is not really possible in our election system to have the narrow, specific focus for an intense period of four or six or eight weeks of a plebiscite campaign on a specific question. This is a great opportunity for Canadians to become educated as they hear the pros and the cons of the question before the country, and they have the personal interest of becoming informed because they know that next Monday that man and that woman have to go and mark a ballot with an X beside "yes" or "no". That is something which leads all of us into a positive educational process which I think can be very important for this country.
A third point, and somewhat related to that, is that the campaign period can be a time of self definition for individuals and for all of us as Canadians. For example, three years ago in Prince Edward Island, Premier Ghiz submitted to the people of that Island a question about a fixed-link crossing. Although there had been debate and in five elections people had been promised some kind of tunnel or bridge, this was the first time in the history of PE.I. that the men and women, the citizens, had the opportunity to debate among themselves whether it was good, whether it would help the economy, but it would hinder the island psychology, and so on. They sorted it out, just as in Quebec 10 years ago when Quebecers had to sort out and self define auto-definition who they were and what it could mean to be a Quebecer or a Canadian or the two together. In the Northwest Territories the
June 18, 1991

people went through the same thing in deciding how to vote in their plebiscite to divide the territories.
This is very important. In our country too often people are permitted to stay passive spectators. I see this as a positive opportunity for Canadians to become active participants and in the process define more robustly who we really are as Canadians.
Another point has to do with the opportunity that a plebiscite campaign provides for ventilation of feelings within the Canadian public. Why wait three or four or five years between general elections to say to Canadians that is the only time that they are going to have to come out and really get involved in issues? I think anyone here in this House of Commons knows the current mood across our country. I think it is highly appropriate from time to time-not on every question, certainly not, but on those issues of transcending national importance-to put the question to people so that they can all become involved in this and get out of themselves and express publicly their feelings on the issue. Ventilation on some of these issues is a very important part of Canada's nature as a democracy.
A further point is that I think the participation of people is fundamental because Canada has a parliamentary system which is based ultimately on the consent of the governed and not the coercion of those people. For there to be consent on the way the grand lines of our public policy are proceeding, the greater the participation and the more robust our democracy, the more authentic that the participation and consent will be.
Finally, I want to say I do not think that holding referendums and plebiscites is a magic solution without risk. It certainly has to be exercised with wisdom and care and statecraft, but it is a part of what is possible for our country as a democracy. The history of our country shows that on balance, the uses of direct voting have been positive and constructive.
If members in the House can consider and support this bill we will serve our country well by providing the enabling legislation, so that when it is appropriate and when there are issues on which Canadians from coast to coast to coast must be consulted directly, we will not have an eleventh-hour flap about how it should be done.

The hon. members took a lot of clauses out of the elections act, and I see that he has made a lot of changes to bring them up to date, and that is a good thing.

I want to say, however, that I have grave reservations about the whole idea of referenda in general. I set these comments aside from his bill. I feel that in a parliamentary democracy a referendum must be a very rare occurrence indeed. I do not believe that it is something that should be resorted to lightly or on a frequent basis. I believe that the electoral system we have in this country, with the system of representation that we enjoy, generally ensures that Canadians are well represented through their elected representatives in Parliament and in provincial legislatures.
I recognize, as I know the hon. member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore does, that in the last few years there appears to have been some breakdown in Canadians' views about their elected representatives. I realize that there is a sense of unease, a sense perhaps of lack of representation of divergent views in this place. I regret that that is so. I think it is in part because there is a perception that the government is not responsive to the views of Canadians. I agree that in some cases that is so. In others, I think the government can be responsive and occasionally is.
I have plenty of occasions to criticize the government and I am trying to avoid any of that in this particular debate, but I think that is part of the lack of confidence that Canadians feel in their system because, as I have said, they feel the government is unresponsive.
Certainly as a member of the opposition I would prefer that the government pay closer heed to our comments on bills in this House. On minor matters I feel that as a member I get quite good co-operation, by and large, from the government on matters relating to my constituents. However, on major issues and bills I feel that perhaps the views of the opposition warrant further consideration.
Certainly the arguments about referenda fit into this because the argument of those who believe that Parliament is not representative is that that lack of representation can be cured by running to the people with bills or with questions that can then be decided there. While occasionally resort must be had to such an unusual remedy, I suggest that the usual practice must always be that the elected representatives in Parliament make the decisions respecting the introduction and dealing with bills, that the legislation of the country is passed and adopted here in this House and in the other place in the normal legislative process, and that opportunities for public involvement in the legislative process be expanded, be looked at, rather than use the referendum as a means of deciding issues.
The difficulty with referenda that we have seen in recent years-and I think we can look at the recent Quebec examples-is the emotion that can be developed in a campaign so that rational discussion, rational thought and rational behaviour become more difficult. When it is practised on a nation-wide basis, it becomes increasingly difficult to control the running of emotions, the involvement of mass enthusiasm and perhaps discord and disillusionment with the system when people's aspirations or hopes are built up in the course of a campaign.
I see that as a peril and one that if it were to be used frequently would cause grave disorder in our country. I do not think it is particularly helpful as a means of resolving disputes because people simply do not sit around in referenda, if they are being held constantly, and vote rationally and discuss everything on a rational, plain and simple level. It becomes more involved and convoluted than that in most cases.
Nevertheless, I think that the bill the hon. member has introduced represents a very good effort at providing for a means of conducting referenda quickly and efficiently in Canada. It is a start. I would be glad-and I know our party would be glad-to have this matter go to a committee where it could receive further study. We could review each of the provisions and the clauses, possibly improve it in places, look for ways that it could be fixed and possibly improved further. We might not find many. We might be well satisfied on clause by clause study in committee.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to say a few words in support of the bill that has been put forward by the hon. member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore. Bill C-201 is a very excellent bill dealing with referendums and plebiscites in Canada on questions of public importance. I stress that fact: questions of public importance.
I do not think I really have to tell you that the concept behind this bill of referendums and plebiscites is one which I believe, and I trust you believe as well, that the public of Canada is wholeheartedly behind. That is demonstrated by the participation in the Citizens' Forum on Canada's Future. The interim report of the Spicer commission, the Citizens' Forum on Canada's Future, quite clearly points out that the majority of the people who participated in that process feel that politicians lack awareness of their accountability to their constituents. As a result of that lack of awareness, the people of this country quite clearly put forward to the Spicer commission a number of ways in which that awareness of their accountability to their constituents could be put forward very forcibly to their representatives, you and I and the members of this Chamber.
One of those suggestions was, quite clearly again, the idea of a referendum. It was not just a referendum on
everything. It was a referendum specifically on constitutional issues and on other major issues or, as the hon. member has framed it, on issues of public importance.
Of course this bill is particularly important at the present time when we are dealing with the issue of unity and the constitutional crisis that we now face. We have seen throughout the previous Meech Lake debate that as time went on Canadians became quite disillusioned with the process of dealing with constitutional change behind closed doors. They wanted a process in which they could participate. It is interesting to note that as time went on it was not just the Canadian public that felt that way. The participants in the process itself, premiers and prime ministers, had comments about the fact that we could never go through that kind of a process again. We had to do it differently.
How do you do it differently? I have not heard any better way suggested which involves all of the public of Canada than the referendum process.
You know that I put forward a suggestion for dealing with the constitutional process that involves a constituent assembly. I am certainly not the only one who has put that forward. A number of others have, but the concept that I have suggested would involve a constituent assembly which makes recommendations that are then submitted to a federally sponsored referendum, tabulated on a province by province, territory by territory basis. The results of that referendum would then be submitted to the federal, provincial, and territorial governments to be dealt with in accordance with the 1982 amending provisions of the Constitution Act.
In that way it seems to me we would make sure that all Canadians were involved in the process. We would also make sure that provincial and federal representatives were clearly aware of what the people who elected them thought on this particular issue. Not that it would be a one majority vote that would govern the whole country but, if it were tabulated on a province by province basis, the provincial and federal representatives would clearly know how their electors felt on those issues.
The problem of course with the process that I have suggested is that we do not have any legislation in place for a referendum. That is where I have to congratulate the hon. member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore for putting

forward this bill at what I think is an extremely significant time for legislation of this sort. It is not the first time, as the hon. member has pointed out, that we have had referendums in this country. It is not the first time that there has been legislation at one level or another. We do have it at provincial levels; we do have it at municipal levels. We had a referendum in Quebec in 1980 on the question of separation. We have debate going on right now in the National Assembly of Quebec on Bill 150 on the issues of sovereignty and having a referendum in October 1992. We have had referenda in this country on conscription in the First World War and the Second World War. There is nothing revolutionary about this concept. It is something we have done before. There is no reason why we should not have legislation in place to do it again and do it when we need to do it.
The fact is other countries have this in place. To the south of us in the United States some 30 separate states and the District of Columbia have this in place. They go beyond the scope of this bill. They do not go to referenda that are sponsored by governments, but to referenda that electors themselves can initiate by petition. The state of California which has a population of 26 million, exactly the same as Canada, has such legislation in place. It is called direct democracy where electors can petition to have a question put on the ballot. If 5 per cent of the people who voted in the last election for governor of the state of California had petitioned then that question would have had to have gone on the ballot. The most famous of those was Proposition 13 in the state of California dealing with the issue of property tax reform. In the 1990 state election in California there were actually 14 separate propositions or 14 separate referenda on the ballot. California is not alone in the United States. Many of the large states have that sort of thing as well.
What we need is something similar in Canada. We have heard the critics this evening. We know there are critics of this process who feel that this might be a way for the majority of people to run rough-shod over the minorities. It has been said that we elect members of Parliament to represent us because they can look into the details of all of the issues that require legislation. Of course there is the Edmund Burke theory of democracy

Mr. Speaker, for those who have forgotten, the Canadian experience goes back to 1898, when Canadians were consulted on prohibition, alcohol. You will recall that the population was consulted and, if I remember correctly, 51 per cent voted in favour, and 49 per cent voted against, more or less. Therefore, the government did not do anything. They dropped the issue and it became history.
Canadians were consulted again in 1942. This time it was about the conscription. The results were rather decisive, since 65 per cent voted for it, while some 35 per cent voted against it. Because of those results, it took two years before the government decided to do something and, in 1944, Mackenzie King used the conscription as a means to force or incite Canadians to participate in the war effort.
Mr. Speaker, these two plebiscites in our history have left bitter memories in the minds of the Canadian population. For us, French Canadians, I should say Canadians speaking French, it was synonym with division among groups, among families, among people, among regions and among provinces. This caused numerous problems. Therefore, I would be somewhat hesitant to hold a referendum or a plebiscite regarding a Canadian issue. Anyhow, seven provinces already have legislation allowing for going to the people. It is probably not a bad thing that a country like Canada considers the need for such a legislation. I congratulate the hon. member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore for putting this before the House.
Personally, as I said, I have serious concerns. I believe that a referendum binding on the government ought to be on a question worded with extreme caution, a short
and clear question, a question without ambiguity of any kind. Maybe we could go to the people to ratify an accord or a constitutional amendment which has been carefully explained. But this is a prerequisite.
Second, I think it would be useful that the question, when put to a referendum or plebiscite, be endorsed by the political parties and that, as I said a while ago in another intervention, the question be such that it does not diminish existing rights and fundamental rights of Canadians, and in particular minority rights.
I will end my remarks on this, I think that any question put to a referendum or plebiscite should require a double majority. By that I mean that the majority at the national level might prevail, but that where a regional element is involved the four regions-Ontario, Quebec, the East and the West-of the country would have a say. This kind of double majority, along with the other conditions, might convince me that we could use a plebiscite or a referendum to get the view of the people of Canada on a given issue.
Mr. Speaker, I think that it might be advisable to refer all of this matter to a committee. I will support the motion for second reading so that this bill can be read and referred to the committee.

What is being questioned here is the trustworthiness of the government and of the official opposition which are looking for every possible means, with the help of the New Democratic Party, to prevent men and women in Quebec to express themselves clearly and to get to their sovereignty according to their own schedule without being subjected to the threat of a national referendum as proposed by the hon. member for Beausejour.

Why that proposal today, at this very moment, when Quebec has decided on a course and timetable, do we want to pass this legislation on the sly.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words in this debate today.
Before us is a motion to establish another parliamentary committee to look at the next phase of constitutional change in this country. I want to say at the outset that the priority for all of us, not only members of Parliament but Canadians, is to ensure that we find a package and a mechanism to keep this country together.
The most important thing is Canada. The most important thing is national unity, and the most important thing is trying to find that accommodation, that package to keep this country together. That is the most important issue.
The only way we are going to do that is to build a national consensus in all parts of this country, in the provinces and the territories, and among all peoples of this country with a package that I would call the Canada round which would make all parts of this country at home in Canada, and want to stay together. That is the objective.
I hope every member of this House would put the country first before his or her political party. The way to do that and ensure that has caused some differences in this House. We suggest in our party that the most likely way of having a successful conclusion, a national consen-

June 18, 1991

sus, is to establish a constituent assembly. It is not good enough to have only another parliamentary committee.
A parliamentary committee in itself does not well represent all the people of this country. There are many people who are under-represented in the parliamentary system. Look around the House. We do not have anywhere near gender equality in this House. There are very few visible minorities. The ethnocultural community in Canada is under-represented. There are not the number of aboriginal people there should be proportionate to their numbers in Canada. There are many other social groups, particularly poor people in this country, who are vastly under-represented by the parliamentary system.
We are saying as a party that we cannot support the motion before us because it is exclusively a parliamentary committee. Instead of that, we have talked often in our joint committee on amending the Constitution, in this House and across the country, in publications and so on, about the need for some sort of constituent assembly.
As a member of the amending formula committee, I can tell you that the overwhelming majority of Canadians who appeared before our committee said that we need a constituent assembly. We have to broaden out the process and have more than just members of Parliament as part of that process.
We are saying as a party that parliamentarians have a very important role to play. As parliamentarians we should represent about half of that constituent assembly. We then fill out that constituent assembly by adding on the other half representing the important minority groups in this country, in particular the aboriginal people, the ethnocultural reality of Canada, the official language minorities and the visible minorities. They are very important players. Those four or five groups are people in this country who are minorities under-represented in this House. They should be part of that constituent assembly.
In addition, we must make sure we have a proper balance between farm groups, business groups, labour groups, fishing groups, poor people and other people of this country. Gender parity would be easy to strike if we had a constituent assembly.
The idea of a constituent assembly is not a radical one. There have been many constitutional assemblies around the world after a revolution, when new nations are formed or when a nation is in a crisis situation. Our country now is in a crisis situation. We need more than just the parliamentarians or politicians to try to pull together that national consensus.
There must be at the end of the day a national consensus involving the major political parties and the major players at both the federal and provincial level if we are to succeed.
The reason for that is we have an amending formula now which for most amendments requires agreement of the federal Parliament along with seven of the provinces representing two-thirds of the population of those provinces for that amendment to carry. For five more important things, including the amending formula itself, we need unanimous consent.
It is obvious that even for the legal and technical amending procedure of the Constitution of Canada what we need in this country is a national consensus on a package. We are much more likely to achieve that national consensus if we have a broader group participating and pulling together that national consensus.
If we have the aboriginal people represented as fully participating members of that committee, or that constitutional convention or whatever we call it, we are much more likely to have the support of the aboriginal people of Canada and not get into a situation like we did last year in Manitoba in which a member of that assembly felt he had to try to stop the Meech Lake Accord because it did not address the needs of the aboriginal people of Canada.
I appeal to my friends across the way, to the minister in particular, to consider the arguments of the constituent assembly: the overwhelming majority of people who appeared before the committee on the amending formula and process-

The reasons for a constituent assembly are the following. First, as I said, the overwhelming majority of witnesses who came before our committee wanted a constituent assembly. Second, public opinion in this country wants a constituent assembly. If one looks at the most recent public opinion polls, we see that approximately 70 per cent of the people of Canada want a constituent assembly, they want to open up the process.
Third, a growing number of premiers are in favour of a constituent assembly or are very, very open to the idea of a constituent assembly. I think of Premier Rae in the province of Ontario, I think of Premier Devine in Saskatchewan who is open to the idea, Premier McKenna, Premier Cameron of Nova Scotia who is open to the idea of a constituent assembly, and I think of Premier Wells in Newfoundland who has been calling for a constituent assembly. These premiers are either in favour of a constituent assembly or they are open to the idea of opening up the process and working in that direction.
What about Bourassa?

What about Bourassa? Mr. Bourassa said no to a constituent assembly.
What we in our party are saying is that you cannot isolate any province or any part of the country. What we are saying in our party is that this constituent assembly must be drawn from the four or five groups that I have mentioned. If we cannot get all of the provinces to send MLAs or MHAs or MPPs to an assembly, then we should not have any provincial representatives there, because we cannot afford to isolate any one of the provinces. We made that very, very clear from the outset.
Government Orders
Like Belanger-Campeau in Quebec, we had a committee there of 18 members who were elected in the Quebec National Assembly, and then through a consensus of the two parties there was the addition of another 18 members who represented a good cross-section of Quebec society. It can be done in the province of Quebec and it can be done in the rest of the country as well, including people from all regions, territories and provinces. If the provinces do not want to participate officially, there are a lot of people who have experience at the provincial level who could be on the constituent assembly.

For instance, I am thinking of Raymond Gameau who was a member and a minister at the provincial level, in Quebec, in the previous Bourassa government. He has a lot of experience and could represent Quebec and the Liberal Party of that province. There are many people in the province of Quebec who can very well represent that province, as there are many in Saskatchewan and elsewhere in Canada.

These are the reasons we need a constituent assembly, to open up that process.
We have always said in our party that the constituent assembly would not be enshrined in the Constitution. We would not want a constituent assembly to deal with all constitutional issues from here on in: whether we should enshrine property rights or aboriginal rights or change some of the rights in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms; dealing with the notwithstanding clause or with other issues of importance, or saying that it should be a one shot deal.
We are in a serious situation of national disunity in this country and because of that we need to have a constituent assembly at this time, but it should not be a permanent part of the amending process. We have made that very clear. It should not be enshrined in the Constitution as part of the amending process and we have made that very clear as well.
The constituent assembly would do no more than this parliamentary committee is supposed to do. A constituent assembly would try to draw together that national consensus, the accommodation that will keep this country one.

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
That is exactly what the parliamentary committee is supposed to do as proposed by the government across the way. It is supposed to draw together a national consensus, to draw together a package to keep this country united.
All we are saying in our party is that the composition of that committee must be different than what the government envisions it to be. The composition of that committee must be a mixture of parliamentarians and non-parliamentarians. The ministers across the way say they do not want non-elected people on it and that it should be a parliamentary committee.
In the motion presented to us from the government it is proposing that there be 20 senators on that committee but senators are not elected. Senators have no mandate from their constituencies, from their provinces, from their regions. They are not elected. They arc appointed by the Prime Minister of the day.
As individuals, I know a lot of these senators can make useful contributions, like Senator Beaudoin or Senator Gigantes du Parti liberal. As individuals they are very good people, but they are not accountable to anyone. If the government can appoint 10 non-elected senators then why can't we, as the House of Commons, make sure we appoint the Grand Chief of the Assembly of First Nations, for example, as a member of the constituent assembly and have full voting rights in that assembly like the member of Parliament from our party or the Conservative Party or the Liberal Party of Canada.
I ask the members of this House to open up their minds to the possibility of flushing this out so that the people of Canada feel some ownership to this constituent assembly, so they feel some ownership to the process that we are to embark on come September of this year.
I believe that the chance of success will be a lot greater if we had as fully participating members the aboriginal people of Canada, people representing linguistic minorities, more women, visible and multi-racial minorities, ethnocultural minorities and the like. I think that is the way to go.
We cannot risk failure. The Meech Lake Accord failed and a lot of people in this House, including the overwhelming majority of members of all three national political parties, were in support of the Meech Lake Accord.
It failed because of a couple of reasons. It failed because there was a perception in the country that the people did not have ownership of that particular accord, that they did not have access to the process, that the accord was negotiated by 11 First Ministers and presented to the House of Commons and to the various provincial legislatures as a fait accompli.
We could not change anything. We could not amend anything. It was called a seamless web.
I would assume that everybody has learned some lessons from that experience and that the next package will come to us as a package that will be amendable by members of the House of Commons as well as by the legislative assemblies of this country, including the Quebec National Assembly.
It seems to me it would be a lot easier to build that consensus if not only members of Parliament, but nonparliamentarians are also part of the process. There is no law and there is no precedent in this country that says that the Constitution belongs to the parliamentarians. There is no law in this country that says only the parliamentarians should be involved. There is no law that says only elected parliamentarians should be involved. There is no law that says senators should be 40 per cent of that particular committee.
I remember last spring when Jean Charest was the chair of the committee looking at a companion resolution for the Meech Lake Accord. We had 15 members on that committee. There were no senators. They were all elected members of Parliament representing the three parties of the House. So why do we bring back senators into this particular operation?
In the past we have also had non-members of the House of Commons involved in parliamentary committees. I remember the former Liberal member from Cochrane, Keith Penner, chairing a committee on aboriginal rights a few years ago and the participating members of that committee were people representing the aboriginal peoples of Canada.
We do have a precedent for that happening in the past. I say to the government across the way: "If you really want to be non-partisan, then do not be afraid to lose your government control of that committee". I think that is the big problem.

If we had a committee that was made half of parliamentarians and half non-parliamentarians, there would be a government minority on that committee. At the end of the day, for the new agreement to pass through the amending process, it has to be reflective of a national consensus. Let us start off that way and try to have a committee that is reflective of the national reality of this country, one that mirrors Canada and the real world.
I conclude by saying that to us, in our party, the process itself is so important that we have to vote no to this particular resolution to establish a committee made up uniquely of parliamentarians. We feel that if we set up a committee made up of parliamentarians only, we jeopardize the very process itself and the exercise, which is to find a national consensus and a package that is acceptable to all political parties in this House and different political parties across the provinces and territories of Canada.
If we can enhance the possibility of a national consensus by bringing more people into the committee, then why not open up our committee and involve more than just parliamentarians? That is the simple crux of the argument because the important thing is to keep this country together.
Having travelled the country extensively in the last four months as a member of the committee on the amending formula, I can say to you that I am much more optimistic now than I was a few months ago.

I believe, Mr. Speaker, that there are changes not only in the province of Quebec, but also in the rest of Canada. I believe that most Canadians want to reach a consensus and find a national accommodation, and I have a feeling that most Quebecers would accept a renewed federalism if Quebec is recognized as a distinct society, if we can do something about the division of powers and other important matters for Quebec and its people. I also have the impression that the nine other provinces and the two territories are now more open than five or six months ago. I believe that most Canadians outside Quebec want to find some accommodation, that they wish to find a compromise with Quebec in order to keep the country together and strong. I also have the feeling, Mr. Speaker, that most Canadians want to see the three national
Government Orders
parties and all other political entities of the country as well as all politicians work together in order to find a solution to this national problem.

I believe we can find that solution. The Canadian people want, above all, Parliament to lead the way, Parliament to put aside some of the partisan fights and clashes we have in this place every day as a natural, normal part of our endeavours, and put the country first and find that national consensus and national bargain.
I know it is there. Even last spring, with all the difficulty of Meech Lake, through the parliamentary committee chaired by Jean Charest we had a unanimous report that came up that we thought was a national consensus and a national compromise. It was scuttled because of certain events, including the defection of the now leader of the Bloc Quebecois from the government benches and also of the intransigence of some of the first ministers to consider some new options on how to solve the national crisis.
Let us not let it slip away again. We may not have another chance. This may be the last chance. I argue and we argue that we can increase and enhance the possibility of a solution to the problem that tears this country apart if we broaden the process and have, instead of just a parliamentary committee, a constituent assembly of parliamentarians and non-parliamentarians, working together to try to build a truly national consensus and find a solution to help this country get over its constitutional problems and get on to the real issues facing Canadians in the modern world.

Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to the speech by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville who is known on this side of the House as a friend of Quebec.
He made several speeches in the same vein during the debate on Mecch Lake, and I must say I enjoy my exchanges with him.
However, one of the points he made was that we had to have a constituent assembly to represent all minority groups, all visible minorities in Canada. This is a very high-sounding principle, Mr. Speaker, but I have some trouble with it.
For instance, there are about 75 different nationalities in Canada, if I am not mistaken. Does the hon. member mean that a constituent assembly would have to have a representative of each of those nationalities, including the Vietnamese community, the Italian, the Chinese, the Mongolians, in fact, every country in the world? Is that what he wants? Is that how he sees this assembly?
Mr. Speaker, I think we are wasting a lot of time looking at the kind of forum we need to deal with Canada's constitutional problems. Perhaps we should go on to discuss the problem itself and not waste our time trying to decide what would be the best formula for this forum.
My second point is that a constitution is important to a country. Everybody says so. However, I don't think we should get carried away, Mr. Speaker.
I remember when I was at the University of Ottawa, my professor of Political Science told our class one day that the most impressive constitutional document on this planet was the Constitution of the Soviet Union. However, if ever a country made a complete mess of it, it certainly did, Mr. Speaker.
That being said, would the hon. member for Yorkton- Melville reconsider his demands for a constituent assembly and opt instead for the Parliament of Canada, a constituent assembly lawfully elected by Canadians every four or five years?

Mr. Speaker, the hon member for Saint-Maurice is negative about the concept of a constituent assembly, but the Belanger-Campeau Commission in Quebec is a constituent assembly. It was a group of 18 elected representatives and 18 non-elected members, and this commission found a

consensus in the province of Quebec and made a number of proposals on behalf of Quebecers.
We suggested having a similar model at the federal level, to have a process that is more open or more democratic for Canadians. Like the Belanger-Campeau Commission, which had members representing labour, the business community and many other Quebecers. If I remember correctly, they also said they offered a seat to native groups in Quebec, but the offer was turned down. In any event, this group was a representative sample of the population of Quebec. We can do exactly the same thing here at the federal level, across Canada.
We have many organizations.

He mentioned the ethnocultural groups, the Chinese Canadians and the Vietnamese Canadians. There is the Ethnocultural Council of Canada. Let it decide which two or three or four members should be in a constituent assembly. Our party suggests 80 to 100 people on that constituent assembly.
One of the premiers has suggested between 70 and 80 people on a constituent assembly. There are national organizations representing aboriginal people and ethnocultural people. There are linguistic minorities-

I am thinking of Francophones outside Quebec, of Alliance Quebec which represents English-speaking Quebecers in the province of Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise today in the House of Commons to speak to the motion put forward for our consideration of appointing a special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons to inquire into proposals for a renewed Canada.
First of all, I have to point out that the constituency that I come from is in the Northwest Territories. The national constituency that I deal with is aboriginal in my capacity as the critic for the Liberal Party of Canada.
It was veiy clearly put before the Beaudoin-Edwards committee that there are six principles which should be dealt with in dealing with the whole constitutional issue. That was put forward by the Minister of Justice of the Northwest Territories. He indicated that the mandate is one that is very integral to the success of the whole inquiry. He said that governments must have a clear mandate to proceed with any fundamental changes to the Canadian Constitution.
He then went on to the role of the people. Any new amending formula, he stated in that specific case, must guarantee that Canadians will be involved at all stages of significant constitutional amendment.
He then went on to say that the role of legislatures, any new amending formula in that specific case-but we are dealing with many other things here-must ensure that a significant majority of members of each legislature are required to ratify amendments. He suggests that a free vote would be part of this approach.
Any new amending formula must clearly and carefully balance the role of the executive arm of the government with the role of Canadians and their elected representatives sitting in legislatures.
He said that aboriginal nations must have a guaranteed role in any constitutional amendment process affecting aboriginal interests.
Then he discusses the role of the territories, because the territories are an extension of the federal government. They are indeed not provinces. They have an act under which they operate. It is a very unique situation posing very specific challenges which constitutional experts and the legal community have to confront in dealing with the territories' aspirations to fit into their rightful place in nation building and within Confederation, such as it is.
June 18. 1991

He states that in this case any changes to the current amending formula or any new formulae must provide for the involvement of territorial residents and their elected representatives in matters that directly affect constitutional development in the territories, and the role of territorial residents in national affairs.
Any new amending formula that might involve regional representation must recognize the Northwest Territories and the Yukon as distinct regions within Canada and not as interest groups to be consulted in some other less formal way. I particularly feel that we have gone through a proliferation of committees and groups.
I sat on the Charest committee with our chairman Mr. Charest and a number of my other colleagues. We criss-crossed the countiy, consulting with people. I felt that in a time of great challenge we demonstrated some leadership and the spirit of compromise, but our advice was not heeded. The particular process we engaged in was pretty conciliatory. It is not that we agreed on everything.
I think there is a lot to be learned from engaging in this kind of work as parliamentarians and legislators. We get to know the people and their concerns, and there are some very diverging views across this country that are difficult to reconcile with the best of expertise or any legal body of opinion that exists out there.
I must say we demonstrated that we could agree because we have come to some consensus on a number of very difficult issues. We were charged with the responsibility of responding to the New Brunswick resolutions and I guess ours was to pick and choose. The picking and choosing, although there was a list of recommendations, were not the simplest things to do because of the diversity that exists and because when you are dealing with the heart and matter of a country it is generally the extreme that tends to prevail. There were some very differing opinions on that committee, but from my experience I would say that anything dealing with the future of this country is worth engaging in.
I have a number of concerns. With regard to representation on the committee, I would like to see greater gender equality, I would like to see a far greater role for women, I would like to sec a far greater role for

aboriginal people and I would like to see equitable participation. Participation has to be that they are equal partners in all of the negotiations and all of the consultations regarding what exactly goes into the body and the preamble of the Constitution in the end.
There are a number of issues which have to be dealt with in terms of the Northwest Territories and in terms of the aboriginal peoples. If we talk about equitable participation, we need to know that any of the other activities that prevail at this time will essentially not undermine or usurp the whole essence of the kind of role that, for instance, the two government leaders of the Northwest Territories play in forging ahead with a constitutional agenda that spells equality for all Canadians, including the northern people and the aboriginal people.
Our aboriginal leaders are elected leaders. They also have to be present at the table and they have to be equal partners in these negotiations. Gone are the times when we can ignore the voices of aboriginal people and the disaffected regions of this country. This is not a Constitution for one region of this country. This is a Constitution for the whole of this country and every Canadian must have a part of it.
We talk about the Americans many times. It amazes me because in my travels to Central America and to the Middle East last summer, I came in contact with Americans who talk about their constitution as if it were a part of their skin and a part of their flesh. It should not be the responsibility of a select group of individuals who would disaffect the rest of the nation to change the Constitution, to make fundamental amendments to the Constitution. My concern has to do with the participation of these two particular leadership regimes. We have elected a new leader for the Assembly of First Nations, Mr. Mercredi. I am sure that Mr. Mercredi sees a role for himself, as well as his representation on behalf of 600 chiefs in any kind of constitutional amendments that are going to take place.
The other thing that I see specifically is that the north, because it is not yet a province, is looking for a basis of equality. It is looking for equality in terms of how it participates and equality in terms of how its substantive issues are dealt with.
