It has been agreed in principle that the north will be divided some day into two separate areas, one being Nunavut and the other being a separate territory which might go by another name.
In doing that, we may eventually opt for becoming a province. If the Northwest Territories does become a province, it is felt by all northerners and by our leaders that we should have the equality and the fairness that was afforded to all other provinces. All the other provinces, pre-1982, were created with bilateral negotiation directly between the particular applicant and the Government of Canada and we feel that is what should prevail.
We also feel strongly that if there are going to be any changes of the boundaries of the two territories, the territories have to be consulted and the pre-1982 conditions thereto also have to prevail.
We look in the aboriginal constitutional agenda and we see a complete forging of opinion last week when we elected a new leader that aboriginal people do want to see the inherent right to self government entrenched in the Constitution. This fundamental move is not one which would allow for a continuing succession of laws that either oppress or suppress the rights of these people. What this would do is replace an archaic way of dealing with the rights of aboriginal people.
I guess the most formidable aspect of the inherent right would be the inherency. What does it mean? Canadians want to know what it means. Essentially what it means is that you give the people a right to carve out their own future and to eke out their own destiny. You give the people the right to make their own mistakes or to make good for themselves, politically and otherwise. We are talking about political power and political representation.
We also want to talk about the provisions afforded to other Canadians within the Constitution. If there are going to be provisions on the basis of culture and linguistics, we want to have our languages. There are 53 aboriginal languages, only three of which are not threatened: Inuktitut, Ojibway and Cree. All these other languages are indigenous to this country. Once they disappear, there is no way of repatriating or rejuvenating
those languages elsewhere in other countries. We cannot go to another land and retrieve those languages.
There have been many suggestions in the area of the preservation of language and culture for which aboriginal people have been excluded. They are not part of negotiation for our cultural industries or cultural properties in the free trade agreement. This has to be considered and I think these are the kinds of things that aboriginal people have concerns about.
The other aspect is that aboriginal people want to be part of the First Ministers' Conferences. I believe that there is some movement and some receptivity to the whole idea of reinstating the original agreement of the Government of Canada, I think it is section 37(1), which affirms that their right to this round of negotiation would be reinstated.
There is some receptivity to that whole idea. That is yet to be brought out in forthcoming reports and whatnot. I have no idea whether that is the case, but I believe with the amount of negotiations, consultations and expert representation that we get from our elected leadership in the aboriginal community, that has been brought out very clearly by the aboriginal leadership.
The other thing that I think is quite interesting is that we have perpetuated the whole mythology of two founding nations. I was at the Assembly of First Nations leadership convention and there it was put to rest that this is not the way that Canada should be perceived historically. We are not co-founders, we are the first peoples of this country and this is the way that Canadian history has to be reflected. If there are going to be future constitutional negotiations, this has to be given paramount consideration.
I guess one of the more dangerous aspects of constitutional dealings are the kinds of words and the kinds of phraseologies that are employed. What happens here is when you use a certain phrase like "two founding nations" you are bound to exclude someone. I think these are the sensitivities that have to be employed when we are going to appoint a joint Senate and House of Parliament committee. The Northwest Territories is an area which best reflects the tolerance that we are known for as Canadians. In the Northwest Territories there are eight official languages. Along with French and English there are the aboriginal languages which are deemed official. If you get on an airline in the Northwest

Territories you will be provided the safety instructions in the various aboriginal languages.
You can go into a hotel and look at the bar of soap and all the toiletries offered and they are all done in syllabics in Inuktitut. I believe we set an example. There is tolerance there. There is acceptance of diversity. I think the people who come forward from our part of the world demonstrate that we are not tunnel visioned, we are not closed-minded, we do not exclude other Canadians. We keep the doors open and prove that we have the ingenious creativity to be able to allow room for everyone in Canada.
We do not predicate our constitutional dealings on the basis of being single-focused, on the basis of being intolerant. We are flexible. We understand that the whole political end of the constitutional reform process is one of the art of the possible. The art of the possible includes an element of compromise. We understand that.
The one fundamental exception which must prevail is that we cannot ignore the rights of northerners. We have to include northern leaders on an even and equitable basis with all of the other leaders across this country in dealing with the Constitution. We have to allow for the political aspirations of the north. There has to be dialogue. We cannot let things like the royal commission-it is a very good idea which I support and will be one of the tools to, perhaps, providing one building block for a new relationship between the Government of Canada and the aboriginal people.
We must not allow that to supersede bilateral negotiations between our elected aboriginal leaders or any kind of negotiations with the north. There have to be provisions for both. I think there is room for both. There are a number of issues that can unite us, not just our linguistic aspirations or our linguistic goals and priorities. If that was the case, why do we not have an aboriginal language foundation?
There is a lot of symbolism in telling people that the language which is indigenous to your people and to your country is important, it is you, it is how you communicate. It is your psyche, it is your psychology. It is the heart of your people. That is very important. Why has that not been done. That can be done outside the realm of the Constitution.
These are things which would symbolically ease a lot of the tension and frustration that is there.

Having said that, I believe that there are a number of concerns. We have concerns about the inherent right to self-government. We also have concerns about the whole issue of extinguishment. Aboriginal people feel that they are people who keep their word.
They have agreements. They have engaged in treaties. They have engaged in a number of specific and unique arrangements with governments, with the Queen in previous years through the Royal Proclamation. There are specific arrangements that they have honoured and they feel they are people of their word.
They feel that major, comprehensive land claims, given a good deal and a fair shake concerning the compensation and land base they get, is good enough to guarantee certainty. Certainty can be had with the kind of treatment you give a people, with the kind of fairness within the process. You do not need to extinguish aboriginal title to ensure certainty. That is a mythology. It is the wrong way to go at it.
For years and years it was the aboriginal people of this country and the northerners who have been willing to share their land, who have not hoarded the resources of the land, who have given access. Now we come to a point where they have not benefited economically. They have been marginalized.
We look at the whole issue of political representation. We are now in a situation where we are putting forward an all-party proposal to have aboriginal electoral districts which would perhaps produce nine members of Parliament from the aboriginal community.
This proposal is not to make aboriginal MPs special or give them special status, but to remove the structural barriers that are there. The Indian Act was a suppres-sionist document which would not allow aboriginal people to vote until 1961. These are the things which have happened and which we have to change and make even.
One of the ways in which we can measure the equality of a people is by their socio-economic status. Let me give one figure that is rather glaring. In my community only 5 per cent of aboriginal students make it out of high school. That is a very, very abysmal figure. There are some places across Canada where non-aboriginal communities say: "Well you are tax exempt. You guys have a lot of money because you hoard money". However, when you live on a reserve with 90 per cent unemployment, what good is the tax exemption, especially when there is

system, to find ways to participate to the fullness of their potential.

It is more than the population certainly of P.E.I., New Brunswick and Newfoundland, and perhaps equal to some of the western provinces. Can my colleague fill me in and perhaps take a little bit of the cynicism away from me that I feel, particularly tonight, in this House, on this motion? She mentions that it was 1961 before they were allowed to vote and participate. Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague for bringing forward his concerns and the questions about why it is that aboriginal people would feel that such a process would bring any different results than the numerous attempts that there have been at constitutional reform and amendments.
My feeling and my belief is that after our experience at the failure of Meech, the government has had to re-examine, not only the process, but the substance of what has been debated in terms of the Constitution. Not only that, but there has been an emerging sense of urgency among the aboriginal population out there. We cannot have a country in which they are the first peoples where they, essentially, will be carved out of the Constitution.
The aboriginal population wants to feel, and does feel, that they have emerged over the last 20 years into the strongest kind of leadership which is a combination of education, experience and political moxie. We have out there 600 chiefs who are to be reckoned with. We have out there the various locals of the Metis who are to be dealt with.
We have a strong group in Manitoba. The Manitoba Metis Federation has people in it who will not allow another constitutional process to go by which would exclude them and which would not deal with their issues. The Metis, for instance, are adamant that they are going to get recognition in section 35. That will be part of their constitutional agenda.
There is a different wind blowing out there now. It is not the hot winds of Oka in 1990. It is a warm, gentle wind that is giving a velvet tap on the back of Canadian politicians saying: "Listen, there is another regime of leadership out here and it is the leadership of the first nations". We elected a new leader and that leader has something that was not there till recently, that is, a unified, complete group of people which believes that solidarity is going to be the quality or component that puts it over the edge in terms of what it can achieve. Also, there has been a real delineation of fundamental issues. These people are not talking about a proliferation of details. What they are speaking about is their political aspirations, their political representations and their inherent right to self-government being entrenched in the Constitution. Their culture and their languages have to be recognized.

Well, I remind them that the simple fact of opposing the motion-I think I heard the official spokesperson for that party say that they would vote against it, because it is not a constituent assembly-is not good enough. I tell them, Mr. Speaker, that I cannot understand that they refuse to make any compromise, that they cannot take a more reasonable position which would give Canadians a chance to make their opinions known.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments are now over. The hon. member for Saanich-Gulf Islands.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate this evening. In fact I am honoured to do so.
The Constitution of our country goes to the very essence of how we view our country. I am saddened, however, and even somewhat embittered that we have to oppose this government's proposal.
There are two reasons why we are going to be opposing this resolution of the government. First is timing and second is the composition of the committee. Let me first address the timing.
As a member of the Beaudoin-Edwards committee, we were reassured on many occasions that the government would not pre-empt the Beaudoin-Edwards committee, nor would it pre-empt the Spicer commission report. These are committees established by this government, the time frames of which were established by this government.
I have some quotes. On May 15 of this year the Prime Minister, in response to a question in the House, said: "We want to be consistent. We should wait until the reports on these massive consultations have been tabled before proceeding with a government initiative".
On May 17 the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs said: "I have no intention of judging the Beaudoin-Edwards committee report before it is received, and I have no intention of rejecting the suggestions it may contain".
The timing is a bit curious. If the timing has suddenly become inconvenient at this time and if this government refuses to listen to what these reports have to say, then what confidence can we have that it will listen to the next committee?
The second point, and the main thrust of my argument tonight, is regarding the composition of this committee: 15 members of Parliament and 10 senators. I have two words for that. It is "an insult". As a member of the Beaudoin-Edwards committee, I speak from personal experience. At the outset of our hearings I was not convinced that a constituent assembly was the way to go, although my party had advocated this as early as last summer. I too was concerned with many of the arguments being put forth from both the government and the Liberals that a constituent assembly would further denigrate our parliamentary system. As an elected member of Parliament who has a lot of respect for our parliamentary system, I did not want to contribute to that further denigration of our parliamentary system; it is too fragile.
On the Beaudoin-Edwards committee we heard a lot about what is wrong with our country and about the enormous challenges which we face constitutionally. I will give some examples: first, the whole division of powers, particularly with my interest in the environment, the jurisdictional disputes that we have been embroiled in on the environmental stage in our country. Second is the relationship with the aboriginal peoples. We just have to look back to last summer to know how fundamental that question is and how we must address it. Third is the relationship with Quebec.
These are just some of the agenda items which the next phase of the constitutional debate must address.
As I said, we heard much of what is wrong with our country. We saw much of what is right. As someone who was patriotic before becoming a member of Parliament, I can tell you my experience on the Beaudoin-Edwards committee has reinforced that patriotism. It has strengthened that patriotism. It has given a whole new definition of what patriotism is.
We saw a land of breath-taking beauty, of awesome diversity. We also saw so-called ordinary Canadians, I call them extraordinary Canadians, grappling with these very complex issues. They were an inspiration. The majority of the witnesses who came before us advocated a constituent assembly. They gave me the confidence that this new device, this dramatic departure, could
June 18, 1991

provide a way of giving us a credible process where we had none in the past.
On the antagonisms we heard so much about, which exist in our country against aboriginal people and against Quebec, I did not see those in many instances at all of those hearings and on those many long days. What I did see consistently was antagonism to politicians. People do not trust us, and with good reason.
The process which we have here has not addressed our constitutional malaise. Why do we not see it? Why do we not realize that we must have the courage to try a new way? I now believe that a constituent assembly must be made up not only of elected politicians. I respect elected politicians, some of them, most of them, but it should also include the public.
This blending of that much maligned public with the elected politicians in our country would not denigrate our parliamentary process, it would reinforce it. This is what this government and the Liberals do not seem to be able to grasp.
The government's proposal is unwilling to invite unelected Canadians to participate in the recreation of Canada unless they happen to be unelected Canadians appointed to the Senate from either the Liberal Party or the Progressive Conservative Party.
Do you not see the irony of saying that you are standing up for elected politicians when you are willing to have ten unelected political hacks included on that committee? I think that the people of Canada can certainly see the irony in that if it escapes the members opposite and the members from the Liberal Party.
It is not just the government that thinks this way. This morning the hon. member for Papineau in his remarks in this debate referred to the concept of a constituent assembly as a flight of fancy. Such arrogance is not new to Liberals and Conservatives but it is particularly offensive at a time when all politicians are being tarred with the same brush.
I wish to dissociate myself completely with such a condescending position. We must have a new way. We must have a process in which all people across the country can see themselves reflected. Obviously they now do not see themselves reflected in the government
Government Orders
or Parliament. We need a credible process. We must find a way to restore the confidence of the people in the institutions which govern them.
I have news for the old parties. Our institutions cannot be saved by ignoring the people who put us here. All we will do is further erode the public trust. Canadians want politicians to clean up the mess that politicians have created.
The Liberals and the Progressive Conservatives want to criss-cross this country one more time and then return to the safety of Ottawa to close the doors on reality and issue a report which in no way reflects the public mood.
New Democrats say the time is long past for a new approach, one which includes Canadians, not excludes them.
It is a time for courage. The situation demands courage and this is why we oppose this motion. This is not a courageous motion. This is an entrenchment of old ways demonstrated by both the government and by the Liberals. It is a demonstration of intransigent thinking.
We must have a new approach. We must have the confidence in the people of Canada that they will do the same as I did, take the problems before them and find a solution. On the Beaudoin-Edwards committee, I had the courage to change my mind on a constituent assembly. I hoped the government would do the same.
In conclusion, I want to say that Canada is not as fragile as some would have us think. It is a strong and vibrant land with strong and vibrant people. It has survived many, many things in the past. It may even survive another parliamentary committee examining the Constitution.

Mr. Speaker, I am surprised to hear the NDP talking the way they do today. Two years ago, they criticized the way Quebec had been treated in 1982 by Trudeau, Chretien and Ouellet, who signed and imposed a Constitution without the assent of Quebec. And today, these same people from the New Democratic Party who, obviously, have absolutely no knowledge of what is going on in Quebec, these same people propose a constituent

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
assembly without the Quebec National Assembly being part of it. They propose the same thing as the Liberals did in 1982 and which led to the constitutional crisis that we are in. These people say publicly and try to lead Canadians to believe that they want to help save Canada. Well, I tell you, Mr. Speaker, perhaps they are saving Canada, but it is going to be their own Canada, because Quebec will then be elsewhere, Quebec will then be a sovereign country.
I might even ask them to continue in that way. They help Quebecers understand that this country does not make any sense, which does not mean, Mr. Speaker, that English Canada does not also have a right to its own country. An English Canada looking like the NDP, that is fine with me, but they should never lead Quebecers to believe that they represent them, when they try to give them a repeat of the coup de force they did in 1982.
So, I ask them: how do they think they could sell that message to Quebecers today? Show the real face of the NDP to Quebec! I also ask the member for Chambly to go and explain to Quebecers this new vision of Canada that excludes Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, I would be only too happy to. I think that having had the experience of visiting Quebec City for the first time during this Beaudoin-Ed-wards trip and seeing the beauty of that place and listening to the very moving testimony of the witnesses from Quebec, one rings in my ears. That was the witness who said: "Bourassa does not own Quebec, nor does Parizeau own Quebec. We want a voice in the constituent assembly of Canada".
It is the old way, the old politicians which brought wrath on the heads of Quebec. We want to open up the process to get the elites out of control. The Bloc Quebecois, on its high horse and in its own parochial way, thinks it is the only one that can speak for Quebec. They do not speak for Quebec. I know that now because I heard the voice of Quebec in Quebec City.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I would just like to say that I wanted to ask a question of the member to clarify her point of view on that very issue of Quebec. But I think
her answer is very clear and I am not going to ask a question.

Mr. Speaker, I will not respond to the hon. member right now. I prefer to wait, maybe I will do so later.
But I want to ask a question of my colleague. I listened to her speech and I am pleased that she could see the real picture of Quebec while she was there. I realize also that there are a lot of people who are speaking up loud and clear for Quebec, and it is not only the Liberals who are doing it, nor the Bloc Quebecois, the NDP, or the Conservatives. There are a lot of people who do not belong to any of these political parties but who still want a certain logic, a Parliament in which they can believe.
The question I want to ask my colleague is as follows: keeping into account the work done by the Beaudoin-Edwards Committee, what are the main reasons that pushed her to change her mind on the constituant assembly, and why was she originally for or against it?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for Chambly for that question. It is a good one. I think that having seen and heard the voices of Canadians during that process, I trust Canadians. I wish that the government and the Liberals would trust them as I have learned to trust them. I think that we should have confidence in the people who send us to this wonderful place, and I wish that the government and the Liberals would trust them the way we have learned to do so.

Mr. Speaker, I have a short question for the member for Saanich-Gulf Islands.
I heard today the spokesperson for the NDP tell us that the NDP would vote against this motion. I understand that she is very upset with the process and I want to ask her if this motion is carried or passed by this House, will the NDP participate in the process?
Mr. Speaker, we will be holding caucus discussions on that very issue tomorrow morning.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Questions and comments are now terminated. Debate.
June 18, 1991

Mr. Speaker, I have spoken today but not on debate. I asked a few questions.
I would like to speak on the motion mainly because I think the question of a constituent assembly is a very important one and we have had a lot of things bandied about here today as to whether we should have a constituent assembly or not. I cannot vote for the motion without the provision for a constituent assembly.
As a parliamentarian, to exclude the public in the way that this motion does I find is arrogant and wrong.
I read a newspaper report about the Leader of the Opposition where he says: "A constituent assembly? Nobody knows what it is, how long it will take, who will be on that, will they be elected or not elected." He explained that they had one in Australia that was a great success. They debated for 13 years and reported nothing.
Well, you can have a constituent assembly that does more than nothing and, as I said before, I believe the Belanger-Campeau commission in Quebec did a great deal. I think it pretty well outlined what are the choices facing Quebecers. I was quite proud to be a Quebecer, as I am now of course, but to be in Quebec at the time that the Belanger-Campeau commission held its hearings.
I find that when you are looking at setting a commission up to study a problem as complicated and as important to a country as a Constitution is, you need to have members of that commission or that committee who are not just parliamentarians, but who are representative of the unelected.
When I am talking about the unelected, I am not talking about unclected senators. I look at the numbers we have here. We are looking at 15 plus 10. We are looking at 15 members of Parliament and 10 senators, for a total of 25. Now that is an insult to Canada because just Quebec by itself in the Belanger-Campeau commission had I believe 36 members.
Now I was impressed with the 36 members. We had members from the union side, members representing business and even representatives of the Equality Party if I am not mistaken. It was important to have all sides being heard. These are elected as well as unelected.
Government Orders
The thing here is that it worked well in Quebec, but this government does not seem to have confidence in Canadians sufficiently to the point where they would allow this to be done on a federal scale. Now that bothers me a great deal because I do not see what we would lose by having-hold on-a constituent committee or a constituent assembly in the sense of the Belanger-Campeau commission. What would we lose? The government could still try to find the best representatives of the diverse groups, unelected people but who are very good.
I was impressed by the Group of 22 which came out with a number of suggestions which were dealing primarily with decentralization, but they had their other suggestions as well which I felt, for unelected people, my god, these people were on to something. I really felt, as I feel right now, that if we can plug into Canadians and get this information, not only does the process get revitalized and democracy is well served, but we do get some good information and some things that we can deal with.
When you have people participating in this way, these are people who see the process working and then who believe in it. One of the problems with Meech Lake, and I think this is one time we should put one myth to bed, was that it was a process which appeared to be closed-door. I have heard often, these 11 men making the Constitution in a closed room one night, well that is not exactly the truth. This was really a lot of consultation over many years. This was not a closed door deal, but the perception-and we have said in politics that perception is reality-to the Canadian people was that it was. So that is what people believe it was.
If we were to have the perception as well as the reality of having an enlarged committee, as they did in Quebec, we would bring in these people. I know it will not be perfect. Who is a perfect representative for the native peoples, for women, for senior citizens and so forth, but we must make the effort, because to do otherwise we are selling ourselves short and we are certainly selling Canada short.
There are Canadians who want to participate.
I want to respond to what the Liberal member for Ottawa-Vanier said that the motion, as it stands right now, will do all of those things.

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
The motion will bring in Canadians and the government will be able to talk to these representatives and get the information from them. That is not what I am talking about. I am talking about members with power, powersharing, empowerment, people who are at the table and who are negotiating, who are talking about what they feel is important in a Constitution and have a direct say. They are not just to be patted on the head as someone who would be consulted and then told: "Okay, now go back to where you were because we are finished with you", but must have a direct say in the creation of a Constitution which is a Constitution for all the people of Canada. That is the perception and that is the reality that we want to create.
I believe that it would not be that difficult, as I said before. All we have to do is enlarge the parameters, all we have to do is add in the motion of the government a form of constituent assembly or a constituent committee. I am sure that we could seriously consider that. We just do not want people consulted in a very unserious manner, a manner where people would not really have any power whatsoever, where they would just be used and, I think to a certain degree, abused.
When examining the question of membership, the numbers of members on this committee, if we look at 15 elected parliamentarians, 10 unelected senators, we are really not dealing with that many people. When we are drafting rules for a Constitution, the Constitution that we are going to be living with for many, many years while at the same time trying to deal with the separatist threat from Quebec, we have to be more serious than just having 15 parliamentarians and 10 unelected senators.
I do not have a partisan objection to the Senate per se. I just feel that if we are going to have unelected people on it they should be people from the constituencies, people who have a certain amount of competence in their area of concern. I believe that, as we are talking more and more these days about decentralizing government services and decentralizing the way we deliver these services and the way we govern, it is a good way to show our good will to the people of Canada by asking them to be active participants on the committee.
I do not believe that choosing this pathway instead of what the government in its motion has chosen is going to cause the government a great deal of problems. I feel all the government side has to do, as I said before, is just amend its motion and just make some kind of an effort to
include a constituent committee. It must ensure that it is one with power and that it represents people from communities who have, as I said before, a particular competence in their area.
I want to respond to what my colleague from Ottawa- Vanier said about the NDP's failing to be on side or not being a team player. That affects me particularly because I can remember the same criticism when I was in the United States and I was against the war in Vietnam. I said I had reasons why I was against it. There is a kind of love it or leave it. You have to be a team player or you are off. I left it. I felt it was wrong.
I am not going to leave the debate here today. This debate is an essential one about democracy. It is about bringing the power to the people. On something that is as important as a Constitution-I cannot even believe I am here arguing in favour of a constituent assembly or a constituent committee, a kind of Belanger-Campeau enlarged, to a government composed of a large number of members from Quebec. I cannot believe that I have to tell them what they should know almost in a reflex manner. Yet, here I am saying: "We did it in Quebec". We do not have to be team players. All we have to do is expose the logic and the pragmatism of such a decision on the government's part. If it were to include a constituent assembly or a constituent committee, it would be very pragmatic.
I believe that through a constituent assembly we can bring in people from the Caisse Populaire, we can bring in people from the unions. In Quebec, particularly, we can bring in people from the grassroots who want to participate.
I do not believe for one minute that sovereignty is inevitable, as my colleague from Lac-Saint-Jean said earlier. I do not believe the separation of Quebec from Canada is inevitable.
I believe that, through including people from Quebec who are knowledgeable in their respective areas, we can deal with the question of the threat of separatism. That is the best way to deal with it. Not hollering insults here in the House or one party against the other or saying: "You have to play ball. You have to be on the team". This is not a team sport. We are talking about the future of our country. I am talking about a very pragmatic suggestion made by my party that we have a form of a constituent assembly or a constituent committee in order
June 18, 1991

to include Quebec, to include people who have never had a voice.
I am not talking about appealing to what I call the constitutional cottage industry of professionals who come before the committee and who oftentimes-I guess it is no longer publish or perish, I think it is testify before a committee or subcommittee or perish. I am not talking about these people, although there are many who are good and who are doing their job well. I am talking about the people who are not normally part of the power structure, who do not have a voice and who must have one.
In conclusion, do not mistake the position of the NDP for one of partisanship and do not mistake our motion as something which is going to be difficult to apply. It is not going to be difficult. It can be done. It is very pragmatic. It has been done in Quebec. We have seen the fruit of that. Just simply try. If you do not try and say: "Well, it is our way or no way", then you force us as a party to vote against your way because your way, in our humble opinion, is not the democratic way.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Chambly for having had the courage tonight to give his own personal opinion about the process that led to the negotiation and the signing of the Meech Lake Accord.
I know from first-hand experience that a lot of people have presented the signing of this accord and what happened subsequently as being something which happened between 11 men in a room. He has had the courage tonight to say that that is not true. I choose the word "courage" to describe his affirmation, because he is directly contradicting, as we all know in this House, the leader of his own party, the member for Yukon. She is one of the persons in this country who repeatedly propagates in her speeches and in different interventions the myth he has had the courage to confront and destroy tonight. I want to congratulate him for having had the courage to take on the leader of his own party in that respect. I think I agree with him. I know it is difficult for any member of Parliament to directly contradict on the
Government Orders
floor of the House of Commons most of the members of his or her own party and the leader of his own party.
I want to say that I disagree profoundly with him on what the concept of democracy should be in the case of a constituent assembly. I have heard members allude to the fact that there is some absence of legitimacy because a House of Commons committee is struck. I disagree with that. I fundamentally disagree with that. Members, by making that argument, diminish the importance of our basic institutions in our country, our democratic institutions.
The truth of the matter is that this Parliament and the members who sit in this Parliament, no matter what their leanings may be-and that includes the Bloc Quebecois, the Reform Party, the Liberal Party and the Conservative Party- have been democratically elected by the people of Canada to this institution. It is the basic democratic institution in our land out of which a parliamentary committee is formed, and members go on to do their work. That is the way the British parliamentary system has worked. It has worked successfully, and I think what we are undertaking to do through this committee is very much in line with that.
I have difficulty with the member's argument when he says that we can open up the process. I think he would recognize that at the end of the day, in the spirit of democracy and in recognition of the institutions that have served us so well and that are there now, it is the National Assembly of Quebec that speaks for the people of Quebec in the areas of jurisdiction which are now attributed to it.
If we are in some difficulty today, I would argue that it is because in 1982, when we patriated our Constitution, an argument was made that the government of the day in Quebec because it was a Parti Quebecois government was not a legitimate government and that for some reasoning the federal members of Parliament elected from Quebec spoke for the National Assembly in their areas of jurisdiction. I think that is the fundamental error that led to the constitutional difficulty we are in today.
Whatever the process may be, I think that at the end of the day members of this House have to recognize that it would be the National Assembly of Quebec that will

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
choose in which way it will proceed in the name of the people who elected its members.
Where I have some difficulty is that the National Assembly and the Government of Quebec have clearly said that they will not participate in a constituent assembly. The member may not like that, but to proceed otherwise would mean that they would eliminate from the process the province of Quebec. I cannot understand how he comes to that conclusion. He speaks of Belang-er-Campeau. Belanger-Campeau did not propose that the National Assembly or the province of Quebec participate in a national constituent assembly. Belanger-Campeau did not do that.
I ask the hon. member: How can he say that today when he knows very well that what he proposes would eliminate 25 per cent of Canada's population?

Mr. Speaker, in an editorial published in Le Devoir, Lise Bissonnette clearly states that Quebec is waiting for proposals from the rest of Canada. Now is the time for the rest of Canada, all of us, all the other provinces, to decide how we wish to change the Constitution and what proposals we can offer to Quebecers.
In her editorial, Lise Bissonnette says that Quebec is certainly waiting for us, the rest of Canada, to try to solve our problems together. After reading her editorial, I also agree that we must do just that. Let us see how we can improve the Constitution, how we can change the federal system so that Quebec could better fit in.
I see no problem with that. I also recall that, in 1981-1982, when the Constitution was repatriated, Quebec indeed suffered a coup de force, but do you remember who was among those who rejoiced most, who even congratulated Messrs. Chretien, Trudeau and company? Yes, Brian Mulroney. If one reads carefully the speech he delivered immediately after the repatriation of the Canadian Constitution, one sees that Brian Mulroney was in the same boat as Chretien, Trudeau and company.
So, be careful when speaking of coup de force. I clearly remember that one. Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that I know it is always risky to offend or oppose one's leader. I will choose my words carefully, Mr. Speaker, I have said that perception is tantamount to reality.
According to a certain perception, eleven persons participated in the Meech Lake process and tried to satisfy the five basic demands of Quebec, and we were all under the impression that they were the only people involved. Reality was different. However that perception was shared by my leader, several members of my party, and most Canadians.
So, it did not require so much courage. I simply wanted to clarify the facts.

Very well, Mr. Speaker. I would like to ask my colleague if he recognizes that the real voices for Quebec, now, are the National Assembly, Premier Bou-rassa, and Mr. Parizeau, Leader of the Opposition.

With pleasure, Mr. Speaker. I think that the real voice for Quebec, is now the National Assembly, of course. I have no quarrel with that, but it is not only Mr. Parizeau, it is all the political parties that make up the National Assembly. Finally, I have also in mind the people who have been elected to this Parliament, the Bloc Quebecois, the only NDP member in Quebec, the Liberals or the Conservatives. They too represent Quebec, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands -
Canso): Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see that this resolution has finally come before the House. I am glad to see that this government has finally brought forward a mechanism for resolving the constitutional impasse that has for the past year and more sapped our will as a nation. I am glad that finally the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs has launched, as he declared in his remarks this morning, the Canada round of constitutional renewal.
We can quibble about the details. We can argue about the number of members who should be on this committee. We can argue about when the committee should report. We on this side of the House have made suggestions about that. We have made recommendations as to the process that the committee should undertake. We have made suggestions in a spirit of being constructive for dealing with this very important and critical process of constitutional renewal.
June 18, 1991

However, it is essential-and our leader has been saying it for months now -that Canadians finally come to the point of resolving this constitutional impasse.
What I think has so dissipated our will as a nation over the last several months has not been so much the substance of constitutional change. If we look at the points of differences among the parts of Canada, between Quebecers and Canadians elsewhere in Canada, between Canadians in the west and Canadians in the east, between aboriginal Canadians and the rest of Canadians, what separates us as people are really not profound in a constitutional sense. With a certain will to resolve these differences, the points of constitutional differences are really minor when we look at them in the broad scheme of things.
One irony has constantly been referred to by observers of the Canadian scene as they watch Canadians and their governments torture themselves with constitutional wrangling, as we have over these last several months. They continue to remind us that Canada is rich in resources and really the envy of all the world. People everywhere, millions of people from all over the world, would happily give everything they own in order to have the privilege of living here. Refugees are lined up and are back-logging our refugee system in order to be allowed to come and live in Canada. The irony is that a country with this potential is spending so much energy wrestling with fine and rather insignificant constitutional points of difference. Much of our problems as a society has been amplified and magnified by being brought into a constitutional discussion.
I think that that is really what is at the bottom to a large degree of the difficulties that we have faced as a country in the last several months and perhaps the last several years, although I think in the period preceding Meech Lake that problem has been exemplified.
What I think happened was that in an attempt, and I think give the Prime Minister credit, as he saw it to bring Quebec into the constitutional family, he raised the stakes to such a level and raised the level of the consequences of a failure in producing agreement to such a high pitch that an agreement, first of all, was virtually, as it turned out, impossible and the consequences, the fall-out from that failure to produce
Government Orders
agreement, was so dramatic that it has really taken months for Canadians to recover from that process. Really, I think that that is one of the sad facts which has surrounded the whole Meech Lake process.
In the period following the failure of the Meech Lake Accord when, of course, Quebec retreated and took it very badly that the accord was not signed, the acrimony has been perpetuated, I believe, by the discussions which followed in the months after Meech Lake.
I think it is important that finally we are setting forth some mechanism. I agree, it is probably imperfect, but at least there is some mechanism in there that we can begin to deal with the substance of constitutional reform and to I think de-dramatize the issues, and as we have so often said, certainly as our leader has so often said, be able to put this affair behind us so that we can begin to deal with the other more pressing problems of the country.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak for a few moments as an Acadian. As you know, one of the very important aspects of these constitutional discussions is culture and especially the desire of the people of Quebec to have control over the protection of their language and culture.
Mr. Speaker, I can easily understand where that will to acquire the levers of power in linguistic and cultural matters and to protect their language and culture comes from. I am not a Quebecer. I am an Acadian, and for four centuries, since they came to Canada, Acadians have waged a constant battle to protect and preserve their language and their culture. We have managed to do that in spite of very difficult circumstances. Those who know the history of Canada know about the deportation of Acadians; they know that we were scattered all over the United States and that when we came back to Canada, we settled in various parts of the Maritimes, and they know the consequences that that fact had on the survival of our population.
I come from a part of Cape Breton where for three generations now, we have seen the gradual disappearance of the French language, which was currently spoken in some villages. We have always had to fight to preserve our language in our small villages.

June 18, 1991

Government Orders
For example, my maternal grandfather and grandmother did not speak English. My mother and father spoke French, but nowhere near as much as my grand parents. Those of my generation, myself, my sisters and brothers, my cousins, we were almost completely assimilated. We did not speak French at all. I had to learn it over again, since I did not speak French when I was younger.
So you know, Mr. Speaker, that we have lived with the problem of assimilation and that we must always cope with it outside Quebec and inside Canada. I can tell you that it is thanks to the programs and the will of the central government of the country named Canada that we were able to preserve our language and our culture in our region, and proudly keep our language alive at home.
I think we must not forget that, especially when we speak of preserving French, what we are all anxious to do in Canada. I think that all the Canadians are proud to be part of a society with two official languages, and we are proud of that because everyone knows, all over Canada, that this fact makes us different as a society and that it helps preserve the French language and culture in Quebec.
If the francophones outside Quebec think seriously about the aim which everybody agrees with, the preservation of their language and culture, they will see like others did the only way to maintain a French society in Quebec as well as outside Quebec is to be part of a strong Canada, a Canada with these two languages. This is one of the reasons, one of the elements at the origin of the constitutional debate.
However, we must avoid to over dramatize the constitutional issue. Mr. Speaker, this is a very important and interesting motion that is before the House.
The motion deals with the setting up of a committee to look into making recommendations to Parliament and the Government of Canada on proposals for a renewed Canada.
As you will recall, in the original document which was agreed to by all of the provinces, the original document I am referring to was the document which was signed by the former premier of Newfoundland, the Lion. Brian Peckford.
There was a clause in that constitutional agreement which said that every year there would be a review of the jurisdiction of the federal government in one of our primary resources, which was the fishery. However, consequently, after that signing took place, that particular clause was removed, it was no longer there. It was removed because it was thought by certain premiers, after what they said were consultations with the fishing industry, that the jurisdiction of the federal government should not be questioned on the business of the fishing industry.
I want to put on the record my concern that this particular item must be revisited. It must be examined, impartially, by the members of Parliament and the senators who are on this committee, from the point of
view that it is constitutionally unworkable to have provincial governments with total jurisdiction over fish plants and the federal government with total jurisdiction over the fish.
In other words, everything presently under our present Constitution that happens on land is in the total jurisdiction of the provincial governments. Everything that happens in the water or on top of the water, in the ocean, is under the total jurisdiction of the federal government.
The problem we have today in Canada, in this primary industry of the fishery, is we have fish plants that are closing under provincial jurisdiction under the Constitution because the federal government is cutting back on the quotas, that is the amount of fish that can be fed into those fish plants to keep them operating. Obviously, this is an unworkable situation.
The provincial governments, it is said, went too far in giving approvals to have numerous fish plants built around the coastline of eastern Canada in the past 10 years.
It is cited by many experts that that is why now there are so many fish plants in trouble and that is why they are closing: because the provincial governments have total control over the issuing of all licences for onshore facilities.
The fact of the matter is that the federal government today sits down. The people responsible sit down in the federal government. They make the decisions on fish quotas and how much fish will be caught by Canadian fishermen, by what boats, by what companies, and in what manner.
In other words, the federal government determines on an annual basis whether or not fish plants will be open in Quebec, in New Brunswick, in Nova Scotia, in Prince Edward Island and in Newfoundland, and in British Columbia. The federal government is in total control over that.
I noticed just the other day some good news for the Canadian fishery. Here I must give some credit to the federal government. I have not ever given the federal government, this present government, any credit for anything it has done in the fishery because, as you know,
I have a great objection to this government issuing

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has raised many subjects in his question. He has raised many subjects and I would need, as any member would, hours to address each one of them.
I might suggest to the hon. member in his suggestion on the constituent assembly idea that the first constituent assembly that we had in Canada was what was called the National Assembly in 1947. The hon. gentleman might be surprised that I remember this quite well. In 1947, '48 and '49 a constituency assembly met in the nation of Newfoundland to consider the options. It talked for three long years. There were campaigns and every evening around the radio-we had no television in those days-everybody would tune in and you would always go to the house of someone who had a radio, a battery radio. Not everybody had a radio, and the batteiy would only last for so long because there was no electricity. You would go to this person's house, tune in and listen to the recording of the day's proceedings on these very large long playing recordings at 78 rpm.
For three years those discussions went on in that constituent assembly. They went on and there was a final vote taken. It was a fascinating thing to listen to. After those three years-the point I am getting at is this-of discussion, the National Assembly, the constituent assembly of representatives from all over the province decided against even looking at Canada, after three years. It did not want to look at Canada.
Do you know how Newfoundland became part of Canada? Do you know what happened, Mr. Speaker? What happened was that the advocates for joining Canada went around with a petition to all Newfoundlanders outside of the constituent assembly and got permission to place union with Canada as one of the options on the ballot for the national referendum which took place in the province of Newfoundland.

I want to quote from my speech on that night when I
said:
Let me begin by saying that I too believe it is important to get the signature of the Quebec Government on the Canadian Constitution. However, it is not sufficient a priority that nothing else matters. The real priority is a good and sound Constitution for Canada.
Near the end of my speech I said:
I favour the recognition of Quebec as a distinct society in order to protect the language and culture of Quebec. But the Meech Lake Accord goes beyond Quebec's distinctiveness. This is the essence of the Accord for me. -share a greater loyalty to Canada than the sum of the loyalties toward the provinces. That is the flaw in the Meech Lake Accord and that is why it has to be rejected.

We have to insist on national standards for social programs. That is how we get medicare. That is how we will get national child care in the future, day care. That is how we will get national environmental programs. We have to lead the fight on that.
Second, at the same time we have to stand up for a distinct society in Quebec. It will not be easy to say that all across Canada. Quebec is distinct. It has been distinct since 1774. Quebec is where the French language is predominant. The civil code is a distinct legal system. Quebec has its own pension plan. Quebec collects its own income tax. Quebec has a special agreement on immigration with Canada. We should not be afraid to recognize Quebec as a distinct society.
How far do we go? If we want to face the real question, how far do we go to accommodate Quebec? I think the answer to that is: We go some distance without sacrificing Canada and its institutions in the process. There is a line, but as an English Canadian politician who voted against Meech Lake I want to say clearly tonight that we want Quebec in Canada. We need Quebec in Canada. We are prepared to make the reasonable accommodations to have Quebec in Canada. It will take some courage to say that in western Canada and in other parts of Canada.
Third, I think a great contribution we can make in the debate is to keep insisting, as we did in 1981-82, that aboriginal peoples have a real place in this Constitution. It is their Constitution too. We should insist that they not only be part of the constituent assembly but that they be in fact a part of the Constitution in the sense of recognizing self-government.
I want to conclude by a quote from Tom Berger, a former judge who was speaking in Calgary at the Mart-land lectures. I quote: "I want to see Canada survive with Quebec. Staying together is important not only to ourselves. If people of different languages, cultures, races and religions can live together harmoniously within a great federal state, perhaps they may learn to live together harmoniously in a wider world. In Canada, we have democratic institutions. Et je dis cela au Bloc quebccois, we have democratic institutions, the rule of law, and an educated populace. If we cannot find a way to live, what peoples, what nations can?
Quebec, like English Canada, has a stake in the survival of these ideas in the world. I think he is right.
Let me conclude, if I might, by saying that we advocate a new process, a radical process, a different and creative process, as the member for Yukon said, to include Canadians, to have a constituent assembly, to get a framework of constitutional ideas, to take that perhaps to the people and then to Parliament, and we will have a new Constitution for Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with care and did not interrupt my friend for Port Moody-Coquitlam, but I should say that while I do not agree with his point of view I know that all of us bring with us our certain political philosophy into the debate. As much as we want to be non-partisan, we carry that with us.
What disappoints me about his remarks is that he camouflaged them so much in his speech. I think the true philosophy of my friend is the one which he expressed during his leadership race, about two years ago I think it was. I watched him on local cablevision here in Ottawa. I had the thrill of watching my friend as he was contending for the leadership of his party, and he said that the Meech Lake Accord had to be defeated because it was a threat to the future of the welfare state.
That is the bottom line for this member. I wish he would come clean with all of us and say that is his obsession with any kind of government structure, that he wants to preserve the welfare state and the future of the welfare state. Aside from a very pessimistic view of the future of Canada, to make that the ultimate goal, what bothers me is that he stands here tonight and says: "We want Quebec, we want Quebec". However he sacrificed it a year ago in order to preserve the structure of a welfare state.
I wonder if the member would tell us tonight if that is still his bottom line, that regardless of what structure we have, whether it is a constituent assembly that he proposes and very few other people want or whatever, the format is for coming to a decision as to the future structure of the political system in Canada, whether his bottom line still is the preservation of a welfare state.

May I please respond. I might say that the member mentioned he had the thrill of watching me

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
on local cable television. I am sorry, I did not realize that suffered from insomnia and needed my help to put him to sleep.
My bottom line is not a welfare state. Of course I am partisan and biased and I have my positions, and I will set them out in a minute. I want to preserve a civilized Canada.
Hear, hear.

That is what I want to preserve. I think Canada is a civilized country and I think this government is destroying Canada, quite frankly. With the combination of Meech Lake, with the decentralizing forces to the provinces, taking the power away from the national government and letting the provinces into the federal institutions to control the Senate, to control the court, to have the premiers conference institutionalized, and so on, I think is going to incapacitate the federal government.
That is what his party wants to do. It believes in room for capital. It really believes in less government. That is his position, that is his bias and his government. People say: "The Prime Minister does not have any vision". I think he does have a vision. He wants to deregulate, to privatize-
A corporate vision.

It is a corporate vision of Canada and it is wrecking this country. You decentralize the way Meech was doing, and then you add to it the free trade deal in which Canadians start looking north-south instead of east-west, and gradually all those national institutions and the rope that holds Canada together begins to slip. We can see it happening. We are losing this country.
I have my biases like he has his biases. I want to see a civilized Canada with good social services. That is what makes Canada different from the United States. That is what makes us a great country. That is why they said we are second only to Japan in being the greatest country in the world to live in, but his government is taking it apart. I pushed and I will continue to push for a strong government which can hold Canada together, one government which acts for Canada and is above the sum of its parts.
Mr. Speaker, in all the years that I have been sitting in Parliament, I have tried to understand the philosophy of the New Democratic Party.
It's impossible!

I have made considerable efforts. I have a lot of respect for the New Democratic Party, I have a lot of respect for most of the hon. members sitting on that side; those people have a notion of what Canada could be.
Very briefly, since I know I have only a few minutes, I would like to ask the hon. member, as well as all those who are watching me from the other side-I have circled their names but perhaps I should not name them-but I ask them to try to understand, as I was saying this afternoon, what Canada is all about. What could make us build a country called Canada?
For 27 years-and I ask the hon. member to think about it-for 27 years, ever since I have been a member of Parliament, I have welcomed here hundreds of young people every year.

I hear from hundreds of young people each year for 27 years. Sometimes I do not know how to explain Canada, so I invite them for a walk around Parliament and show them what Canada is all about by showing them three monuments. "Go behind the Library of Parliament", I say that to English Canada.

I tell those who speak French not to get angry if, when speaking about Canada, I prefer to do it in English because those are the ones I have to convince that this country is worth saving. Go around. I almost apologize to my fellow French-speaking compatriots, but since Mr. Bouchard now does it with elegance, so do I.

Go and see the first monument behind the Library on the Senate side. Why are there monuments to two people there, Baldwin and Lafontaine? It goes back a long way.
By the way, I asked the Speaker to have their names reprinted because they have faded over the years, and it is shocking. I hope tonight that Public Works and others
June IS, 1991

will make sure to reprint the names of Baldwin and Lafontaine. That was the spirit of prior Canada.
Then go back, as I said this afternoon: Why is it that we have those two monuments? Parliament is only supposed to honour Prime Ministers. I say to English Canada to come here and go around Parliament. I say to the NDP member that he should go around Parliament tonight and ask why there are two monuments, Baldwin and Lafontaine, together. In 1867 there was Mr. Cartier and Mr. Macdonald. This is not supposed to be, but that was the spirit of what built Canada.
I say that to the millions of new Canadians whom I have always defended, whom I always will defend for their pride, like mine. They must understand the history of Canada, and the history of Canada is right here on the Hill.
We do not need to go to the library. We do not need to be a scholar to understand the spirit of Canada. Go around the building tonight and you will see Cartier and Macdonald. One was a Prime Minister; the other one was not. Yet they are there together.
Go behind the library, young colleagues and friends. I am not aggressive, but when you talk about Canada I cannot do otherwise but say; "Open your eyes. Go back to the spirit and the rest will follow, but go back first to the spirit of what built this country".
What built this country was an entente. Call it an agreement, call it a pact, call it a law, call it what you want. Constitutionalists will make a debate on each of the words I have used tonight. I am not interested, even though I have some experience in law but never practised in reality.
I am not interested. Canadians are not interested. They want to have a country that works, that functions, in which people are not the same. First we have to go back to the beginning, the history of Canada, the spirit of Canada. Dear colleagues, and I could name Mr. Friesen, Mr. Domm, Mr. Vankoughnet, Mr. Horner, Madam Feltham and others, please, all of you, just walk around Parliament before you go and get your inspiration there. Come back tomorrow morning. Get your inspiration and you will see that if we all make an effort to go back to the

spirit that built this country, we will show the rest of the world.
The rest of the world will know that together we can have a different kind of country in which Marcel Prud'h-omme will remain Marcel Prud'homme and Benno Friesen, with whom I fought vigorously on certain issues, will remain Benno Friesen. Horner, who I see there, will remain Horner. With all due kindness, as I always say, the Paproskis of Canada will remain the Paproskis of Canada.

speechtext: I do not think that really requires a reply, but I will allow 30 seconds. The hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam.

I am delighted, and I want to thank the hon. member for Saint-Denis who is respected in this House for his wisdom. He asked me to go and look at the statues of two great Canadians, and I accept his invitation. Perhaps we could go together after the debate.

Mr. Speaker, earlier, I heard an NDP member explain that as a member of the Beaudoin-Edwards Committee, she had been to Quebec city for the first time in her life, and that all of a sudden she understood -Imagine what that says about this committee: A member from the West who goes to Quebec City for the first time and all of a sudden understands - A revelation from Heaven? A revelation, my eye! No wonder the New Democratic Party has lost touch with Quebec, a New Democratic Party that wants a constituent assembly without Quebec, without the Quebec National Assembly, and that claims to understand Quebedlt is just a repeat of the political manoeuvre by Chretien and Ouellet in 1982. You are making the same costly mistake that shocked so many Quebecers, but you don't seem to realize what you are doing. However, I have known you for the past seven years I have been here.
Basically, you are good people and good Canadians. I think you just don't understand what is happening in Quebec, because these people live in other provinces. Am I going to blame them because I don't want a country in their image? Of course not. Let them have a country in their own image. I hope they will have the kind of country they want, with the laws they want, with their own culture and their own traditions and their own

June 18, 1991

language. And we in Quebec will also have our own country with our own culture, our traditions, our language and our business.
Never!

Not never, my friend from Western Canada, but soon. Soon we will have our own country, because this country is two countries. These are two totally different visions of the same country. Since the conference in Victoria 20 years ago, we have had 20 years of constitutional negotiations and we are no further than we were then. We were unable to come up with an amending formula except in 1982, but this was at the expense of Quebec. That was the last time. It was the second, the first and the last time because this will never happen again, whatever the NDP may think, whatever the Conservatives, the Anglo establishment party of this country may think, whatever Jean Chretien may think, who has just concocted an agreement today with the Conservatives, probably another plot to shaft Quebec.
This, Mr. Speaker, is entirely unacceptable to Quebecers. For 20 years -and the hon. member for Saint-Denis who has been here for 27 years has seen quite a few constitutional conferences. He saw Quebec's Premiers try to make some headway, starting with Duplessis, Lesage, Johnson, Bertrand, Bourassa, Levesque, and now again Bourassa, but they never got anywhere. And you really think we are going to go on like this? We are bankrupting this country and Quebec as a result of this situation.
In the 70s, to buy peace and camouflage the fact that Canada was coming apart at the seams, Trudeau started borrowing billions and billions and gave a few hundred million to Newfoundland and a few hundred million to the West to mollify the farmers and to the Maritimes, a little bit to Quebec, mostly peanuts. Today, in 1991, we have a country that is in debt to the tune of more than $400 billion. Mr. Speaker, do you have any idea how many zeros that is? Four hundred billion dollars worth of deficit? This year we are going to pay nearly $45 billion in interest alone. While Canadians are paying $110 billion in taxes, $45 billion of that amount is used to pay the interest on the debt. Why? Because we have not been able to deal with the fundamental problem in this country which is the Constitution. Because we keep
tiying to solve a problem that is impossible to solve. Everything has been tried: the strong arm method a la Trudeau and the conciliatory method d la Mulroney. All Quebec Premiers have tried. We have tried any number of things, but it was no use.
Today, we spent the whole day talking, not about what Quebecers would like to talk about the economy, jobs and the environment no, we still hear people of good will say that after 20 years, we have to persevere like the bull in front of a 20-foot thick wall who keeps saying: It doesn't matter, we will get through somehow. This has got to stop. We can no longer afford to go on like this. Quebecers can no longer afford to ignore the real problems.
The time will come when people will have to decide. In Quebec, we made our decision. In Quebec, we appointed the Belanger-Campeau Commission. Thirty-six people, eighteen elected and eighteen representatives of all groups of Quebec society. The unions were represented. Business was represented. We were generous. We even let Andre Ouellet in. Not bad. We even let Jean-Pierre Hogue go to the Commission. Of course, he didn't speak. When he did, it wasn't worth much, but in any case, we let him come as a representative of the Progressive Conservative Party. We even let Lucien Bouchard from the Bloc Quebecois in. At the Commission, he managed to establish a consensus. The consensus, Mr. Speaker, is on a referendum on sovereignty, by October 1992. If you want to know what is going on, it takes more than just a short visit to Quebec City like the hon. member for the NDP thinks she got a revelation from heaven, like Mr. Ryan.
Come and live in Quebec for a month, even just two weeks. Come and visit the countryside in my riding of Megantic-Compton- Stanstead. Come and see us. The people will tell you themselves that they are tired of governments like this one, of their beating about the bush, of measures that achieve nothing.
The people of Quebec cannot stand it anymore. I remember, during the 1983-84 campaign, Mr. Mulroney was travelling across the province-back in those days, we thought he was going to be so great -and referring to the Liberals as "those 74 morous".

Mr. Speaker, I want to say to my friends in English Canada that they have the right to have their own country. Sovereignty is not a concept too difficult to understand. Sovereignty, Mr. Speaker, is the right to pass your own laws. It is normal to make your own laws, to collect your own taxes and to reach agreements.
In Quebec, we make our own laws in about half of the total jurisdictions. We have our own taxes. We already have international agreements. I think we would be able to take the same responsibilities, but in all jurisdictions. Once English Canada has the right to pass its own laws, to preserve its own traditions, its own culture, I see nothing wrong in the fact that Quebec and English Canada, Upper Canada and Lower Canada as we used to say in the past, join together and build an agreement
based not on our differences, as we have been trying to do for the last 25 or 30 years, but try to build an agreement, a superstructure as a Premier calls it, or other kinds of agreements based on our similarities, Mr. Speaker. Mr. Speaker, it really is a sad moment in this House to hear the member of the Bloc Quebecois. I do not believe his comments reflect at all the sentiment of the majority of Quebecers who, like the constituents of London East, are proud of this country's heritage, proud of what this country has done for each and every one of us.
I do not believe that this member speaks for anybody other than himself. It really is hypocritical, because last year not only he, but his leader, accepted the largesse of the Canadian people and the Government of Canada. In fact, his leader from Lac-Saint-Jean accepted $800 million for his riding to get into this House of Commons in a by-election. Really, the Canadian people have been more generous to the member than he has been to the Canadian people tonight. It is absolutely unbelievable that a member in this House can speak of this country in such a fashion.
I believe that this member is stuck in a time warp. This country has been built on generosity and tolerance from all people, from Quebec, the west, Atlantic Canada and Ontario. That is what has built this country. I am not at all sure that he reflects the sentiments of the majority of Canadians at all.
Let me ask him one simple little question. The Bloc Quebecois essentially wants a Quebec without Canada, very much like its counterpart, the Reform Party, which wants a Canada without Quebec. I want to ask him how he can reconcile the fact that he wants the good things of Canada, such as our dollar, our trade, and the economic links to this country and yet is prepared to disavow himself of all the good things that have built this country over the past 124 years.

Hear, hear.
June 18, 1991
Of course, we are ready to pay a portion of the huge federal debt which we inherited from that wonderful Canadian federalism.

I have a comment tonight about how the Quebec National Assembly speaks for francophones. It is true in Quebec. It is a provincial government and it speaks for the majority in Quebec. There has been a tradition in Canada, enunciated by Henri Bourassa and Sir Wilfrid Laurier, that in the federal House, Quebecers and federal politicians have a responsibility for the French fact and francophone rights throughout Canada. That was the dream of Henri Bourassa and Sir Wilfrid Laurier. It is wrong to say that this House does not play a role in protecting the French language and the French fact. Someone has to say that. It is a revisionist view of history.

Does he not realize that if there is separation there will not be representation by Quebec in a federal bank because the bank will be controlled by English Canadians in the new country of English Canada and Quebecers would have no control over it? Is it not misleading the Quebec people by saying that separation will be easy? Quebec would not be in a federal bank. There would not be a common currency. There would be some question as to whether his farmers would get access to markets in the rest of Canada. So, why are you misleading the Quebec people on this?

You tell me that the Bank of Canada would be controlled by English Canada. That would not be very different from the present situation. The Bank of Canada serves the interests of Toronto. Look at all the decisions that the Bank of Canada took to help Toronto, to bring the inflation down in Toronto; it had an extremely negative impact on the economy of Quebec and of Montreal. Look what is done in research and development. It's always done in favour of Toronto. You, New Democrats, a party mainly based on regional interests out of Toronto, should be able to understand that Quebec has been a victim for many years. We have thought for a long time that by reforming the Constitu-

We are debating tonight a motion to create a committee of this House and members of the Senate, with some provisions to include other people, to discuss further proposals for a Canadian Constitution. This committee will finally receive in September the proposal from the Government of Canada in terms of what we see as their proposal for the future of this country.
I appreciated the comments made earlier by the member for Saint-Denis who very passionately told the
House about his vision and what he saw as some of the sense and origin of this country and from where he gets his vision. I would like to share with him an equal vision of this country. As I travel through the part of the country that I represent, I see a vision of my country through the mountains, the forests, the rivers, the people who live and work in that world, and I understand what he said about Parliament and what it should be in this country.
I suggest to any member who has wanted to try and shape this country through a career in politics to go past the Peace Tower when it is lit up at night and feel like one very lucky person to have had a chance to share in the debate about the future of Canada. I would hope that all Canadians who from time to time watch the debates on television, or those Canadians who have an opportunity to come to Ottawa to see their capital, that when they see the Peace Tower it means more than just the top part of a building where a bunch of politicians are trying to figure out how to run the country. The Peace Tower should stand for something in this country, for peace, for unity in Canada, and for their own vision of what our country is trying to establish.
I think it is important that there is intense debate in the country and in this House between our members, members of the Bloc Quebecois, and others. I would hope that we would want to fight over Canada. I would hope it would be important enough-that we would be passionate enough-to have the sense to really fight for what we believe. Thank goodness that people do have some emotion about the country. It would be terrible if this Chamber passed in one sitting all of the stages necessary to pass a Constitution in this country. What a boring thing that would be if we treated our Constitution in that way.
I do not think we should have to apologize if members in this House and people across the country get emotional about what they believe in and what our country should stand for. I am glad about that because clearly those people believe in something, as we should as well.
What are we doing with this committee? I would say that it is with some regret that we speak on this motion presented by the government. Since the failure last June of the Meech Lake Accord, we have had very intense

discussions led by the Prime Minister.
