That was just a year ago, but that has been a long time in terms of the debate we had in the country on the Constitution.
I say with respect for all of the comments made by learned members and with the effort made by my leader and my party in terms of outlining a broader process to involve more Canadians in the constitutional process, I would hope that after a year we might have done a little more, that maybe tonight rather than debating what may end up to be-we hope it becomes more than that-yet another parliamentary committee. It is unfortunate that tonight we could not have been debating and fine-tuning perhaps the components and aspects of a constituent assembly that I think would go some distance toward showing Canadians that not only do we respect the advice and opinions of Canadians from all walks of life, members of Parliament, members of legislative assemblies, representatives of local governments-a group quite often missed in this debate-but that we want them to be part of a process. A little goes a long way when it comes to showing Canadians that we are prepared to consider their views when we are writing and dealing with the Constitution of Canada.
If there is one constant that we will be faced with from now on, that constant is the change in our Constitution. This is not something that will be resolved by September or the fall of next year, or into 1993 with a spring election. We have the ability to change and to amend our Constitution at home on our own, now.
Others were here before in that historic debate when we brought home, as it was said, our Constitution. So, change is with us constantly now and we have to be prepared to deal with that.
I have mentioned some of the groups that I think can and should be involved in this debate. I have talked about members of legislative assemblies, and I have talked about local governments. Their voice has not been heard a lot lately. I also want to mention because it is so important that aboriginal people in this country have their role as well in the makeup and the writing of our Constitution. We cannot allow another failure in that
Government Orders
area. I hope we have a commitment from this House and others that that will in fact be the case.
We have had an example, one small step perhaps, but an example of what a government can do. I am referring of course to the recent announcement by the Government of Ontario that has signed a statement of a political relationship with the First Nations of Ontario. The Ontario government has done what the President of the Privy Council and the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs ought to be doing as they continue their discussions with the legitimate leadership of the national aboriginal organizations. Our member who represents Port Albemi has spoken eloquently on this issue previously in the House.
I would hope that as we consider this motion and the debate that we are having that we do look beyond the confines of the rules as we have known them and have become comfortable with. Let us not be afraid to experiment, let us not be afraid to listen to some new ideas.
One new idea we debated this afternoon. The member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore presented his bill on referen-dums and plebiscites. Let us not be afraid to consider a couple of ideas from time to time. We are a young nation. Next year we will be celebrating our 125th birthday and we have many years to go. We have survived a great deal as a country. We will I hope survive our current fracas or discussions. I am hopeful that we will, and I am particularly hopeful of course that in writing this Constitution that we be inclusive, as is being said, that we include aboriginal people and the groups that we have mentioned before. We will not accomplish that- or, I would hope that we have to go some distance to ensure that we do-with the motion before us now.
I would ask that the House give serious consideration to our proposal for a constituent assembly. Our leader has said that it is not perfect. What is? But it is an attempt, a signal if you like, a call on the government to lay out in some detail a message that we are prepared to reach out to Canadians, to have their say, to have their view and to participate in the writing of our Constitution and to share some of that emotion and some of that vision for Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Before I recognize the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park, I would just

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
like to advise hon. members who are waiting for the adjournment proceedings that under Standing Order 38(7) they are today cancelled.

Mr. Speaker, I believe all members in this House received a document in their offices yesterday or a few days ago called "Some Practical Suggestions for Canada: Report of the Group of 22". I compliment this group because rather than sit around and complain as many do, it got together and did something.
It put this report together with 28 recommendations of what should be incorporated in the Canadian Constitution. I do not agree with all of them, but as I say, I compliment it for doing something positive.
I would like to ask the hon. member whether he agrees with recommendation 14 which reads: "We recommend that full and complete recognition of the four economic freedoms, the freedom of movement, labour, capital, goods and services be stipulated in the Constitution so that the Canadian economic union can be fully established and citizens can have recourse to the courts to ensure that these provisions are met. We suggest that consideration be given as well to the creation of an administrative tribunal which would oversee the practical realization of these essential economic principles and would assist in the resolution of the problems."
Coming from the constituency which he represents, does he see that this will be a positive thing into the Constitution or a negative thing, this building in the free movement of labour, capital, goods and services?

Mr. Speaker, let me respond to that question first of all with just a brief comment on the member's preamble to his question.
That was on the proposal from this group as it is called, in which there are some learned people who are presenting their views of Canada and suggestions on how we can take a look at the country.
The member mentioned that in his preamble with a suggestion. These people are making their proposals and suggestions in a positive way, or adding to the debate.
Let me make one comment about what I hope is one small way that I am helping my constituents in this debate. During the discussions on Meech Lake, it was very interesting to ask how many people had actually read Meech Lake. In a room in which everybody in my
riding would have got up, howled and screamed about Meech Lake, not one may have read it.
As a practical solution or attempt at that, I have made an effort to my constituents to ensure that those people who are interested in the constitutional debate are sent a package once a month of pro and con debates. We will be including this Group of 22 submission in that package for my constituents. We have about 300 people in my riding now who have written to me. I invite anyone else in the country who is interested to write. I would be more than pleased to put them on that list so that they can make an informed decision about the Constitution.
A "more informed decision" means we will have a better vision of the country. Specifically, to his question in terms of some of the four components in the Constitution, I would certainly be prepared to look at them. On first hand, I do not see any reason necessary to reject them. I suppose some debate would be with the provinces which have their own challenge in terms of attempting to break down the barriers they have between their jurisdictions.
We have had some cases in which that has been almost ridiculous. On first glance, I would not have a problem with that. I suppose we would have a better Canadian economy if we had better coast to coast to coast trade than we do now.

Mr. Speaker, I know the hour is late and I do want to thank all the members of this House for the latitude given in extending the hours of the debate so that remaining speakers, my colleague and I, have an opportunity to address this really important issue.
Canada is a country which faces troubled and difficult times. It is a nation which today is at a crossroads. It is a nation with an uncertain future. It is easy to point fingers at who or what is to blame for taking us to this critical point. It is easy to blame this government. It is easy to blame this Prime Minister. I think we have to recognize that in some measure we are all to blame. That is precisely why we all must be part of the solution.
Canadians are a people who are rather uninformed about their country. That is possibly due to the fact that we are constantly submerged and inundated in a wave of culture from our U.S. neighbour. We do not have a healthy sense of national identity. We are a vast land, a land with a very sparse and a very diverse population. We tend to view ourselves from two distinctly separate
June 18, 1991

realities. The problem, when you look at it, goes right back to the beginnings and the foundations of Canada.
Before Confederation there were essentially two Canadas, composed of two founding nations: the French of Lower Canada and the anglophones of Upper Canada. As this land grew and spread westward the perceptions of Canada evolved. The francophones of Quebec remained within the frame of reference of a Canada of two founding nations. The anglophones, the English-speaking Canadians, particularly western Canadians, began to perceive our land as an equal partnership of provinces and territories.
Canada today, as a result of that evolution of realities, has become a land, if you like, of two solitudes. It is a Canada of vastly different realities. That is why the Meech Lake Accord failed. It had essentially competing objectives and it was assisted by a Prime Minister who chose to roll the dice with the future of this nation. The demands of Quebec to be essentially a nation within a nation, with special privileges and powers, in the perception of western Canadians, of English Canadians, was unacceptable.
The application of the notwithstanding clause to impose French-only language rights within Quebec was the straw that broke the camel's back in western Canada. That is why western Canadians are now railing against the concept of bilingualism. The question they ask themselves is: why should English Canada be attempting to accommodate Quebec through a national bilingualism program when Quebec is trying to override equal rights within the province? That is the perception. It is the reality in terms of a western Canadian perspective. I want to try to bring that perspective here on behalf of western Canadians so that we can attempt to deal with this difficulty.
Quebecers, to present the other view, if they cannot follow their own perceived sovereign destiny within the national framework then they do not want to stay in Canada, they want to pursue their own future. To westerners, if they cannot have an equal partnership, then perhaps it is time that Quebec leaves. There are certain sentiments in the west which take that viewpoint. The reality is that we tread in very dangerous waters. It is a situation which threatens to rip our young nation apart.
Government Orders
The failure of Meech Lake last year has paralyzed this government and it paralyzed this nation. We do not have the kind of constitutional tools to deal with the kind of crisis which besets us today.
The current parliamentary structure is incapable of resolving this crisis. Canadians know that we as parliamentarians have in some measure failed them. There has been a clarion call for change in the way that this country runs itself.
There has been a request, a demand, for a mechanism to resolve this constitutional impasse.
One thing Meech Lake has taught us is that the Canadian people themselves are no longer willing to sit idly by on the sidelines while the process evolves behind closed doors. They want to be active. They want to take an active role, to be fundamentally involved with the process of solving this crisis, despite the anger and the frustration that is out there in Canada on both sides.
There is also, I feel, a growing desire to heal the wounds that have been left from the Meech Lake fiasco. There are genuine efforts coming about toward real national reconciliation.
I want to point to a small community in my riding, on the western edge of my riding in the Okanagan-Shu-swap, the community of Falkland which is now becoming known internationally as "the little town that could". This small community is trying to reach out to our francophone friends in Quebec with an "I care for Canada" campaign. The little town has been flying hundreds of flags. There are T-shirts. There are buttons. There are letter writing campaigns going on. Falkland has challenged other communities in my constituency and throughout the west to open up a dialogue with communities in French Canada and to tell our francophone friends, the brothers and sisters in Quebec, that we want them to stay. We want them to remain a part of Canada.
Other communities have taken up the challenge which Falkland has levelled. Falkland's sister city in Utah is even proudly flying our own Canadian flag and is taking up the challenge of the need for national unity in Canada. Falkland's message to Canada is that despite

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
our differences, and granted they are real, together we are stronger.
I believe there is a growing hope for a united and a stronger Canada which will include our friends in Quebec. That is why my colleagues and I support a renewed process of reconciliation. We very much want to see a renewed Canada, a just Canada, and in particular, a united Canada.
It will take more than simply a commitment to constitutional change. It means a commitment to building a fair and a prosperous economy. It means a commitment to maintaining our national health and social programs. It means a commitment to restoring health to our natural environment.
Today we are debating a constitutional resolution and how we as a Parliament will seek consensus which will hopefully lead us more united into the 21st century.
Both the Liberal opposition and the Conservative government have adopted the proposal for this committee of self-interest. My colleagues and I have to reject this proposal. There is a need for involving the Canadian people at a fundamentally different level, and that is ignored in this committee proposal.
My colleagues and I have proposed a constituent assembly, a process where Canadian people can become involved and can take part in the decisions that affect the future of this nation. A nation can only create a Constitution through a process of social consensus, and the best way to reach that social consensus is through such a constituent assembly.
Earlier this evening the Liberal member from Papi-neau called a constituent assembly a flight of fancy. If our Liberal and Conservative friends call listening to the voice of the people of Canada a flight of fancy, then I submit we are in deep trouble indeed.
The success of Canada is dependent upon the full participation of Canadians in the process of national renewal. Regrettably, this motion before the House does not allow that full participation. The people of Canada have spoken loud and clear. They want to be involved. They no longer trust this government. They no longer trust the politicians. They want to have a hand in the process in a very fundamental way. They do not want to leave their future and the future of their children in the hands of the political process because that political process has failed them before. They do not want it to fail again.
Enough of the back room deals and enough of the rolling of the dice, they are not willing to have their children's future simply gambled away.
The government response to this challenge levelled by Canadians, after all the commissions and studies, is to strike another parliamentary committee, a committee in which the government has control, a committee in which the government calls the shots, a committee in which the government shuffles the deck and deals the cards, and in which unelected senators, believe it or not, will have a say and perhaps the balance of power in the outcome of this process. It is a committee of politicians speaking to more politicians. Once again the Canadian people are on the outside looking in, and that is unacceptable. It is time to bring real people into the process.
The Constitution of Canada, the future of this nation, does not belong to this government. It belongs to the people of Canada and, by God, they must be able to have a say and be able to participate in that future.
As was mentioned earlier tonight by my colleague for Port Moody-Coquitlam, 68 per cent of the Canadian people want a constituent assembly. Canadians are calling for a larger role in this process of constitutional reform. The government's response has been to appoint another committee and to appoint 10 unelected, unrepresentative senators to that committee who may well hold the balance of power in the deliberations of that committee. That is unacceptable to the Canadian people. More politicians and more hidden agendas are unacceptable.
My colleagues in the New Democratic Party and I are not opposed to the concept of parliamentary committees, but this constitutional impasse, this crisis that we face, is an extraordinary situation. It is time that we explored new solutions and explored the utilization of new tools to resolve those problems.
We have to turn away from the old ways and from the old ideas. A constituent assembly, I submit, could w'ell be that new way Canadians are looking for. It would bring Canadians back into the process of national renewal. The voices of Canada would most assuredly be heard.
*

	
June 18, 1991

The Conservatives and the Liberals argue that a constituent assembly would mean that we are not respecting the parliamentary tradition and the parliamentary process, that we are usurping parliamentary power.
Parliament would not be by-passed by a constituent assembly. It is in fact Parliament that would make that final decision. My leader had said earlier tonight: "The buck stops here". Although the constituent assembly would involve Canadian people in the process, that final decision still rests with Parliament.
I might add that once that final decision had been made by Parliament, we could well go back to the people for a final ratification of that consensus through a national referendum. This would ensure that Canadian people were involved in the process from beginning to end, that they had a stake in the results of that process, and that they had a stake in the future of this country.
What we are talking about here is fundamental reform, constitutional reform and parliamentary reform. We are all participants in the painting of a grand design for this nation. It is a challenge which we must share and it is a challenge which all Canadians must share. It is a challenge at which we cannot afford to fail.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague for Okanagan-Shuswap alluded to the 101 legislation which is trampling on English language rights in Quebec in his opinion. Perhaps, my hon. colleague read too much from a certain press in English Canada and perhaps he has not tried hard enough to understand what really went on in Quebec under the 101 legislation. The only people's rights who were trampled on were the Francophones like myself who could not send their children to an English public school because both themselves and their wives were French unilingual, even though they were supporting English public schools in Quebec with their taxes.
My colleague seems to have forgotten the many anglophone universities, high schools, elementary schools, kindergardens and hospitals where every Anglophones can be served in English, even in Quebec City where they barely represent 4 per cent of the population. My colleague cannot say that in his region of Canada,
Government Orders
Francophone minorities receive the same treatment as the Quebec Anglophone minorities.
Moreover, the hon. member mentionned the Meech Lake Accord and the vision we had of our country. The Meech Lake Accord were proposed as a mean to undo a wrong that was done in 1982 when the province of Quebec was excluded from the Canadian Constitution. I think that the Meech Lake Accord was fair to every Canadian. And the hon. member's party should have supported it. That is all I had to say.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague makes a very compelling case about his own particular situation as a unilingual francophone. I sympathize with the arguments he has made.
It is not possible within the time structure of the debate to expand upon my comments more fully than I did except to say that what I was reflecting is not my personal bias about the situation in Quebec but rather the perception people throughout western Canada have of the whole situation with regard to the notwithstanding clause and the imposition of Bill 101.
That brings me back to the point I was making earlier. We have two realities in Canada and we have a problem with communication between our francophone friends in Quebec and the English-speaking western provinces. There are different perceptions. If Canadians could travel more across this country, if there was more opportunity for cultural exchanges, for educational exchanges between students from schools in western Canada, the prairies, the maritimes, Quebec, those communication barriers would begin to break down.
We have French immersion schools in my constituency. My two youngest daughters went to that school. Often that particular school does have exchanges with schools in Quebec. It is a great opportunity for those students to learn about other cultures and to learn the differences between francophone and anglophone Canada. That is precisely the issue. We have to learn to bridge that gap. I hope someday we can say that we have accomplished that.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the debate of the hon. member for Okanagan- Shuswap. We had the pleasure of representing our country at the United Nations at one time so I know he

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
speaks with sincerity and has the best interests of our country at heart.
He quoted my colleague from Papineau-Sain t-Mi-chel as running down the constituent assembly idea. What he fails to do is put it into full context.
The member for Papineau-Saint-Michel asked how the constituent assembly can work when one of the provinces has already publicly stated that it will not participate in the process of a constituent assembly. I would like him to tell the House how his party plans to resolve this? It is pushing a constituent assembly at almost every debate I have heard. That is the one idea they have, yet one province has already rejected it.
I would like to hear from the hon. member just how his party plans to resolve this.

I think the member has a very relevant point. I appreciate him bringing it up and trying to place some parameters around the comment that the member for Papineau-Saint-Michel had made earlier this evening.
Hie fact is that the argument the member makes refers to the political elite of that particular province. Although that political elite says they will not participate in a constituent assembly, when you ask the people of Quebec how they feel about a constituent assembly, 57 per cent of say "yes" to a constituent assembly, and 68 per cent of the people outside of Quebec say "yes" to a constituent assembly.
Clyde Wells of Newfoundland, Frank McKenna of New Brunswick, Bob Rae of Ontario, Grant Devine in Saskatchewan, all say "yes" to a constituent assembly. Just because Mr. Bourassa says "no" does not mean it is not possible. The people of Quebec also say "yes."

Mr. Speaker, I was listening with interest to the speech by the member for Okanagan-Shuswap. I heard him mention the two separate realities in this country. I feel that he is over-dramatizing the differences some people think exist between Canadians.
I am a Quebecer and I do not detect these two separate realities. We are all human beings. We are all Canadians. Canada means something to many Quebecers, to the great majority of Quebecers I would say. What has been missing in the past few years is someone who can adequately articulate what Canada is all about to all
Canadians so that all Canadians can see themselves within this great country.
Someone reminded me that it was Pierre Berton who defined a Canadian as someone who could make love in a canoe. I think we should reflect a little bit on-the Minister for International Trade suggests that I have the quote somewhat wrong, but that is almost it. I would suggest that we ought to think a little bit more about the things that we have in common, rather than the things that may set us apart.

Mr. Speaker, in the speech from the throne, the government indicated its intention to tackle on the constitutionnal issue. The government said that it would put forward new proposals designed to focus the debate on a more united and more prosperous Canada.
Some proposals were submitted to the Joint Committe of the House and the Senate on September and that committee will be required to consult Canadians. It will be asked to report to the govemement or to the Parliament within a five months timetable.
We are talking today about the terms of reference and membership of this joint committee. During the debate on the Speech from the Throne, the Prime Minister mentioned the need to think of the national interest. He underlined that it was up to the Parliament of Canada to think of the national interest.
For a long time, Mr. Speaker, members of my party, the Liberal Party, have recognized that only the Parliament of Canada speaks for all Canadians. The provincial legislatures only speak on behalf of the citizens of their respective provinces. Some national organizations represent the interest of women or native people, but the only assembly speaking for all Canadians is the Parliament of Canada, and this is why I said a moment ago that we need Canadian leaders who are capable of championing the national interest in this House.
We have to remember, Mr. Speaker, that we have here 295 elected members who represent all Canadians. Who could know better the wishes, the needs and the interests of Canadian voters, of the Canadian people, than the hon. members sitting here, in the House of Commons? Our duties give us a good appreciation of the general interest, on top of the particular interests of our constituents. Who could better than us reconcile the interests
June 18, 1991

of our constituencies, our provinces with the national interest, than the people in this place, Mr. Speaker?
I am glad that the Prime Minister recognized that no constituent assembly could be better than the House of commons, but we are not talking about that today, we are talking about the membership of the joint committee. This committee has to represent all Canadians. To this end, it must have enough members to be a good sample of the population. Without giving undue importance to the differences, let me say that it is necessary for the committee to be representative of the various regions, languages, genders, ethnic origins, ages and interests of Canadians.
However, the government proposal will not allow that representativeness. Let us look at our party, Mr. Speaker. We will have four members on the committee. We will have to select one member from each of the four regions. We will have one member from the Maritime, one from Quebec, one from Ontario and one from the West. The member from Quebec will, most certainly, be French-speaking. With only four members, the Liberal Party will not be able to have an English-speaking member from Quebec and it is unacceptable, Mr. Speaker, that 800,000 English-speaking Quebecers be without representation on the Liberal side.

Perhaps a Conservative anglophone would be picked, but I believe that many anglophones in Quebec would agree with me if I said that their point of view of the country has been better represented by Liberals in recent years than by Conservatives.
That is for sure.

Their interests would be better represented by Liberals on this committee. One would not think that the government needs to be told that anglophones in Quebec feel a certain anxiety about their future and would want to make sure that their views are expressed as we go about making important decisions about the future of this country.
In addition to the criteria I mentioned above, namely that attention be paid to the language of the members of the committee and to the regions that they will represent, I think it will be important to consider the interests and background of members of the committee. Of

we will never agree on some aspects of federalism. We should be careful-and it was true long before my honourable colleague, the hon. member for Saint-Hen-ri-Westmount, arrive in this House-with those who think that everything beautiful, noble, great and intelligent always comes from Ottawa.

I have travelled enough in your province and in every other province of Canada to know that a lot of good can come from provinces. That is why I am not an absolute, total centralisateur and I believe that this country will only survive if we understand that on various levels of government a lot of good could be created.
It reminds me of when I arrived. My father told me: "Beware of people whose policy is 'Father knows best and the rest of you all across Canada know nothing.' "
There is a tendency for those of us who are here in Ottawa to neglect and not recognize that in various parts of Canada there is a lot of good that can come from various provincial governments.
Earlier, to a colleague of mine from the Atlantic, I said: "I am afraid some morning we may get up and see Canada does not exist any more". Simply out of boredom people will be so fed up they will give up. Or others, and this is more dangerous, will say, like the hon. Minister of Transport, and I am astounded that my hon. colleague and the Minister of Transport may have something in common, that there is no problem. The Minister of Transport keeps saying there is no problem and so he is not going to address how bad the situation is in Montreal.
I can tell him that he has members of Parliament from the government, the member for Bourassa and the member for Outremont, who are better prepared. I am going to ask the Prime Minister of Canada to ask these people if they think that the situation is so great in Montreal. I would not like to embarrass them by saying that, but I know they realize the situation is bad. My colleague seems to say: "Oh, do not worry, there is no problem".
The situation is very serious. I am not preaching: "Do not go to bed tonight, you know bad things are coming tomorrow morning". The seriousness, however, of this
debate is real. We must not encourage people to go to sleep too easily and say: "Do not worry, everything will be all right; big daddy in Ottawa knows what to do."
I would hope my colleague will at least share that with me; that the situation is serious. He should recognize, point number one, that the situation is serious and point number two, that simply because we are in Ottawa does not mean that all the public servants know all the answers. A lot of good can come out from the provinces. That is why I am a decentralisateur-federaliste.

I never said that Ottawa has all the answers, Mr. Speaker, far from it. But I think it is necessary to maintain a certain balance between the provinces and the federal government. That is the essence of federalism. I can give my colleague the example of medicare, which may have come from Saskatchewan, but which was developed nationally by the central government, which, ultimately, is the only government capable of acting at the national level, for all Canadians.
I will remind hon. members of the resistance that our province of Quebec opposed through the years to different social initiatives of the federal govemement. In the 1930s, Quebec governments were opposed to family allowances. They quoted approving by Clemenceau who said that the State had too many children to be a good father. In the 1950s, Duplessis opposed medicare. He said that good health was God's business and had nothing to do with the Reds in Ottawa.
So, it is important to recall our history-
That is not what he said. He said the only insurance against illness was good health.

That's right. He said: "The only insurance against illness is good health and that's God's business and has nothing to do with the Reds in Ottawa".
So, it is important to recall our history, Mr. Speaker. [English]

Mr. Speaker, "Ask not what your country can do for you. Ask what you can do for your country". We all know where that statement came from. It will live on, probably, as long as there is life on this earth.
June 18, 1991

Government Orders
The one thing lacking in the whole constitutional debate, in the whole process of setting up a committee of 15 members and 10 senators, is this very question: "What can I do for my country?"
I rise to put this on the floor of the House as an idea for the committee as it travels across this country, to sensitize Canadians to ask: "What are my duties to my country as a Canadian citizen? What are my obligations to my country"? People bom in Canada very seldom ask themselves that, because they are automatically Canadian citizens. People who come to Canada and apply for citizenship do at least take an oath. In that oath they stress their duties to this country.
My obligations, my duties to this country can be summarized very simply in one word.
Let us hear it.

The member says: "Let us hear it". Well, here it is and I hope you will remember it for as long as you live. The one word is "respect". Respect for others, respect for property and respect for authority. If we can build that into our Constitution, a simple rule that children in kindergarten can learn and will be better Canadians for the rest of their lives. Respect for others. Yes, respect for our aboriginal people. Respect for the anglophones, the francophones, whether they be in a majority or a minority situation. Respect for allophones and their languages and their cultures. Respect for the physically handicapped, the mentally handicapped.
When the provincial government turfed out the mentally handicapped from Queen Street Mental Hospital without any support services there was not much respect shown by politicians for those mentally handicapped. I have many of them in my riding of Parkdale who are still suffering.
Respect for seniors, to ensure that for as long as they live they have respect and security and an adequate income in this country. Respect for children providing adequate day care.
If we can build respect for others into the Constitution, it is my duty to respect others and to ensure that others are provided for. Respect for property. If Canadians grow up from day one with this respect for property, they will respect the water to make sure it is clean for drinking.
They will respect the air that we breathe and not put pollutants into it. They will respect the land that grows our food to feed not only Canadians, but the starving, the dying in Ethiopia and in other countries. Respect for property means respecting our forests, our trees.
Just three weeks ago I was with the Canada-Europe delegation in British Columbia and the members from the European Parliament were horrified to see the clear cuts on our mountains. I hope they do not pass a resolution boycotting our forest products. We tried to show them the excellent reforestation programs we have; planting two trees for every one we cut out. Respect for authority has to be built into the Constitution.
As a Canadian citizen, one must go off with respect for authority, for this House and for all the parliamentary traditions that you, Mr. Speaker, try to preserve. You did that just this afternoon because one member was breaking the rules of this House and you drew it to his attention. I am sure he will respect this institution much more from now on. There must be respect for the legislatures, for the laws, for the courts, the police who enforce these laws and for the Constitution which we will finally hammer out for Canadians.
I do not want to take much more time, but I do want to put on the floor of the House that somehow in this process of coming up with a revised Constitution, we must put in: "What is my duty and my obligation to this country?" And not just: "What can I get out of this country?" Every group and everyone is trying to milk it for all they can. No, let us turn it around and say: "What can we do for our country?"
I think we can summarize it in the one word "respect", respect for others, respect for authority, respect for property.

Let us not kid around on this motion tonight. I debated whether I should even participate in this motion because I understand the desire of Canadians from all parties and all segments of the country to try to put this place back together again.
Humpty-Dumpty was on the wall a year ago. June 23 was the catch line and the demarcation line and the deadline. Humpty-Dumpty fell off, Meech Lake fell off, and the country was going to be forever ruined. Yes, the country has been forever changed.
Humpty-Dumpty fell off the wall because of rolling the dice and all those things we are not supposed to speak about now. We are not supposed to be negative. We are not supposed to talk about all the things that happened but look ahead and try to solve the future.
I agree with that but unless we realize what happened we are not going to solve the future.
That is why this motion tonight introduced understandably at the eve of our summer recess is not going to get the attention it deserves. However, I give full credit to the government this time, not last time, because at least this time it is allowing an open debate. Some of the members opposite, especially the then Whip and a friend of mine, now the Solicitor General-he was the government House leader. I sat in the House for three days to make sure there was at least a debate on Meech Lake.
Finally the government House leader acknowledged my presence and was honest with me and there was an abbreviated debate. My friends opposite, and my friends across this country I think we know now that the fundamental problem with Meech Lake, with all respect to the Prime Minister with whom I have great problems over Meech Lake, was not just the rolling of the dice. The problem was that there was not a full debate in the House of Commons on Meech Lake before June 23. You can say what you want about free trade, but there was a very vital debate concerning free trade in this House. There was an election campaign and then there was another debate in this House, as we all remember, as things were forced through before the gong came down before Christmas and it was put in place. There was a debate.
I am not going to castigate my colleagues who speak sincerely on something so fundamental to us but I have
Government Orders
never heard so much claptrap in my life on something so fundamental. At least there is an opportunity to ventilate what some may think is claptrap but what others may think are interesting ideas.
I think the fundamental thing from all the speeches on this motion-I give full credit to the government for bringing the motion in and it is an open-ended motion to which all members can speak. There is no cut-off. There is no little deal. There is no little back room agreement to cut it off when all parties had the conspiracy of silence. I say to the supine, sterile NDP and/or the Liberals and/or the government we did not have the debate in the House of Commons then but at least we are having the debate now on setting up the committee.
I think, without getting too involved emotionally- which I am-at least there is a feeling in this House and there is a feeling across the country that people should participate. Not just the frigging politicians, not just the frigging sterile premiers, not just the Prime Minister- who is a tremendous poker player with the premiers- but the people. The great problem is how do they participate. Is it with another address to an august joint committee which travels around the country?
If the member from Vancouver or wherever wants to speak to the Chair let him speak to the Chair in his time. Otherwise I will call him what he is, but I would not dare because I am very serious on this issue, and he was too and I give him full credit. He was one of the few members in this House who was against the conspiracy of silence on Meech Lake. Therefore, I am very disturbed that he is trying to interrupt the Chair when I am trying to speak on something so fundamental because the government has allowed us to speak and I guess, when the motion comes, I will vote for it.
Frankly, time has moved beyond the motion and this is what is sad to me. While we all talk about the public participating, the public has participated until it is coming out of their ears. Constitutionalitis has become a fog over Canada. All the experts are talking about this and that. We all know it is important. The fundamental thing is that this Parliament of Canada, this high court of Canada, this Constitution of Canada that is here in the House of Commons is dead. It is beyond the boards. Other things have happened, be it Quebec and the Belanger-Campeau commission-and I wish a member from Quebec would say, and I wish the member for

Portneuf would say, or the other member who was on the Belanger-Campeau commission would say, Dr. Hogue, the member for Outremont, and he is a good friend of mine-I wish someone would say, especially on the Liberal side, that the Allaire report was commissioned by the Liberal Party before Meech Lake fell.
As I understand it, the Allaire report was there to study the options with or without Meech Lake. Then we had the Belanger-Campeau commission and now we are going to have the Spicer report and now we are going to have the Beaudoin-Edwards report.
Is it any wonder that Canadians are totally confused as to what really is going on? Here we are, on the eve of summer recess. When we all met here in all our rhetorical flourishes-and it is important, it is fundamental-but the sadness is I think a lot of Canada has gone by us. This is why the Reform Party has arisen and that is very dangerous. This is why the Bloc Quebecois has arisen and that is very dangerous.
I am not a Reform person but I can tell you that when the Parliament of Canada is silent on fundamental issues no wonder-nature abhors a vacuum, it is a law of science- the Reform moves in with superficial messages that frankly have to be analyzed. It is a seductive message. I say this for all of Canada because there may be someone watching tonight regardless of who is in this House. One of the beguiling messages of the Reform, which is close to being anti-Lrench or anti-this or anti-that is that it says: "Hey, Quebec, we will deal with you if you decide to come into Canada. Then we will talk to you and/or run candidates in Quebec".
Mr. Speaker, you are a lawyer, and there are some other lawyers around here, and we are all practical people, because we all got elected and we all understand people. Where did you ever hear of a situation where you are going to talk about the living arrangements after the divorce? That is part of the beguiling seductive message of Reform: "Hey, we won't talk to you until you come in". I am scared to death of Reform because of its seductive, beguiling capacity to woo English speaking Canadians in English speaking Canada and the Bloc Quebecois-which I won't waste much time on because I don't understand them-that is Quebec and that is French Canada. Yet, that is not the totality of Canada that we all love.
Yet, a lot of English speaking Canadians are supporting the Reform Party-and the Reform Party was not even mentioned in this motion which talks about Canada because we are all supposed to be too nice, we are not supposed to talk about the realities.
I am going to talk about a fundamental reality in my closing, which is not going to make any members across the way happy-and I shouldn't perhaps say what I am going to say. I am on-side in terms of trying to figure out what the answer is. I do not have the fundamental answers.
I agree with some of the comments made opposite, and here, that perhaps this parliamentary committee is a pseudo committee which has been committed to death, and a quasi-constitutional assembly.
Quite frankly, if I had my way I would have done it a little differently. We are trying to play catch-up ball. I must say that you have to accept the blame where the blame is, because if it wasn't blame you would take the credit. The Government of Canada has to take the blame for the fact that we are trying to play catch-up ball. We are trying to play catch-up ball because of the mess of last year. You can't blame it on Clyde Wells. Oh, yes, it is easy to blame it on Clyde Wells because he is an anglophone, he is a WASP but you do not want to blame it on Elijah Harper, who is an Indian with a feather on his head. He waved the feather all over the Manitoba legislature. Oh, no, it is easy to blame. Let us not talk too much about individual blame but collective blame has to be on the government of the day.
So now we are trying to pick up the pieces. We will have the Spicer commission coming through some time. We will have Beaudoin-Edwards coming through. These individuals are all nice Canadians.
What disturbs me is that here we sit during the summer. I am all for a summer recess. I am glad we are getting out of here. However, if this is the fundamental issue, if this is the issue that is going to break up Canada when we have had wars off-stream that were going to break up the world, why do we not have a Parliament that meets in a national coalition or a union Parliament or something like that? If this is what the stakes are, are we still going to play our partisan games?
June 18, 1991

I think my time is getting pretty close. I guess I will vote for the motion, because at least it is another move, another pause, another deflection in law that we call a traverse. You traverse the issue so that you never have to face it. That is kind of what we are doing here in this Parliament of Canada. We should be involved in it and should have been involved in it right from day one after we knew Meech went down the boards and we had the summer of discontent that we had last summer, but not the summer of zombie land that we are going to have this summer. Then this committee is supposed to be struck by independent means and there are to be conversations with House leaders to get the 15 or 20 members who meet in September. Then they are going to travel the country again, a country that is so travelled out with constitutional committees who is going to listen?
I agree with members of the NDP and perhaps the Liberals. I think, perhaps not tonight or perhaps not when we adjourn Wednesday or Thursday,but when we have the Spicer commission and we have the Beaudoin- Edwards report, that we should have the government response. Let us find out if there is someone to get together. If it is that fundamental, as we all know it is, we could call the Parliament of Canada back and get to work, all of us.
On that uplifting, positive note, I am going to say the following. Maybe I should not say it, because it is not positive or uplifting.
You are telling me, Mr. Speaker, that my time is just about over and I think it is. I feel sad about the Prime Minister. I do not think he feels as sad about me but, frankly, we are two Irishmen. We had a lot to give to each other. I had a lot of parliamentary experience and he had none, and that is part of his problem. I have a lot of knowledge about Canada and his was confined to Quebec and the board rooms of the Iron Ore Company of Canada. Many members will not know that I worked for the Iron Ore Company of Canada before Brian Mulroney ever became the president of the company. I was a surveyor on the Iron Ore centre line, sent up the Moisie River from Seven Islands, before it was called Sept Isles, up to Knob Lake, to Schefferville. It was ironic that he became the president and I just became a member of Parliament; then he became my leader and here we are tonight.

I say this in the nicest way. I am glad the member for Brampton is giggling because he is one of the first to be affected. I say this without getting too political on a fundamental issue, and I really say it seriously. Let us have the Spicer report. Let us have the Beaudoin-Ed-wards report. Let us see where the government makes its decisions and the caucus is going to go. I will not get on the caucus because its members are nice friends of mine. Frankly, this caucus could have had different directions if it had made its decisions and was prepared to bite the bullet, but it did not.
We are now at this stage. We are going to have those reports. They are supposed to be the blueprint for Canada. We are behind the eight ball. Therefore, I should not say what I am about to say. Unless the reports come out and unless the government makes the right move, at a certain stage next year the Prime Minister, my Prime Minister, your Prime Minister, the Prime Minister of Canada, has to decide what is best for Canada. I will accept him at his word, that the next election is not the issue. I agree with that. Canada is the issue.
If he honestly believes that, then I think this Prime Minister at a certain stage, not to be a lame duck totally, when and if we can get certain things done has to do the same as President Johnson of the United States and say to Canada: "Look, Canadians, I am not here for the next election. I am here for the sake of Canada. Let us hope that we can get some agreement to make this Canada we now know work in a fundamentally changed form"-and I am prepared to agree-"but I am not here to reap political benefits".
If we cannot get a union coalition type of situation, which I am afraid we cannot, I think that is naive, then I think my Prime Minister, your Prime Minister and the Prime Minister of Canadians has to decide at the right time and it has to be within a year. He must be able to make the unity message and to get the polls to turn around to say to Canadians: "Look, Canada, I have put this together. I have tried. I have done all of these things. We have got these people working. This is what we have come up with, Quebec, if you want it or not."
Whatever the responses are, the Prime Minister by this time next year if things have not turned around totally, and I do not know who said what there but I am very serious and this is a very serious thing to say, has to

decide to do the honourable thing, not only for the country but, my friends, to save the Tory party.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very, very brief. When my friend speaks he knows the affection I have always had for the Nowlan family because I sat with his father and his father was a good friend of mine when I was a student at university. He taught me so much about parliamentary process and procedure and many other things which were interesting to learn when you go around Parliament.
I cannot do otherwise but be highly interested in the suggestion he made. The beauty of the parliamentary process is that we listen to each other. Some people do not listen, but I like to listen to what people may have to say and you forget if there is nothing to remember.
He made two proposals tonight and if he would be kind enough, I would like him just to elaborate for a few minutes because I know other members would like to question him. He made a proposal that it would be advisable and possible, if if we are to adjourn tomorrow night, to be sad that we will not have a chance to debate the Spicer commission report and the Beaudoin-Ed-wards report. I would not mind if Parliament were recalled for a day's debate on each of these reports. Would he kindly elaborate on this new and fresh idea? He is the only one who made this suggestion.

I appreciate the comment from my good friend from Saint-Denis. That is the point. I agree, let us not open this place to have the opposition run riot with a multitude of problems. I do not see why the House leaders, who have made so many interesting agreements tonight to get us out of here tomorrow, could not make an agreement provisionally to come back here. I do not want to come back here, but this is a fundamental issue.
I think this would at least flag the fact that the Parliament of Canada, the Prime Minister, in a very good speech he made here in the House and one in Toronto and one in Quebec, said that parliamentarians were going to be fundamentally involved. I think it is unnatural. What is the alternative? We have these reports coming in and we sit here in the slumber of summer and then we stagger back here in September all fit and gung-ho with all our other individual problems which
affect members and/or aim criticism at government. We all understand this because you and I, and I hate to say it because you, Mr. Speaker, are supposed to have a halo in the Chair, used to sit in opposition. I am still there in this interesting hybrid situation.
I am glad for the question from my friend because I think it would be an impetus to get the Parliament of Canada involved in this issue, not in a multitude of issues and perhaps not even Question Period unless it were on the Constitution. You can devise certain ways to do it and at least we would be back in the ball game rather than trying to catch up. I can say this; come September we are not going to be catching up. We are going to be very partisan and we are going to be behind the eight ball. In some ways, Canada is behind the eight ball.

Mr. Speaker, during his speech, my colleague from Annapolis Valley-Hants said that I did not understand very well what happen with the Meech Lake Accord and that it might somewhat be unfortunate for me.
I would like to say something to my colleague, for whom I have a lot of respect-he is an old timer in the House of Commons-and I also have respect for the decision he made when he decided to sit as an independent because he was opposed to the Meech Lake Accord. I respected his decision. I must tell him that I, like the majority of Quebecers, have never perceived the failure of Meech as a denial, by English Canada. Quite the contrary.
All that Quebecers and the rest of Canadians saw on TV, was that ten provincial premiers and one federal prime minister signed the Meech Lake Accord. Everybody saw that. What was difficult to understand or to recognize for Canadians was the fact that two premiers reneged on the deal. The first one did not do anything and let the aboriginals representative take the blame rather than assume his responsibilities as premier. The other one simply did not keep his word.
That is what I perceived, as a Quebecer and as a Canadian, and I believe that the majority of Canadians had the same perception. I would like my colleague to

give us an explanation, because he added something else in his speech when he talked about the silence plot on Meech. I have never heard about such a plot. Mr. Speaker, my friend, who is a very conscientious member, has asked me a very serious question. Actually, there are many parts to this. I used his name because I heard his earlier intervention when he commented about Meech Lake and said that this was a denial of English-speaking Canada against Meech Lake. That is really why I mentioned the name of my colleague earlier. It was not a denial of English-speaking Canada against Meech Lake. As he says, there were 97 per cent of Canadians, representing all the provinces except one, and then there was Manitoba in between that were sort of for Meech Lake. But the conspiracy of silence was very definite. And if the hon. member does not understand that by now, then that is part of the problem with the Conservative caucus. There was an agreement between the Prime Minister, the then leader of the Liberal Party and the then leader of the NDP Those two have changed. I can tell you I sat just about where the member was sitting, only about two seats up in the corner, and I sat there for two days to make sure that we at least had a debate on the motion to refer the Meech Lake matter to a joint committee that sat in the summer. That is what I mean about the conspiracy.
Don Johnson, the former member from Westmount, or wherever it was, by this time, was out of the Liberal Party. He was seated around here. Now he happens to be president of the Liberal Party, but that is immaterial. He and I, and I was here longer than he, I have to say, in terms of my attendance in the House, tried to force a restricted debate. We have had a better debate already on this motion and more participants than we had on the Meech Lake proposal, if you will check Hansard.

I was reminiscing with the hon. member for Yorkton- Melville earlier this evening. When I celebrated my 30th birthday, we were in the middle of a constitutional crisis in this House in 1981. I hope that when I celebrate my 50th birthday in this House that we will be beyond this.
I had a comment for the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants. If I could get people's attention, particularly the member for Brampton who was part of this debate. When the member for Annapolis Valley-Hants made his suggestion as to how the Prime Minister could help the situation by considering whether or not he ought to resign, by considering whether or not he is part of the problem, the hon. member for Brampton said that the Prime Minister was not a quitter.
I respect that view that the hon. member for Brampton has of the Prime Minister, but I think there does come a time when quitting is not necessarily a disgraceful thing to do, particularly when there is a widespread view that is held in a widespread way that the Prime Minister is part of the problem.
We can leave it to the historians to debate whether this is in fact the case, but it is also the case that the Prime Minister should consider this. I think that the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants has made a suggestion that should be taken seriously by the Prime Minister.
I am sorry there are not more members here, and I am sorry the Prime Minister is not here to hear what has been a very good debate about this. I think that we should do this more often, have a real debate, the kind of debate that we have threatened to have tonight.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly agree with more or less everything the hon. member from Bird's Hill said. I have a great respect for him.
He has been a member of the constitutional committee of this House of Commons for years. He was one of the members who was in opposition at the same time as I was. That is the point about the member from Brampton. The fundamental problem of the Tory Party today in government is it forgets from when they came.
You can have the Prime Minister. I agree there are certain things that I will take exception with the Prime Minister on. But the fundamental thing is that the public
of Canada in 1984 and in 1988, but especially in 1984, went for the Tory Party for a change. We were good opposition people.
Long before the member from Brampton came out of the Chamber of Commerce down there in the southwestern horseshoe, and got into the House of Commons, there were some of us here carrying the torch. We were carrying the torch and we carried it pretty gosh-darned well.
Then we get into government and there are so many new members of government and a new Prime Minister, none of whom understand Parliament. They think that they can hoodwink the Canadian people by just abusing and contradicting in government what we used to say in opposition. You can shake it all down. There may be night sittings that we do not have so that we can get to know each other and some of us know each other too well. There may be a multitude of things, but the fundamental thing, I will be here long after the next election which the member from Brampton would be at the present time.
The fundamental thing is this, that unfortunately, the members of opposition who became government, and especially got inoculated with cabinet juices, and started to drive cabinet cars, and started to have cabinet perks and then told caucus what to do, they forgot that what we used to say here was so nasty. With television, good or bad, an educated public, they are not going to put up with that any more and that is one of the reasons for the malaise.
Coming back to the question from Birds Hill, I agree with the member obviously, but the member for Birds Hill and other members on both sides, and there are some members even on the government side today, and that is one of the reasons I broke with the government in a sense. The member from Brampton will never experience this. He never wanted to ever vote other than what he was told to so that he could get his-

Mr. Speaker, might I say that, while we send the pages home, I am grateful as a member of Parliament to have an opportunity to speak in the House on what is, I think, a veiy important issue for our country. I am grateful not just to the pages and to yourself and to colleagues for permitting the debate to go on, but also the other staff who are here to keep us functioning so that many of us who would like to talk about this have an opportunity to do so. Although we have had a little bit of debate, often we do talk for the record. We also, as part of our functions as members of Parliament, I believe, have an important responsibility to express for the benefit of those who elected us our views on important issues.
I think that as we talk about the resolution that is before us to create a constitutional committee to again look at proposals for a renewed Canada, that there are some things that, as one member of Parliament, I would like to talk about.
I am conscious that many Canadians, and I am sure that many of my constituents, if any of them are still up, are growing very weary of constitutional discussions. I am sure that many of them believe that only lawyers and maybe political junkies care about such arcane matters as notwithstanding clauses and divisions of powers and section 91 and 92 and maybe they think that politicians should be occupying themselves with economic problems and solving some of the other important issues that confront us.
In a sense they are right. Our economic problems in Canada today are serious and they require a very great deal of thought and insight and determination, perhaps even more than the constitutional problems that we face. I think that this is not a matter of losing sight of what is important. I think very often people are not interested particularly in insurance until they realize that their house in on fire. To my constituents I say: "I believe that perhaps our house is on fire and it is time we started to look for our insurance policies".

The failure of the Meech Lake Accord and the subsequent developments that have occurred in the province of Quebec have made this a very important and perhaps a watershed time for Canada.
None of us knows what will come of these significant developments, but what is clear is that significant change is going to come. It will be certain if Quebec decides that it will not continue in Canada, and it will be necessary if Quebec decides to stay.
My concern and my hope is that Canadians are going to realize before it is too late that Canada really has to be preserved. Canadians do not make it a habit of flaunting their patriotism as some other nationalities do. We have a rather small country with a pretty short history. It has been said that we have too much geography and not enough history. We are a nation not because of a war, a revolution, but as a result of a series of conferences that resulted in a vision of compromise.
I suppose it is even true to say that we tend to define ourselves more by what we are not than by what we are. We are surely the most reluctant nation on the face of the earth. Do we not appreciate the value in what we have? Have we become as a nation so weary of our pitiful problems that we cannot celebrate the greatness that is Canada? Can we not see what we have to offer to our children and to the world that is so valuable, a view of the world that says "bigger and stronger is not always better", a view that says we need to look after our poor and weak and sick while rewarding talent, skill and enterprise, a view that says it is no shame to see compromise where others see only conflict?
Do we not understand that it is not by chance that we have played a role in the world and in its institutions far in excess of what our size, our population and our wealth would dictate.
I know that our problems are not going to be solved by blaming anybody and there is lots of blame to go around, but I think where we started down the wrong road on this was when the Prime Minister of Canada said that the Constitution of his country was not worth the paper it was written on.
Can we imagine the President of the United States making such a statement? As a result of that, I feel a great deal of anger and frustration that we can stand here and contemplate the dismantling of Canada.

June 18, 1991
