I think there are some fallacies that underlie the problem we are in. One of them is that opposition to the Meech Lake Accord represented a rejection of Quebec by English Canada. First of all, there is no such monolith as English Canada. In addition, many things that were criticized about the Meech Lake Accord had nothing to do with Quebec. They concerned aboriginals, the north, the rigidity of the amending formula and other things.
Another of the fallacies that I think we hear repeated on and on is that Canada is not working. I think we are at a period of change in our country and we should be prepared for reform, but to glibly say as some people do that Canada is not working is simply wrong. Maybe Yugoslavia is not working. Perhaps the Soviet Union is not working. Canada is working. Canada, despite whatever the flaws may be that people want to talk about, is one of the wealthiest, most prosperous, most successful nations on the face of the earth.
I believe that today's problems are in no small part a result of the fact that we have dwelt on some of these fallacies too much. We have become too negative on ourselves, too critical. It is time that maybe Canadians put on a face of patriotism and talked about some of the things that are good about Canada, some of the things that make this the nation of choice for so many people around the world who want to come here.
Throughout the protracted and distasteful death throes of the Meech Lake Accord, it became evident that the need to look to Canada's future could not be satisfied by a confrontational or incremental change without knowing where Canada was going to end up. The polarization over Meech Lake was surely based upon a disagreement over whether Meech was going to contribute to Canada's unity or whether it would lead to a weaker Canada and thus inevitably to further disunity.
I object to the crisis atmosphere we have ourselves in over this issue which tends to prevent rational and reasoned argument from being part of the process. I think it is clear that certain fundamental changes are going to have to be made. Some of these changes arise out of concerns of Quebecers. The Allaire report correctly points to some of these, but there are other concerns as well.
These changes are going to be difficult for us to address in the context of the uncertainty in which we now find ourselves. The continuing threat of separation from Quebec creates an atmosphere in which the result can only be bitterness and recrimination. In a protracted period of disintegration, if that in fact is what we embark upon, is going to result in nothing but economic hardship and political and constitutional chaos.
I believe that Quebec's linguistic and cultural goals are more likely to be achieved within Canada. I also believe that the Canada that would remain, if Quebec were to separate, would be significantly poorer in every way and much less influential in the world. In the arithmetic of separation ten minus one does not equal nine. Canada without Quebec would be smaller. Out of the G-7 group of the largest industrialized nations, Canadians would be known as a people who could not keep a country together that was one of the most fortunate on the face of the earth.
Anyone who thinks that the remainder of Canada would be easy to govern after Quebec left should think again. The ease with which Preston Manning and his like talk about the existence of a Canada without Quebec should be a warning to people about how false those assumptions are.
Seeking a solution to Quebec's concerns as a preliminary step to dealing with other constitutional issues was attempted in the Meech Lake round and failed. This was most definitively not a rejection of Quebec. Rather it was a failure of process and a clear statement that Canadians will not be bullied into accepting ad hoc changes to their Constitution when there is little prospect for other grievances to be addressed in a reasonable time and fashion.
Those as well on the other side, the new allies of Preston Manning and his group, the Bloc Quebecois that proposes an independent Quebec, have a heavy burden of responsibility to speak the truth to Quebecers. Independence will not come easily, and the fact that Jacques Parizeau goes around professing that he believes it will be so will not make it happen easily.
I think there are some issues that have emerged in the course of how far we have come in this debate that are clear. One is that there is an emerging consensus that there has to be a reduction in the over-all level of
June 18, 1991

government deficits and debt, and that this should be enabled by any constitutional reform.
There are other issues as well that are emerging. They emerged in the Allaire report and other places. Duplication and harmonization are clearly becoming issues on which we need to seek a constitutional understanding among us. It makes no sense whatsoever that in a variety of fields federal and provincial governments are occupying themselves with the same concerns, are hiring and employing bureaucrats to do the same things. Nor does it make any sense that we continue to operate our market in Canada as ten little countries with respect to many different goods and services.
The government was right in raising the issue of interprovincial trade barriers in the Speech from the Throne. I only hope that we can make very rapid and real progress in these matters. In terms of competing in the world, Canada already begins with the disadvantage of having a relatively small and veiy spread out domestic market.
Why on earth do we want to make it more difficult for ourselves by chopping that market up into ten little ones? It does not make any sense at all.
The Allaire report in Quebec, which put many people outside of Quebec on edge, makes very clear and valuable proposals on the economic union within Canada. We should seize on those and we should promote them and try to gain a consensus across Canada.
A popular conventional wisdom is developing on where we should go in this constitutional debate that concerns me and I want to talk a little bit about it. That is the idea that the solution is going to be the decentralization of power. The fact that Canada is a large and diverse country is not sufficient reason to divide powers so as to create ten little mini countries when it comes to government powers, at the same time as we are trying to break up the interprovincial barriers.
In fact, the world outside our borders is moving towards broader political understanding, broader consensus and co-operation and greater power sharing. Trade and investment is becoming more and more global. To fragment power in Canada, either through Quebec becoming independent or through massive decentralization, is to abandon our levers at a time when global pressures are growing. We are surely stronger united than we would be divided.
Government Orders
I believe that a vastly decentralized Canadian state would find it impossible to lean into the wind that would blow from Washington. In other words, you may be able to take power away from the federal government but that does not mean that it is going to end up with the provinces. Some of it is going to end up outside our borders.
In embarking on constitutional change I think there are a few principles upon which we can agree. The first is that all Canadians should share a common understanding of their fundamental rights and freedoms as expressed in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Second, all Canadians should benefit from common social programs based upon national standards as a simple right of citizenship so that Canadians can be confident that opportunities are available to all, no matter where in the land they may be. For example, my provincial health care plan must have adequate coverage for me anywhere I travel within Canada.
Third, I believe that all Canadians should have a national government elected by the people, able to give voice to the needs of Canada as a whole and able to speak with authority for Canada on the world stage.
Canadians should be able to enjoy a commonality of purpose based upon national consensus, genuinely sought and formed at a national level. Elected political leaders need to ask what is in the best interest of Canada as a whole and have the power to act on that response. The sum must be bigger than the parts. The national government should be working to bring us all closer together.
I believe that the issues most crucial to our future as a nation on this planet in the coming century require national consensus, national will and international cooperation. These issues are global environmental imperatives, global economic restructuring, including Third World development, and world trade.
Can we really face these global issues as an even more decentralized state than we already are? How can our international representatives speak for us in world assemblies on such vital issues as climate change or ozone depletion or reforestation without having the authority to bind Canada? Would we really enter into another free

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
trade agreement, when we do not have free trade among our own provinces? I think these are the issues that need to be dealt with in a focused and clear fashion in this debate as it evolves.
My concern to this point has been that there did not seem to be any kind of organization or orchestration, perhaps choreography is the right word, about how this was going to unfold. The presentation of the resolution that we are debating now, forming a parliamentary committee to look at specific proposals and to consult with Canadians is a positive move. It gives some shape to what is happening, some hope that this is actually a process that has an end which will result in a product to which we can rally the support of Canadians.
Before I close, since it was the NDP who hoped that we would have real debate here, I would like to say in response to its suggestions today that I regret its position, that it cannot support the resolution because it does not contain a constituent assembly.
As I said to the member for Yorkton-Melville when he spoke earlier this evening, I understand where he is coming from on that issue. I hear some of the same voices, the same concerns of people that somehow the process has excluded them.
When I hear the proposals that the NDP make for a constituent assembly I am, first of all, concerned that it could not be completed in a timely fashion. Second, I am concerned about the notion that Canadians cannot be represented unless a member of their particular group speaks on their behalf. It concerns me to think that the implications of the suggestion of the NDP are that when I speak or vote in the House of Commons I do not do so on behalf of the women in my constituency, that I do not do so on behalf of the people of racial origins other than my own in my constituency. This does not make sense to me and I cannot understand why the NDP insists that elected representatives are inadequate to speak on behalf of the people who elected them, even though they may be different from themselves.
To take his case to an absurd conclusion I would say that, no matter what suggestion is made, children are under-represented. Are we to have children on the constituent assembly? Perhaps we should.
The other thing which concerns me is the implication that politicians are incapable of dealing with these important issues of the day. I accept much of the criticism that has been levelled against all of us, that we for some reason have lost the trust of Canadians. Frankly, I blame the government for a lot of that sentiment but that is not the point of addressing it tonight.
Canada is a country rich in democratic traditions. The cornerstone of those traditions is the fact that we elect our leaders from among our peers. Therefore, those elected to lead in Canada are of the best and the worst and the mediocre of our society. If we constantly harp on the worst then very soon the best will want no part of this process.
I plead with the people of Canada to give us all another chance. To give us the time to deal with these issues. We can find a solution. It will not be the solution that satisfies all 25 million Canadians. There will be dissent, there will be people who do not find their own solution in what comes out. However, for the sake of our country, for the sake of all that we have, let us not lose all those good things because we are unhappy with a few things.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
I want to congratulate the hon. member. That was probably one of the most thoughtful speeches today. I think he put his finger on a number of concerns that we all feel in the House. I just wanted to add my congratulations.
He did get one shot in and I want to correct the record because it was one of the better speeches that I have heard in this House in a long time. He quoted the Prime Minister as saying that the Constitution was not worth the paper it was written on and asked what would happen if George Bush said that about the constitution in the United States.
There is a slight difference, and let us put it in context. The Prime Minister of Canada was referring to our Constitution in saying that if seven million Canadians are outside our Constitution, then it is not really worth the paper it is written on. That was the context in which was delivered. The difference is George Bush doesn't have one of his states of the union outside the constitution of the United States.
If the hon. member, in the mood of the speech that was given by him, which was excellent, would understand and in all fairness place when the Prime Minister said
June 18, 1991

that in proper context to be fair to the Prime Minister, I think he would agree.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for his comments. I do not have the context in which the remark was made, and so I cannot dispute him. My recollection is that it had to do with the notwithstanding clause, because I recall at the time being confused by that since Meech Lake did not remove the notwithstanding clause.
In any event I want to say two things. First, I share the concern I am sure the minister has that the province of Quebec, through its provincial government, did not accept the 1982 constitutional amendments. I am not sure that that leads me to the conclusion that seven million people were left out of the Constitution, given that the Government of the Province of Quebec in 1982 was one that was devoted to separation.
I believe I am also correct in saying that if we look at other veiy successful federations in the world, we find other examples of countries that work quite well without having every state accept the federal constitution. I suggest that Bavaria has not accepted the constitution of Germany and yet it has worked extremely well for the country. I believe that one or two states in Australia have voted to secede from that federation a number of decades ago. Their efforts were not successful, but it did indicate a lack of acceptance by those state governments of the federation. Sometimes you just have to soldier on.
I do not think we have that option any longer. I think we had that option prior to 1986 but we do not have that option now. The task is for us all to come up with a constitution that not only is worth the paper that it is written on but is worth the love and respect of the people who are bound together by its terms.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after moving the resolution concerning the adoption of the amendments and finally the main motion a few minutes ago, I have now lost my audience and that of the hon. member for Ottawa South, and that is unfortunate. Anyway, I am happy the minister is still here to ask questions and correct any mistakes I may make during my speech.
Government Orders
Therefore, the first thing I want to do is to congratulate the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs who has introduced this resolution this afternoon. I believe that it is a very important resolution for our country. He made an excellent speech. I think that, if we can agree on the amendments proposed by my party, we will have a good resolution that we will be able to support. We disagree with the government on only two things.
The first is the time limit. The government has proposed that the committee should have until February 28, 1992, to submit its report. We have suggested December 31 of this year. And I think that this date is more reasonable. It gives the committee enough time, and I think the situation in Canada to-day demands that the committee does its work without delay.
Secondly, we think that the government did not produced any proposals to change or amend the Constitution today or in the past. Our party has made some proposals, but the government has not done anything. It has indicated that its proposals will be tabled before the House or the committee in September of this year. It is the view of the official Opposition that it is too late. The govemement had almost a year since the failure of the Meech Lake Accord and it is time to put an end to this and to make these proposals to this House and to the committee.

In any event, with those criticisms I should also add that I believe the government itself has brought about the current constitutional crisis, as we have said repeatedly in this House. I regret that, but our job now is not to lay blame, it is to proceed to try to solve the problem.
We on this side are pleased to help and I suggest that we have done so. I will come to terms with that in a moment.
Before turning to the proposals put forward by the Liberal Party, I would like to look for a moment at the position put forward by the New Democratic Party, which basically is to oppose this motion on the basis that a constituent assembly is a better way to proceed.
When I first heard the idea of a constituent assembly, I must say it had some appeal. It sounded reasonable. It sounded as though it could be considered as a means of

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
involving the members of the public who seem so enthusiastic in getting into this process.
When I considered it, it was many months ago. Having considered it for a while, I dismissed it as a reasonable means of solving the problem at this time. I did so for many reasons set forth by the hon. member for Papi-neau-Saint Michel this morning in his very able speech, particularly the delay in deciding who is to be in the constituent assembly and how it is to be selected. That will take months, and it will not work.
There will never be agreement as to how the constituent assembly is to be constituted. The hon. member for Yukon, in presenting the views of her party in her speech, was exceedingly vague on this point. There was no indication on how members were to be selected. There was no indication of who would be on it, except members from groups. She stressed that various groups would be asked to send representatives.
Who will agree on which groups? How will the groups choose the delegates to be members of the constituent assembly? Will it be by election? Who will be members of the groups for the purpose of the election? These issues were not dealt with. It is so complicated and so convoluted that it would take months to settle that issue before such an assembly could be brought together.
The hon. member for Ottawa South, in his speech, referred to this particular problem which the NDP is plagued with on this issue. I regret that it has not really concentrated its mind for more than a short time on it because I think if it had, it would have realized that what it is proposing is unworkable.
I want to turn to the argument that it advances in saying that everyone must be represented by one of his or her own kind. It reminds me of Noah's ark. All the animals went in two by two. There had to be two of every variety. If every variety were not there, it would be a failure of representation on the earth afterward because there were none there to reproduce.
It just does not work that way in modem political thought. I think I am safe in saying this is not modern thought, this idea of representation in democracy has been around for a very, very long time; in the British parliamentary tradition for well over 900 years. I do not think I need go back beyond that, but it is not new. This
is something which is old in civilization. For generations, thousands of years, people chose to have representatives do their governing for them. That is exactly what we have had in Canada since our inception as a country under the British North America Act and under the various acts that preceded it. I suggest that it is a perfectly workable alternative for us today.
Members of Parliament can represent their ridings. They are capable of representing their ridings. Some of us may be better at it than others, and the people make judgments in respect of our abilities to represent our ridings. We do have that ability. Some may be better, some may be less, but the ability, the capability is there.
I am white. I am male. I happen to be Protestant. I happen to be a Liberal, not a Conservative or a New Democrat. I happen to have English as my native tongue. That does not mean that I am in any way inhibited from representing all the people of Kingston and the Islands who may be somewhat different. Some might not have English as their native tongue, some might be female, some might be Catholic or some other religious belief, some might not be white and some might not be Liberals. There is the odd Tory in Kingston and the Islands, and there is the odd New Democrat. I am still their representative in this House for the term for which I am elected. I do not say to any Conservative or New Democrat who comes to me for assistance: "Sorry, I cannot help you, you are not of my party". I do not know any member in this House who would ever say that to anyone else who came to him or her for help. There may be one, but if so, I do not know him or her.
We all work as representatives of all the people in our ridings when we work in this House. That is a vital and fundamental principle of Canadian parliamentary democracy. If we have the ability, or at least the capability of representing all the people in our riding, surely we do not need a constituent assembly which is to be made up of all these diverse groups in order to achieve representation.
Why would it be any more representative of the people than the elected House of Commons just because its make-up was made to reflect the various diversities of Canada? The people of Canada make a choice, and if we go to a constituent assembly the choice will be made by limited groups here and there which will be asked to
June 18, 1991

make selections and send people, it will not be done on popular election.
From a straight political point of view, I can understand why the New Democratic Party would prefer the constituent assembly.
Peter.
I am surprised that the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants is obviously supporting the New Democratic Party in this view. It sounds as though he is from his grunts and groans at the back.
A point of order, Mr. Speaker.
This is phoney, there is no point of order.
The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands has the floor.

I appreciated the break.
The fact is that the members of the New Democratic Party are obviously of the view that there is some political advantage to be gained in going for a constituent assembly. They take the view that if there were elections now for a constituent assembly there would be more New Democrats elected than there are in this House. There would be more Liberals elected, too, in my opinion. I suspect, and I think the minister would agree with me, that if there were an election tomorrow we would probably have most of the seats in a constituent assembly and the Conservatives would have very, very few.
The Reform would have more-

I am not out to try to argue this on partisan grounds, I do not think it needs to be. I do think that we need to look at the constituent assembly not from the point of view of partisan advantage, but from the point of view of whether it is the reasonable method to deal with the constitutional situation that we are faced with. I suggest that it is not. What we need to look at is taking advantage of the elected persons we have here, putting them on a committee and getting the job done. That is what the government has proposed. We support it, with the modifications that we have suggested in our amendments.
We on this side of the House say that we strive to represent all of our constituents at all times regardless of
Government Orders
their differences. We seek to speak on behalf of all of them. We obviously fail from time to time. On one issue or another we will have differences. The fact is that we make the effort. I think it is a genuine effort on the part of all members on this side, and indeed on every side, of this House.
The surprise for me is that the New Democratic Party, which calls itself the Democratic Party in Canada and stresses how democratic it is, is abandoning this fundamental precept or concept of Canadian democracy in opting for a constituent assembly, instead of taking advantage of the membership of this House.
I note that one of the principal reasons why it ought to abandon this whole concept is because the province of Quebec, through its government, has indicated its unwillingness to participate in this assembly.
It is not surprising that the New Democratic Party ignores the Government of Quebec. At its recent convention in Halifax, out of 521 delegates only 30 were from the province of Quebec. One-quarter of Canada's population was represented by well less than 10 per cent of the delegates present at that convention. That is a standard pattern in that party. It has not been able to change that position. I suggest that if we looked at the breakdown of delegates, which I do not have, we would find that it was quite unrepresentative of large chunks of the rest of the country as well.
What has the Liberal Party done in order to further this debate? It has proposed, through its leader, a framework for reform of the Constitution. The usual practice for an opposition is to wait until the government makes proposals and then criticize the proposals.
In this case, the Leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for Beausejour, has chosen to go public with a set of principles and proposals to amend the Constitution of Canada. I suggest that it is unusual, but it has been done in this case, and the Prime Minister of Canada has followed virtually every one of these proposals and adopted them as his own. He has agreed, on behalf of his government, that these proposals merit consideration and are sensible and that he is prepared to proceed on them, all but one. That one deals with the question of a referendum.
Let us see what the proposals are.

June 18, 1991
Government Orders

* The first proposal was a statement on the essence of Canada. The leader of the opposition spoke of our attachment to the two official languages, of our varied cultural background, of the distinct nature of the Quebec society and of the role of the native peoples. These are some of issues raised in the statement on the essence of Canada.
[English ]
It sounds like Meech.

That is right, it does sound like Meech, but the Meech Lake Accord did not contain everything.
The commitment to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms was also mentioned and, in particular, the primacy of the Charter, as well as the building up of the Canadian economic union. He said the barriers to interprovincial trade should come down.
He proposed a reform of our institutions mainly affecting the Senate, considering that this renewed elected, equal and effective Senate should be a key component of the constitutional reform.
Equal?

No, he did not say that. He did not say equal,
He also proposed the division of powers, pointing out we would be well advised to consult the provinces on this issue of great importance to every level of government, provincial and federal. All that was proposed.
On the subject of immigration, he proposed that the existing administrative arrangement governing immigration be entrenched in the constitution.
As for the Supreme Court of Canada, he proposed that the provinces be given the right to designate judges, what was proposed in the Meech Lake Accord.
For the First Nations, he proposed that constitutional reform enshrine their right to self determination, and this is the position of the Liberal Party.
Likewise, he proposed that the amending formula-
I am very sorry that the hon. member is not interested in my remarks, but he will be able to read all this in the document prepared by the Opposition Leader's office.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I would have thought the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, a very responsible member of the House of Commons who is very involved in all these discussions, would have communicated all this to the committee when it gets into committee. However, to take the time of the House 12.55 a.m., with all the personnel working here, shows to me an absolute abusive interest in the affairs of the nation.
This speech is a speech not on the motion, but on the Liberal proposals, good ones and bad ones, that should be put before the committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member has four minutes left in his speech. Then we will have questions and comments.

Mr. Speaker, I hope that the time taken by these interruptions by the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants will be added to my time.
I sat here and listened patiently to an extremely boring speech from him. For him to continue interrupting my speech when I am trying to explain these policies, I find unnecessary in the circumstances and I ask him to restrain himself.
I have a question for when you are finished, thank God.

The hon. member can ask questions to his heart's content when I am finished. I will be pleased to answer them, but I also want to say that the amending formula proposed by the Leader of the Opposition, according to the Victoria charter is again, as he suggested, most effective for Canada. It is a reasonable one. He has put it forward as our position.
That represents a framework in which constitutional reform can proceed in this country. It is a sensible, logical approach to the issue. It is one that has found favour with the government. I have no doubt that it will be considered by the committee as the hon. member has suggested, and I hope it will be.

June 18, 1991

I think that as members of this House we have an obligation to do our best to see that this works. I hope that the motion, when it is amended, will find favour with all parties in the House and that all parties will work to ensure that the committee is successful in its work.
I was born in this country and I had that privilege. It is one that I know many of my countrymen enjoy, but many came to Canada by choice. I have travelled very extensively in this country from St. John's to Victoria, to the northern tip of Baffin Island. I have canoed thousands of miles in Canadian rivers and I have visited most of Canada's major cities at one time or another.
My roots in Canada are very deep, and my family has come from various parts of the country. I have lived across this country for various periods of time and in various places, mostly in Ontario but briefly elsewhere. I have a very deep affection for this country and I, like other hon. members, do not want to see Canada divided.
Our aim in the opposition in this case as in many others is to strive to make the system work. We believe that Parliament can work. We believe the House of Commons of Canada does work. Sure, we have problems once in a while with different aspects of government policy where we see the place is breaking down. By and large, the House of Commons works. Its committees work. We believe that this committee studying the Constitution can do a job for Canada that will make every member of this House proud of its achievement if we just give it the chance and if all members work together to make the committee a viable option.
I support the amendment that has been proposed. I hope that the matter will be dealt with tomorrow at the vote on a virtually unanimous basis and I hope that we can all strive, whether we are on the committee or not, to make it the success that it should be.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the hour is late, but quite frankly the hour may be late for the country and therefore the hour being late in this Chamber is immaterial. I therefore take back what I sort of inferred when the hon. member from Kingston and the Islands was concluding his speech.
Government Orders
The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands is one of the more constructive, sincere and capable members of this House, so I have two questions for him.
He is sort of the assistant House leader. I do not know what his official title is, but after the Spicer report, after the Beaudoin-Edwards report, goodness knows that the government is going to respond to those reports because we do not know, but would the hon. member be the leader in his party, which is Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, to try and develop not just a consensus, but to explore with the government a coalition union situation on this matter of the country. That is my first question, a very, very specific question.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's question is very hypothetical. I see no evidence that it will be necessary to form a coalition with the government on this issue. I am optimistic that there will be a unanimous report from the committee as I note there was from the committee that studied the Meech Lake Accord chaired by the present hon. Minister of the Environment.
Obviously, the parties in this House worked together with great success on that committee. Unfortunately, the committee report was not acted upon, and I will say no more in respect to that.
I think it is important that the hon. member realize that there is a difference between forming a coalition with the government on this issue and making a unanimous committee report, which I think is possible. I hope that it will happen and I think all hon. members should work to that aim.

Very good, Mr. Speaker, this is an educational night. I really appreciate that answer of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands which leads me very naturally to my supplementary. I do not know if he was a lawyer, but I used to be.
Therefore, I understand the problems in trying to get a coalition union situation in this very partisan atmosphere here. The hon. member talks about a unanimous committee report and we all saw what happened to that. Therefore, there is the cry outside of this hallowed Chamber of having the constituent assembly referendum process.
I really want to ask the hon. member this question. I heard him talk and denigrate in effect the NDP situation of constituent assembly, and it is not just the NDP situation of constituent assembly, but there are many people without party affiliation who feel-it may be

June 18, 1991
Government Orders
wrong, it may be difficult, it may be complicated-they want to get involved.
Could the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands answer this specific question. When he talks about the constituent assembly, would he agree with me after he signs that memo that there is a heck of a difference between a constituent assembly of people with all the difficulties of collecting them, all the difficulties of organizing them, all the difficulties of having them focus on a report and then perhaps the elected members, most likely properly the elected members developing their recommendations.
I was amazed at the hon. member who knows quite a bit, not more than I, but quite a bit more on constitutional law, on constitutional assemblies.
Does he not agree with me that the fundamental difference at the moment between what we are doing with the parliamentary committee with all its potential and a constituent assembly feeding into the parliamentary process is that with a constituent assembly you do not have any party discipline? In terms of the House of Commons and a parliamentary committee, and I have been through it for 25 years, you have something called party discipline. Does he not think the fact that there is no party discipline in something so fundamental as a constituent assembly is something that should at least be considered and explored and then rejected rather than rejected for the ideological negatives put forward by the negative situation of the Liberal Party?

First of all I want to say I do not think the Liberal Party's position on this is negative. With respect, it is the most positive of any of the parties in this House. We are the only party that has laid on the table a proposal for amending the Constitution and dealing with the situation we are in at this time. No other party has so far come up with such a comprehensive proposal at this stage.
I think that has taken considerable courage from the Leader of the Opposition. It has shown some judgment. That is the first point I want to make.
Second, I do not agree with him that a constituent assembly would necessarily be non-partisan. I think there would be all kinds of partisan divisions in a
constituent assembly and if the hon. member does not agree with that he is dreaming in technicolour.
Constituent assemblies will divide on all kinds of bases. There will not be a party Whip, but at least with a party Whip you are able to whip together differing interests into one concrete group. With a constituent assembly you would have every division going in the country shown up and exposed and members would arguing with each other. It would be very divisive. There is no guarantee that everybody in it would suddenly say that this is exactly what they wanted, that they had hit on a consensus. There is no guarantee of that at all.
I want to point out that in the motion, if he would read it, it sets up this committee. I urge him to look at it very carefully. There are all kinds of provisions-
Subcommittees.

I listened patiently to his questions. The least he could do is listen to my answer.
It says the committee will provide Canadians with an opportunity to participate fully in the development of the Government of Canada's plan for a renewed Canada. The committee will have subcommittees with power to travel and hold public hearings within Canada. The committee will have the power to hold joint sittings with the committees of legislatures or individual members of provincial and territorial legislatures. The committee will develop procedures to ensure aboriginal peoples participate fully in the development of the Government of Canada's plan for a renewed Canada and in particular on issues of special interest to them.
There are all kinds of powers in here which are unusual in a parliamentary committee. They are designed to make this committee react and interact with Canadians across this country. I think it is a reasonable proposition. It is the best we have seen yet from this government. We are delighted to see it has taken this step. We support those aspects of this motion. I think the hon. member, if he looks at it and thinks about it, will realize that in terms of what could be accomplished in a reasonable time with minimum of division and discord the parliamentary committee is a sound, solid approach. There is a risk that the Conservative Whip will lay it on a bit thick but I am prepared to take that chance. I think that the country is prepared to take the chance, and we in the Liberal Party have committed ourselves to working with the government to achieve unanimity on this issue.
June 18, 1991
